#6308. United Airlines CEO Insists He Runs The “World’s Best” Airline. Does That Title Even Matter?

Scott Kirby believes United Airlines is the best airline in the world (he has for quite some time). I understand his argument, and there are aspects of United that compare favorably with just about any competitor. But the claim raises a more interesting question: what actually makes an airline the best? The answer depends on much more than the seat or the route map or any other single quality…and maybe that’s asking the wrong question anyway.

In his recent Cheeky Pint interview with John Collison and Ben Thompson, Kirby made a case for United that deserves more than an eye roll.

His argument is not that United serves the best food or offers the most luxurious seats. He acknowledges that Asian and Middle Eastern competitors do better on the physical product and probably service. He also identifies schedule as the primary reason people choose an airline. But he believes United’s technology changes the overall assessment:

“I say schedule is the number one reason people pick an airline. But, everything else matters for brand-loyal customers. It’s service, product, reliability, and technology. The Asian and Middle East carriers do better than the US airlines on product for sure, and probably service too. I think we do a really good job, but they have different cultures for service, so they do better on that. But I think technology is the differentiator.

“United, that’s why I now believe that United in totality is the best airline in the world, and it’s because of technology. It’s exponentially getting better. Things like being able to do this for customers when there’s a delay and tell them what’s going on. We started it this summer. AI allows us to institutionalize this. But if you’re going to have a delay, like sending customers weather radar maps. In Chicago, there was a day where the weather was over the horizon, but you had to fly. It was sunny at the airport, but you had to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and so the routes were closed. You couldn’t—

“We sent half the people the normal weather delay, which they think you’re lying… Because it’s sunny outside. You must be lying to me. We sent half a picture with the radar map, and you have to fly through this line of thunderstorms, and the routes are closed because of outside. The people with a 1-hour delay, I think the numbers were negative 60 NPS on the normal way of sending it, plus 60 when we send a picture of the map. A 120-point difference.”

His case for United rests on technology: better tools for managing travel, clearer communication during disruptions, and connectivity that makes time onboard more useful. For example, he describes sending passengers radar maps to explain why distant thunderstorms were delaying flights even though the weather at their airport looked fine. His point is that passengers respond much better when they understand what is happening.

Thus, Kirby is acknowledging that competitors outperform it in some traditional measures of onboard quality, but arguing that United’s technological advantages outweigh those shortcomings.

I think he is right that these things matter. I am less convinced that they settle the question.

Start with the most obvious consideration: an airline is not particularly useful if it cannot conveniently take you where you need to go. I love trying new products and will sometimes take an absurd routing to do so. Most travelers understandably do not approach their trips that way.

A nonstop flight at a convenient time can be more valuable than a better seat reached through a connection. Frequency matters too. An airline with several flights a day gives you more options, particularly when something goes wrong.

This is a substantial part of United’s appeal. Its network gives me reasons to fly it that have nothing to do with whether another airline serves better Champagne.

But the best network for me may be largely irrelevant to someone living elsewhere. A traveler in Taipei and a traveler in Chicago are starting with very different choices. There is no universal route map that works best for everyone.

Emirates is a good example of why an airline’s reputation may need to be separated from the particular experience you are buying.

Mention Emirates and many people think of luxury (massive first class suites, showers, and bars onboard with beautiful flight attendants serving you extensive food and beverage offerings). That “halo effect” reputation is understandable.

But someone booking business class on an older Boeing 777 may encounter a product that falls well short of that image. The retrofitted 777s improve the situation with a 1-2-1 layout and direct aisle access, but I would not put that seat ahead of the leading business class products elsewhere.

Singapore Airlines illustrates this as well. Its reputation for service, built in part around the Singapore Girl branding, is extraordinary. Yet some travelers strongly dislike its longhaul business class seats, particularly their sleeping position.

A beautifully presented meal and gracious service cannot entirely compensate for a bed in which you struggle to get comfortable. Singapore’s new cabin reveal on Friday, November 6, will be particularly interesting for that reason.

My recent Emirates 777 first class flight demonstrated the reverse problem: a superb suite paired with service that did not live up to it. I loved the space, but the experience still fell short.

So what about Kirby’s argument that technology is most important?

We sometimes talk about technology as if it is separate from the passenger experience. But an app that lets you solve a problem without standing in line is providing service. A clear explanation of a delay is providing service. Working internet can determine whether a long daytime flight is productive or frustrating.

US airlines deserve credit here. Their digital tools can be excellent, and United’s app is absolutely the best in the business, no question about it. But even the Alaska, American, and Delta apps are–comparatively speaking–much better than their non-US peers.

To be clear, that does not mean every American airline leads every foreign airline or that an attractive app excuses indifferent employees. It does mean that evaluating service solely by how someone pours your wine misses a large part of what an airline does for its customers.

Connectivity is especially important to me. Extra legroom and a better meal are welcome, but painfully slow or non-functioning Wi-Fi can materially change how I feel about a flight. For someone hoping to disconnect and sleep, it may barely register. The features can be measured. The importance each passenger assigns to them cannot be universal.

I also recognize the limitations of my own perspective. Much of my coverage focuses on premium cabins, and those experiences influence my preferences. But what does the airline offer someone in economy?

Some Asian carriers offer a more appealing combination of legroom, meals, and attentive service than their US counterparts. That deserves weight, even if the business class cabin lacks the latest suite.

At the same time, the aircraft still matters. So do the fare restrictions, baggage allowance, and cost of choosing a seat. A generous meal does not tell us whether the ticket represents good value.

For a family paying for several tickets, the best airline may be the one offering a tolerable nonstop journey at an affordable total price. For a tall passenger, a little more legroom may matter far more than the entertainment selection.

An airline cannot claim superiority for everyone based on what it provides a small number of passengers at the front of the aircraft.

A great airline should operate reliably and treat passengers well when it fails.

Those are related, but separate, expectations. I want to arrive on time. When that is impossible, I want an honest explanation and practical assistance.

No airline can prevent every weather delay or mechanical problem. But how it prepares, communicates, and recovers tells me much more than a polished promotional video.

American Airlines is a useful example from my own flying. I would argue that some of my recent meals on American have been the best among the US network carriers. Its free Wi-Fi has also tends to work very well for me. Those are real strengths.

Nevertheless, my experiences with inconsistent service and operational problems place American well below Delta and United in my overall assessment. That is not a claim that every American flight is bad or every Delta flight is good. It is the cumulative effect of repeated experiences. A carrier earns my confidence over time, and it can lose it the same way.

The loyalty program belongs in this discussion too.

Award availability, redemption prices, and the usefulness of elite benefits all affect how much value I receive from an airline. A good program can persuade me to choose one carrier when the alternatives are otherwise similar.

But I try to separate the airline I enjoy most from the program in which I find the most value.

An excellent redemption does not make an uncomfortable seat comfortable. Status does not make a canceled flight depart. Conversely, a wonderful airline can have a loyalty program that gives me little reason to engage with it. Ideally, the program reinforces a relationship the airline has already earned through its service.

Qatar Airways and STARLUX are among my favorites because I have found their overall experiences so compelling. The appeal extends beyond a seat or a meal: I look forward to flying them because of the reliable Wi-Fi, excellent service, and quality in everything.

Air France has also come such a long way. Its newer business class seat is excellent, and the addition of Starlink on equipped aircraft addresses something that matters greatly to me. Combined with the food and service I enjoy, that makes it an increasingly attractive choice.

Yet I still have many reasons to fly United. Its network and technology have practical value in my life that an exceptional flight on another carrier cannot always replace.

That is why my favorite airline and the airline I choose for a particular trip need not be the same…maybe the point is that talking about which carrier is “best” is ultimately futile and our focus instead should be rewarding carriers who do things well and not patronizing those that continually disappoint.

Kirby’s claim is worth discussing because he recognizes that being the best involves more than having the fanciest cabin. Technology and network utility deserve more credit than they sometimes receive.

But I would not crown United the best airline in the world on that basis alone. The seat still matters. So does the person serving you, the reliability of the operation, and what happens when your plans unravel.

For me, the best airlines are the ones that bring those elements together consistently, but at the same time I realize how arbitrary my own evaluation can be. Thus, I tend to think asking “who is best” is the wrong question versus asking “who does X,Y, and Z well?”

What makes an airline the best for you—and which airline comes closest?

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

In Kirby’s world, as long it is said with enough superlatives it must be true

Pretty much. IT is one factor for sure but United is not remotely the best based on it alone and to state the painfully obvious United is not the best airline regardless.

Friends, who cares what a CEO says; I think many of them are going to soon be ‘put in their place.’ Basic consumer protections are long-overdue. No more of this blustering, attention-seeking, etc. Just run a reliable operation.

I mean a lot of people in the comments are about to say “Kirby is wrong and has his head up his own ass” but go ask any airline CEO what the best airline in the world is and 90% will say their own airline. It is literally their job as CEO to be championing their own airline. I don’t know why it is a surprise to anyone that Kirby says his airline is the best in the world.

Also there is no objective measure of the best airline in the world. What matters is what works for you personally. I live near a United hub so of course United gives me the greatest access to destinations. If I lived near an American hub then American might be the best airline for me. Its a throwaway comment, made by a CEO doing his job. His broader point is that just having the best first class seat doesn’t make you the best airline and he’s right on that.

The best airline in the world is American. That’s because they generally fly where I go, hubs where I live, and I’m an Executive Platinum so I get frequent upgrades on the routes I fly. I don’t give a rat’s about IFE, who designed the seat, and whether or not the FA smiles at me when giving me my drink and snack (just that they not show outright hostility to me, like Delta FAs). I also don’t generally fly overseas, so I concentrate on domestic. AA gives me what I need and what I want from the Admirals’ Club network and destinations. That being said, this week, I flew United because a non-stop and a 2.5 hour drive to my ultimate destination was far shorter than a one-stop through Dallas or Denver and a backtrack, then a 1-hour drive. So yesterday they were the best airline in the world. I care about what works for me and don’t care one bit what works for you. So my decision is always right.

“I also don’t generally fly overseas, so I concentrate on domestic. ”

I feel like this goes without saying since you love to rant about the French and just about any non-US country 😉

It’s a big and beautiful world out there if you learn to overcome learned biases. Hint hint. the French actually aren’t any more smelly than Americans, especially if you’ve ever been to Florida in July. 😉

Florida deserves the strays it just caught.

“Their digital tools can be excellent, and United’s app is absolutely the best in the business, no question about it.”

I do have to say, this is obviously just personal opinion. I think the statement above was accurate maybe 10 years ago? It seems like the app is just surviving on past reputation among bloggers.

The United app was leaps and bounds ahead of AA and DL maybe… 2014-2020 or somewhere around then. I personally find the United app to be the worst of the big 3 lately. By no means is it bad and, sure, you can do a lot, but they’ve made it very cumbersome and slow.

It can do a lot of what you need, but it takes longer to navigate to the easy things, in my opinion.

Definitely not a bad app, by any means but I find it more difficult to use vs AA and DL. And it’s not like I’m a novice with any of them

I do use the AS/DL/AA apps often, among others, and the only one that I think comes close to the UA app is the AF/KL app, which has improved dramatically.

Just my humble opinion. I know it’s not mainstream. To me, the United app looks nearly the same (aesthetically) as it did ten years ago. And the changes since then have removed much of the ease of use that I used to like about it.

Just opinions… 🙂 The united app isn’t a bad one. I use it pretty often but I just find it more cumbersome than AA and DL. The layout used to be the best but it isn’t to me anymore.

That said. Why do you think ““…and United’s app is absolutely the best in the business, no question about it.”?

They’ve made a ton of progress, but he needs to focus on continuing to improve the airline’s customer service culture and let the customer’s decide who’s the best.

Andy is correct. Saying you are the best is the CEO’s job. So is correcting the short falls. But the Best gets the headlines.

But you’re right, no matter what he says, it is a chip on his shoulder.

Its childish and he should worry more about running an airline. He comes across as a snake the way he panders to everyone under the sun without any humility or professionalism.

Everyone’s experience is different, but mine is that it’s a happy surprise when I have to fly United and the trip goes well. Too often it’s a story of surly crew and broken aircraft. Mr. Kirby’s daily floods of self-congratulation serve mostly as a repeated reminder of how much United seems to think it’s current standards are ok, and how much I disagree.

They left my bag in Newark. The internet that I had to pay for from Ewr-fco was so bad, I couldn’t get work done for my client and had to apologize the next morning. (Starlink worked great on my domestic flight.) Also why am I paying for internet on a business class ticket? My ticket was expensive.

Customer service and tracking down my bag and getting it back was a nightmare. Lost half a day getting my bag back, bc United couldn’t guarantee that the courier in Rome would deliver the bag to my hotel before I had to depart to another city.

All the technology in the world doesn’t matter if they can’t do the basics right. Get me to my destination along with my bags. I don’t even care that the FAs looked unhappy and it showed. I just need to get to my destination with zero problems and preferably working internet on the plane so I can work.

Technology improvements do not always equate to improved customer service.

United is not even the best domestic airline. How about Kirby worry about beating Delta before challenging international carriers? Customer service at United pales in comparison to Delta, although delta’s customer service has been declining recently.

Pricing, timing of flights, no f ups, entertainment/wifi and good customer service. That is what is important in varying terms of importance for 98% of flyers.

#6307. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

Good thing you did the Edit deal as the Thompson doesn’t honor Hyatt Globalist benefits. So, no upgrade and no breakfast for Globalists.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

Am I the only one finding Edit hotels are north of $1000 a night? Whatever the credit Chase is giving is for staying at an Edit property isn’t enough to offset the exceptionally high rate.

I’ve stayed at that Thompson many times and been upgraded to suites and the Upper Stories. The previous poster is empirically wrong.

doesn’t Edit usually require a two night minimum? How did you get the benefits for only a one night stay?

I had thought I read that the benefits are for stays of at least 2 nights. Is that incorrect?

Actually – just looked up what I read and I think it’s the $250 credit every six months that requires a 2-night stay but not the other benefits. So looks like you could have spent 12,500 points + $250 cash for a second night and gotten the $250 credited back.

#6306. 17 Trips You Should Book a Year in Advance

I'm a firm believer that holidays need a balance of organization and freedom, so that you can enjoy all the long-awaited activities without feeling like they're obligations. Starting to organize and book excursions well in advance can make your experience considerably better, especially when planning trips to particularly popular destinations. Though, that's not the only reason why you should already be thinking about what to add to your 2027 travel bucket list.

Planning a trip a year in advance, long before your suitcase ever leaves the closet, offers up a very particular and potent type of dopamine hit. The moment you confirm a flight or secure a coveted reservation delivers its own quiet thrill, a reminder that the joy of travel lives not only in the trip itself, but in the anticipation that precedes it.

With 2027 shaping up to be a year of more personal, experience-led travel, there's even more reason to start planning ahead. According to Booking.com's 2027 travel predictions, 77 percent of travelers are interested in taking a holiday that pushes them beyond their comfort zone, while 81 percent would choose a destination based on how they want to feel rather than simply where they want to go.

Booking early has myriad practical advantages, too. It can protect you from soaring prices, guarantee access to peak-season experiences, and ensure a plethora of accommodation options that often fill up months before departure. The extra planning room also allows you to seek out lesser-known routes and time your visit to seasonal spectacles. Plus, it offers the underrated delight of months filled with small frissons of excitement every time you think about what is to come. Whether you’re dreaming of spotting wildlife in East Africa or weaving through the Peloponnese in Greece, here's your guide to planning a trip a year in advance for 2027.

This gallery has been updated since its original publish date.

England’s landscapes offer a surprising breadth of adventure for such a compact country, from the rugged drama of the Lake District to the chalk cliffs and wildflower-strewn downs of the South East and the mellow, biscuit-hued villages that string all of this together. A rich tapestry of moors that feel wonderfully remote, market towns that hum with independent food producers, and stretches of coastline where seals bob with the rhythm of the waves can all be woven together, with the added ease of just being able to ring up and book. Outdoorsy types can opt for hiking along windswept coastal paths in Cornwall, paddleboarding through still-water estuaries in Devon, or following ancient woodland trails in the New Forest, while those who prefer a slower pace can settle into long lunches at quaint English vineyards (Chapel Down in Kent and Rathfinny in Sussex, to name a few), wander through sculpture parks or spend languid afternoons in honey-stone villages where the loudest sound is often the church bell.

For those seeking the same sense of escape on a gentler scale, a clutch of estates across England is quietly rethinking the country house stay. Just outside London, The Grove in Hertfordshire is a firm family favorite, amid rolling parkland and its own championship golf course. The addition of two quaint cottages tucked into the grounds in 2025 offers a more private way to experience the estate, with access to its extensive grounds and family-friendly activities, from mini Land Rover rides to archery and woodland walks. Further north, The Tawny in Staffordshire offers a more immersive relationship with the landscape, where architecturally considered treehouses and lakeside retreats complement woodland gardens, dining at The Plumicorn restaurant, and paths to explore across its two adjoining estates. While in Hampshire, Avington Park Estate leans into its historic setting, pairing grand riverside scenery with elegant accommodation and access to fishing, wild swimming, and a range of wellness experiences, including a lakeside sauna pod.

All this, though, with the caveat that some of the most sought-after Great British stays can fill up well ahead of peak weekends and school holidays, so it's worth getting your reservation in early if you have your heart set on a particular property or date in 2027.

The Peloponnese invites a slower, deeper kind of Greek escape, one built around winding coastal roads, mountain passes scented with wild herbs, and ancient sites that appear almost without warning. This southern peninsula feels far removed from the island throngs, yet it offers a richness that rivals any Aegean hotspot. Planning ahead is key, particularly if you want to secure small guesthouses, family-run inns, or farm stays in popular coastal areas during July and August. For a 2027 trip, consider traveling in May, June, or September, when temperatures are generally more comfortable for sightseeing and the roads are less crowded than at the height of summer.

A favorite among avid road trippers, routes here weave through layers of history and landscape. One moment you’re exploring the fortified town of Monemvasia, built on a towering rocky islet connected to the mainland by a narrow causeway, and the next you are wandering through the ruins of Mycenae or the venerable theater at Epidaurus. The distances are manageable with a well-planned itinerary, which leaves ample time to pause at quiet coves, watch fishermen haul in their morning catch, or break for lunch under vine-covered pergolas in medieval villages. Allow at least a week if you want to explore several parts of the peninsula rather than rushing between archaeological sites, and consider choosing a handful of bases, such as Nafplio, Monemvasia, the Mani peninsula, or Pylos, to make the most of the journey.

The Mani peninsula is stark and dramatic, dotted with stone towers and rugged beaches that glow at sunset. To the west, the region opens into long ribbons of sand, olive groves that stretch toward the horizon, and wetlands alive with birdlife. Near Pylos, the Gialova Lagoon is an important stopping point for migratory birds, while the nearby crescent-shaped Voidokilia Beach makes a particularly tempting stop on a coastal drive. Inland, the mountains of Arcadia offer cool respite in summer and timeless hiking trails that trace the contours of rivers and valleys. If you're traveling in 2027, book your preferred accommodation early for peak summer dates, but leave enough room in the itinerary for spontaneous detours. In fact, for travelers drawn to the romance of the open road, there are few places as rewarding or as effortlessly cinematic as the Peloponnese.

For couples planning a celebration trip, Hawaii remains one of the most evocative places to unwind together. The archipelago pairs volcanic drama with serene beaches, vibrant reefs, and an open spirit, while its deeply held sense of community gives romance a grounded, almost effortless quality.

For a romantic escape, the choice of island is just as important as the hotel. On Big Island, volcanic landscapes and stretches of coastline set the scene for a slower-paced holiday, while Oahu combines beautiful beaches with Honolulu's lively restaurants and nightlife. The hotel scene offers plenty of tempting options, from the traditional-style, thatched-roof hale at Rosewood Kona Village and the extensively renovated Mauna Lani, Auberge Collection, to smaller gems such as White Sands Hotel and Surfjack in Waikiki.

For a honeymoon or anniversary trip, it's worth booking your preferred resort and flights in advance, particularly if you're traveling over Christmas, New Year, or during the summer holidays. And if you're hoping to explore more than one island, allow enough time for the additional flights rather than trying to squeeze too much into one trip.

The landscapes of Utah are full of sandstone spires, rust-red cliffs that glow in the late-afternoon light, and labyrinthine slot canyons that twist into shadow and sun. Geology becomes a storybook, particularly at Utahraptor State Park, home to one of the most significant dinosaur bone sites in North America. Located around 15 miles northwest of Moab, the park protects the Dalton Wells Dinosaur Quarry, where thousands of dinosaur bones have been discovered, including those of its namesake predator. Further south, the astonishing petroglyph panels at Newspaper Rock offer a rare glimpse into centuries of Indigenous history, with carvings attributed to Basketmaker, Ancestral Puebloan, and Ute peoples. The rock surface is carved with scenes that feel as vivid today as when they were first etched.

Both sites can be reached from Moab, a small desert hub that continues to evolve. From April to early November 2027, Canyon Spirit, formerly Rocky Mountaineer's Rockies to the Red Rocks service, is scheduled to operate its two-day train journey between Denver and Moab, with an overnight stay in Glenwood Springs. With panoramic windows framing Colorado's mountains, river valleys, and dramatic red-rock canyons, it is a journey that turns the simple act of moving from one place to another into an experience in its own right. Winter, too, brings a different kind of spectacle to Utah, when canyon walls catch the low light and snowfall softens the edges of its famously rugged terrain. For a 2027 trip, it's worth securing your preferred train departure and accommodation in Moab well ahead, particularly if you're traveling in spring or autumn, when temperatures are generally more comfortable for exploring the desert on foot.

Vancouver Island offers a rare kind of quiet that settles over old-growth forests, wild shorelines, and mountain lakes so still they resemble polished stone. It is also a place where Indigenous presence remains central. The lands of the Kwakwaka’wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth, and Coast Salish peoples continue to shape the island’s identity, and planning ahead allows travelers to seek out experiences rooted in cultural respect rather than commercial interpretation. Ferries can fill up quickly during summer, making advance bookings worthwhile on reservable routes and giving you time to curate a thoughtful route. BC Ferries generally opens reservations six months ahead and recommends booking at least four to six weeks before long weekends, so it's worth planning your crossings early if you're traveling with a car or camper van.

On the water, you can join marine excursions informed by generations of coastal knowledge or explore the Salish Sea with Indigenous guides who share their knowledge of the region's history, wildlife, and cultural traditions. Fishing trips with Indigenous-owned outfitters offer another way to experience the island's coastal traditions, while storytelling walks and wildlife encounters reveal how land, sea, and culture are intertwined. Vancouver Island’s landscapes match this richness. Orcas pulse through cold channels, black bears forage along shorelines and in forest clearings, and mist drifts between cedar trees that have stood for centuries. Whether you pitch a tent north of Campbell River or take a slow-rolling road trip in a camper van, this is a destination where the outside world becomes the centerpiece. Summer is a particularly rewarding time to explore, with longer days for hiking and kayaking, while whale-watching opportunities vary by location and season. If you're planning a 2027 escape, check campsite reservation opening dates and arrange popular guided wildlife excursions and Indigenous-led experiences ahead of your visit, particularly for July and August.

Your kids might learn about the rainforest at school—but there’s nothing like seeing it in real life to nurture their interest in nature and inspire their curiosity. Costa Rica is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world, with more than a quarter of its territory protected for conservation, and it’s not just children who are enchanted by bright butterflies, noisy green macaws, bead-eyed tree frogs, and sloths. It’s a relatively small country, so it’s possible to take in the rainforest canopy, pineapple plantations, sandy beaches, and mist-topped mountains all in one trip. From spotting wildlife on guided rainforest walks to exploring hanging bridges around Arenal or watching the waves roll in along the Pacific coast, there are plenty of ways to turn a family holiday into an adventure.

The best eco-lodges, home rentals, and hotels in Costa Rica are worth booking well ahead, particularly for Christmas, Easter, and school holidays. The Pacific coast's dry season generally runs from December to March, with April marking the transition towards the rainy season, making these months popular for beach holidays and outdoor adventures. The Caribbean coast follows a different rainfall pattern, with September and October often among its driest months. Plan in advance and book into one of the country's famous eco-friendly stays—we like the Victorian-style bungalows at Aguas Claras in Puerto Viejo or the luxurious Lapa Rios Lodge on the Osa Peninsula. Aguas Claras welcomes children aged three and over and can arrange activities such as surfing lessons and wildlife excursions, while Lapa Rios, which accepts children aged six and over, offers guided rainforest experiences and opportunities to learn about conservation. For a private stay, there are some truly fantastic Airbnbs in Costa Rica, including treehouses surrounded by tropical greenery and villas near the beaches of Santa Teresa.

For a 2027 family trip, it's worth planning your route as carefully as your accommodation. Winding mountain roads and travel times between regions can make an ambitious itinerary tiring, particularly with younger children. Choose a few bases rather than trying to see everything, and book popular guided activities ahead of time. Some national parks also require advance online tickets, so check the relevant booking arrangements before visiting.

Where to stay: Best Hotels in Costa Rica; Best Rentals in Costa Rica

Though Seoul is famous for its café culture and culinary scene, the kitchens in South Korea's southern regions are drawing travelers down and out of the capital, with tour operators designing itineraries that guide guests through the ingredients, culture, and history of each recipe. Responsible Travel has put together an eight-day experience with departures available throughout much of 2027, inviting travelers to experience regional specialities, spend a night at a Buddhist temple near Gyeongju, explore traditional food markets, and learn to make kimchi. On the coast, Jeollanam-do spotlights fresher, lighter flavors straight from the ocean such as ganjang gejang (soy-marinated crab), plus richer dishes like beef-rib soup. You can also stay in a temple at Baekyangsa, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan (of Chef’s Table fame) has a meditative approach to Korean cooking. The temple offers a separate overnight experience featuring a demonstration of her temple cuisine, with sessions generally held monthly and dates released around a month in advance.

Most arriving by air will travel through Seoul at some point—so factor in a few days to check out chefs such as Jungsik Yim and Mingoo Kang, who have been putting the city on the Michelin-starred map with their internationally-acclaimed menus. Kang's restaurant Mingles holds three Michelin stars in the 2026 guide, while Yim's Jungsik has two, making both tempting additions to a food-focused itinerary. For an authentic stay, book into a hanok in Seoul, perhaps in the historic Bukchon neighborhood, where traditional tiled-roof houses sit alongside galleries, tea rooms, and small boutiques. Be aware that tourist sightseeing is restricted between 5 p.m. and 10 a.m. in designated residential streets, so check the local rules before visiting.

Ask most people what’s on their travel bucket list, and you can guarantee that a trip on Belmond's Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is up there. Long associated with romance and timeless glamour, there are few things as enjoyable as a journey on one of these famous trains through Europe. Thanks to a focus on slow travel, you can now justify your ticket as a greener way of getting around. From the moment you arrive at the station and the lacquered dark blue carriages come into view, you feel like you’ve stepped into the pages of an Agatha Christie novel.

There are 70 routes to explore, including Paris to Verona and Amsterdam to Venice. On the Florence to Paris route, squeeze in a stay at Castello di Casole beforehand so you can start your trip with freshly cooked pizza from the hotel’s 16th-century pizza oven and glasses of wine from their vineyard while watching the sun set behind the rolling Tuscan hills.

Once on board and directed to your cabin, there’s little to do but sit back, sip Champagne, and watch as the train station melts away and towns and fields speed past you. A three-course lunch in one of the three 1920s dining cars is next, followed by an afternoon drinking cocktails in 3674, the train’s Art Deco bar car, before dressing in your finery for the evening.

Time slips away as quickly as the snow-capped mountains whizzing past the window, and after a decadent dinner followed by martinis in the bar car—accompanied by the tinkling of a piano and, if you’re lucky, a sing-song from the bar staff—it’s time to climb into bed and let the movement of the train (and aforementioned martinis) lull you to sleep.

If you don’t quite manage the 6 a.m. wake up to see the sunrise over Champagne, then you’ll stir as the train pulls into Paris and coffee and pastries arrive promptly at your cabin. All that’s left is to wonder how quickly you can save for your next Venice Simplon-Orient-Express adventure. With 2027 journeys already available to book, it's worth reserving early if you have a particular route, date, or cabin category in mind.

Uruguay’s summer runs from December to February, although warm weather and beach holidays can extend into March, so it’s a popular winter break for sun-starved travelers (and when seasonal restaurants and hotels are most likely to be open). While Montevideo offers a mix of city beaches, markets, and culture, further along the coast, José Ignacio—a former fishing village turned bustling beach town—draws a fashionable crowd of locals and foreigners. The area has become a magnet for art lovers, foodies, and design enthusiasts, with places such as Posada Ayana, home to James Turrell’s Skyspace installation, and Luz, a wine lodge surrounded by vineyards and olive groves, around ten minutes' drive from José Ignacio. Guests at Posada Ayana can experience Turrell's Ta Khut installation at sunrise and sunset, while Luz offers wine tastings and culinary experiences that make it worth venturing away from the beach.

Seafront favorite Playa Vik continues to attract visitors with its striking architecture, art-filled interiors, and views over Playa Mansa. Just out of town, the high-design Sacromonte Landscape Hotel offers a more secluded escape in the wild sierras of Maldonado, where contemporary cabins overlook the surrounding vineyards and countryside. Although Francis Mallmann’s restaurants Chiringuito and Bodega Garzón are on many bucket lists, few know that visitors can also stay at Casa Anna, the chef's charming guesthouse in nearby Pueblo Garzón. Alongside regular accommodation, Casa Anna offers separately arranged hosted culinary experiences with Mallmann, including shared meals and opportunities to discover his distinctive approach to open-fire cooking.

If you're planning to spend the last of your annual leave in the South American sunshine, aim for late December to experience José Ignacio at its buzziest, but be prepared for higher prices and limited availability at the most sought-after hotels. February and March can offer a quieter alternative, although some seasonal businesses begin winding down as summer draws to a close. For the festive period, booking in advance is particularly worthwhile, especially if you're hoping to secure one of the area's smaller, design-led retreats.

The ski-in-ski-out Park Hyatt Niseko Hanazono boasts Molière Montagne, a restaurant from three-Michelin-starred chef Hiroshi Nakamichi, an impressive selection of restaurants and bars, and hot-spring bathing facilities for unwinding after a day on the slopes. Sansui Niseko offers a fully serviced alternative to townhouses by Kasara or Airbnb (the latter of which are particularly high quality here), with direct ski access to Grand Hirafu's Family Course, an onsen, and spacious suites for those traveling with family or friends.

The outskirts of Sapporo are stunning in the fall, with koyo (the appearance of autumn leaves) at its most colorful around mid-October, but winter is when Niseko really comes into its own. The 2026 to 2027 ski season is scheduled to begin on November 28, with some ski areas planning to remain open into early May, depending on snowfall. January and February are generally the best months for the famously light, dry powder that draws skiers and snowboarders from around the world, although snow conditions can never be guaranteed.

For a trip during the winter season, booking accommodation, ski lessons, and equipment rentals well in advance is a good idea, particularly over Christmas and New Year's Eve. With four interconnected ski areas, a thriving restaurant scene, and plenty of opportunities to warm up in an onsen after a day in the snow, Niseko is the kind of destination where a little advance planning can make all the difference.

Another blockbuster backdrop, Jordan’s archaeological city of Petra was named one of the new seven wonders of the world in 2007 for its extraordinary rock-carved architecture and the Al Siq canyon. A couple of hours' drive from Petra, the sliver of Red Sea coast around Aqaba draws visitors for its sun, souks, and scuba-diving opportunities, with colorful coral reefs and warm waters making it a favorite among underwater explorers. Beyond the coast, the extraordinary landscapes of Wadi Rum are another reason to add Jordan to your 2027 travel wish list. Here, towering sandstone formations and vast desert valleys provide the setting for guided excursions with local Bedouin communities and nights spent beneath the stars at desert camps.

Spring and autumn are among the best times to visit, with milder temperatures making it easier to explore Petra's archaeological treasures and venture into the desert. If you fly into the capital, Amman, a metropolis of ancient tradition and entrepreneurial spirit greets you, alongside a slew of social enterprises such as SEP, a fashion and lifestyle brand working with Palestinian refugee embroiderers, and Beit Sitti, a cooking school founded by three sisters where visitors can learn to prepare traditional Arabic dishes alongside local women.

For those hoping to combine Petra, Wadi Rum, and the Red Sea in one trip, planning ahead allows time to arrange local guides, accommodation, and transport between the country's most spectacular destinations. It's also worth looking into the Jordan Pass, which includes admission to more than 40 attractions, including Petra, and a tourist visa fee waiver for eligible visitors who purchase it before arrival and meet the relevant stay requirements. With travel schedules and regional conditions subject to change, check the latest official advisories before confirming your 2027 plans.

Antarctic travel is still trying to strike a balance between overtourism and sustainable travel, with the International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators recording more than 113,000 tourists traveling to the region during the 2025 to 2026 season. Once accessible only to wealthy explorers or well-funded scientists, it’s exciting that this stark, striking landscape is now attracting a growing number of adventurous travelers, although its increasing popularity raises important questions about protecting one of the world's most fragile environments. Many choose to visit during the austral summer (November to March), when there’s less sea ice and more sun (ideal for kayaking, wildlife watching and, on certain specialist expeditions, skiing and snowshoeing).

From vast penguin colonies and seals resting on ice floes to humpback whales feeding in the Southern Ocean, Antarctica offers extraordinary opportunities for wildlife encounters, both on land and at sea. For many travelers, a polar cruise is one of the most rewarding ways to experience the continent, with expedition vessels offering guided shore landings and Zodiac excursions, while larger ships may provide scenic cruising without disembarkation. Choosing an operator committed to responsible tourism is essential, although even carefully managed expeditions have an environmental footprint. Consider a vessel with hybrid-electric propulsion, such as Ponant’s Le Commandant Charcot, the first hybrid-electric polar exploration ship powered by liquified natural gas, which also carries two onboard scientific laboratories. Or, book with an operator such as Abercrombie & Kent or White Desert, which offers a different way to experience the continent through its fly-in expeditions and luxury land-based camps, including Whichaway Camp.

With the Antarctic travel season concentrated into just a few months and places on specialist expeditions limited, planning a year ahead is particularly worthwhile. Travelers hoping to visit during the popular summer months of December and January (or to secure a place on a small-group expedition) should start comparing itineraries and booking well before departure.

Trekking in the Himalayas comes with its own set of logistical, financial, and physical challenges, so booking well in advance can make a huge difference. Big groups will struggle with spontaneity, and allowing yourself several months to train and prepare for long days on the mountains is well worth the effort. But physical preparation is only part of the equation: Ladakh's high altitude means visitors also need to allow sufficient time to acclimate, particularly when arriving in Leh, which sits at around 11,500 feet above sea level. Local tourism authorities recommend at least 48 hours of rest before heading to higher-altitude areas.

If you’re determined to spot the region’s elusive snow leopard too, a good local guide is essential, and they book up fast. Hemis National Park is one of the world's best-known places to search for these big cats, with experienced trackers scanning the rocky slopes and valleys for signs of movement. Unlike conventional trekking holidays, snow leopard expeditions are best undertaken during the colder months, generally between November and April, when specialist wildlife tours operate in the region. The conditions can be challenging, with freezing temperatures and unpredictable mountain weather, but the rewards can be extraordinary. Ladakh is at its loveliest, and busiest, during the warmer months, from June to September, for those interested in exploring its Buddhist monasteries.

Consider booking through Voygr Expeditions, andBeyond, or Responsible Travel, all of which offer specialist snow leopard expeditions with experienced local guides or trackers. Some itineraries also incorporate visits to local communities and conservation initiatives, including andBeyond's support for the Snow Leopard Conservancy. With several 2027 departures already sold out, securing a place six to 12 months ahead is advisable, especially for those hoping to travel during the peak winter months.

For decades, safari trips centered around Big Five game, but Rwanda has something that Kenya, Zambia, and Botswana do not: silverback mountain gorillas. As a country, Rwanda has been a champion of ecotourism since long before the term went mainstream, with reforestation, conservation, and caps on visitor numbers protecting the environment and the wildlife within it. These efforts have contributed to a remarkable conservation success story, with the mountain gorilla population across the Virunga Massif, which spans Rwanda, Uganda, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, increasing from 480 in 2010 to 604 in 2016. In the Virunga Mountains, only eight people may trek to visit a particular gorilla group each day, with encounters limited to one hour. Visitors are told to stay at least 23 feet away to protect the gorillas from human diseases, although the animals themselves may occasionally approach more closely (recall David Attenborough’s encounter in 1978, when he commented, ‘There is more meaning and mutual understanding in exchanging a glance with a gorilla than any other animal I know’).

A collection of established luxury lodges, such as Magashi Camp, Singita Kwitonda Lodge, One&Only’s Gorilla’s Nest, and Nyungwe Tea Forest Resort have proven themselves to experienced safari-goers. While Magashi offers traditional Big Five game drives in Akagera National Park, Singita Kwitonda and Gorilla's Nest provide luxurious bases for gorilla trekking, and Nyungwe Tea Forest Resort is ideally placed for exploring the rainforest and tracking chimpanzees. For those wanting to venture beyond the forests, Lake Kivu offers a completely different perspective on Rwanda's landscapes. The Kivu Queen uBuranga, which began welcoming guests in December 2023, takes travelers across the lake aboard a luxury floating hotel, with opportunities to explore its islands and discover local communities and traditions.

Gorilla trekking permits currently cost $1,500 per person for most international visitors, and with only eight visitors allowed per habituated gorilla group each day, booking several months in advance is strongly recommended, particularly during the drier seasons from June to September and December to February. Those hoping to combine gorilla trekking with a stay at one of the country's most exclusive lodges should start planning even earlier, especially if traveling during peak holiday periods.

#6305. Ryanair Weighs Fare Hikes, Pay Freeze As Fuel Prices Soar

Irish discount carrier Ryanair is bracing for a difficult 2027 as jet fuel prices rise and European oil hedges expire.

In its most recent earnings report, the airline said it is considering temporarily freezing pay for workers, lowering crew ratios, and ramping up use of artificial intelligence. The company did not specify how long it would look to freeze wages, or how it would adjust staffing.

Ryanair has over 27,000 employees across its group.

Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said ticket prices will rise across Europe as lower-price oil hedges run out.

“The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months,” O’Leary said. “But those hedges are rolling off. There’s still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year. I believe you’re going to see air fares rise next year across Europe by 10 percent, maybe even 20 percent.”

In its earnings report, Ryanair said that while short-haul air fares will increase “materially,” it will not be enough to offset the expected €2 billion increase in fuel costs, necessitating the additional cost-saving measures.

Fuel prices have prompted several major European airlines and airline groups to cut capacity this fall and winter, and to retire some older, less efficient aircraft. Price volatility also pushed Lufthansa to accelerate the shutdown of Lufthansa CityLine, and made the U.K.’s EasyJet amenable to a roughly $7.7 billion takeover by Apollo Global Management.

The price shock has generally been worse in Europe and Asia than in North America, as those regions are more dependent on Gulf oil and lack domestic refining capacity.

#6303. JetBlue Raises Baggage Fees Again, Now Charges Up To $140 Roundtrip For One Checked Bag

JetBlue has raised checked baggage fees again, and bringing one ordinary suitcase can now add as much as $140 to a roundtrip ticket. With holiday travel approaching, this is another reminder that the fare you see when shopping may be far removed from what your trip actually costs.

JetBlue has increased baggage charges for new bookings made on or after November 3, 2026. The airline’s updated fee schedule lists a first checked bag starting at $50 each way. The price depends on when you travel and when you pay.

For passengers without an included baggage allowance or waiver, these are the new charges within the United States, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Canada. All amounts are per bag, each way:

You can see more particulars here, including pricing for Mosaic elites.

Upcoming peak periods include November 19–January 18. If you booked before November 3, check your reservation for the applicable charges (old rates apply). Here’s the full chart of peak dates over the next year:

That means one suitcase costs $100 roundtrip even at the lowest new rate. On peak dates, it costs $110 when paid in advance or $140 when purchased within 24 hours of each departure.

Consider a family of four traveling over Thanksgiving, with each person checking one suitcase and no baggage benefits.

Pay sufficiently early and the roundtrip baggage bill is $440. Wait until check-in for both flights and it becomes $560.

When does it become cheaper just to buy new clothes at your destination? We certainly try to pack efficiently when traveling with our children, but one standard checked bag per person hardly strikes me as an extravagant amount of luggage, especially for a longer holiday trip.

At these prices, baggage can materially change which airline offers the best deal. A cheaper JetBlue ticket may cease to be cheaper once you add the luggage you actually need…though it would not surprise me to see others follow.

Mosaic 1 members receive one checked bag, while Mosaic 2–4 members receive two. Eligible JetBlue Plus and Premier cardholders receive one bag. Premium-cabin allowances depend on the fare purchased: Base fares include one bag, while standard and Flex premium fares include two.

Those benefits become more valuable every time the underlying fees rise, though it’s still not a loyalty program or credit card product I can get enthusiastic about.

JetBlue’s latest increase pushes the cost of one checked suitcase to $100–$140 roundtrip for passengers without an exemption. For families, the additional expense can reach hundreds of dollars.

Compare the total cost before booking, and if you know you will check a bag, pay more than 24 hours before departure. I want JetBlue to succeed, but charging passengers more to bring their belongings does little to make it an airline people actively want to choose. Quote the contrary, JetBlue is doing a great job of alienating passengers during its great time of need.

Lol, over 60% of the dates in the next 12 months (Nov 2026-2027) are ‘peak’, including every single day from before Memorial Day weekend to after Labor Day. That’s insanity, and I’m guessing that will only grow over time.

This whole peak day bags cost more is ridiculous. It does not cost JetBlue any more money to load bags on an aircraft on January18th verses January 19th. Customers will tolerate different prices when talking about pre-paid verses paying at the airport, but this peak non-peak charge is how you drive customers away because they can see through it and know it’s sham. It doesn’t cost JetBlue more money to load baggage on peak days verses non-peak days.

#6302. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6301. 11 Best Airbnbs Near SoFi Stadium to Make the Most of Your Super Bowl Weekend

With its translucent roof, cutting-edge technology, and $5.5 billion price tag, SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles ranks among the most ambitious sports venues in the world. Since opening in 2020, it has made headlines for its indoor-outdoor design and massive dual-sided video board suspended above the field. It's played host to some spectacular events, from Super Bowl LVI in 2022, when the Los Angeles Rams won on their home turf, to FIFA World Cup matches in 2026. As the official host of the Super Bowl LXI in 2027, SoFi continues to attract fans from around the world. But getting there—and finding the right Airbnb to stay at nearby—can be quite the challenge.

LA traffic is notorious for turning a short trip into an hours-long commute, especially during a big event like the Super Bowl. Add expensive rideshares and post-event congestion, and transportation to SoFi Stadium can quickly become a headache. The solution? The Airbnbs below, which let you stay closer to the action to make the most of your trip.

Every property on this list is less than a 25-minute drive from the stadium (sans traffic), and some are just steps away, so you can skip the transportation stress and spend more time enjoying the big game. Read on for the best Airbnbs near SoFi Stadium, whether you’re headed there for the Super Bowl, the next buzzy concert, or to take a behind-the-scenes stadium tour.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Client dinners, catered lunches and team celebrations can add up quickly. The right business credit card can turn those restaurant bills into a meaningful haul of points, miles or cash back.

From high category bonuses to uncapped flat-rate rewards, the best credit cards for dining can make every business meal work harder.

Here's how our top picks compare based on their dining returns, annual fees and reward flexibility.

The information for the U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus Visa Signature Card and the U.S. Bank Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

To determine the best business cards for dining, I looked for cards with an estimated return of at least 3% on restaurant purchases, based on TPG's valuations. I focused on ongoing earnings rather than welcome offers or dining credits, then selected cards serving distinct use cases, including high category bonuses, uncapped transferable rewards and no-annual-fee options.

Other cards that don't earn at least 3% back in value based on our valuations may still be good fits for your business within a broader rewards strategy, but are less competitive when restaurant earnings are the primary goal.

The American Express Business Gold earns valuable Membership Rewards points. Cardmembers earn 4 points per dollar spent in their top two spending categories each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in bonus category spending per year, then 1 point per dollar), with dining and restaurants falling under an available category.

That means businesses that max out their cap could earn 600,000 points each year. Even if you don't come close to that cap, 4 points per dollar is still a significant return on spend, especially when they come with all the potential of Membership Rewards.

Just be careful: Since Amex rewards extra bonus points on your top spending categories each billing cycle, if other eligible expenses overtake dining, restaurant purchases may earn only 1 point per dollar. You can use that to your advantage when your restaurant spending is low one month, but it could also catch you off guard.

To learn more, read our full review of the Business Gold.

Apply here: American Express Business Gold

The U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus earns 5% cash back in the cardholder's top eligible spending category each month on up to $200,000 in annual eligible purchases, automatically. Dining is one of the qualifying categories, and the cap is high enough that most businesses won't have to worry about it. All purchases outside the top category earn at least 2% cash back, which is also a generous return.

The $295 annual fee makes this card best for businesses with substantial, consistent restaurant spending. Otherwise, a no-annual-fee option may provide better value overall.

If you're looking for a card with no annual fee, The Blue Business Plus earns 2 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on all purchases (for the first $50,000 in spending each year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The simplicity of this card means you don't need to keep track of spending categories; it's just as great for your dining purchases as it is for shipping, advertising and other business expenses. For businesses that can stay below the cap and earn 2 points per dollar spent on all their spending, the combination of transferable points and no annual fee is difficult to beat.

To learn more, read our full review of the Blue Business Plus.

Apply here: The Blue Business Plus Credit Card from American Express

Like the Blue Business Plus, the Capital One Venture Business earns 2 miles per dollar spent on dining and other purchases. Unlike the Amex card, however, that earning rate is unlimited. This makes Venture Business a stronger fit for businesses that expect to spend more than $50,000 each year and can take advantage of double miles well above that spending threshold, despite the $95 annual fee.

Capital One miles are highly versatile, with options to transfer to 15-plus airline or hotel partners, book travel without blackout dates through Capital One Travel and more. In fact, a different set of transfer partners could make the Venture Business a more compelling solution than an Amex, depending on your business's redemption preferences.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Business.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Business Credit Card

The Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card earns 3% cash back on eligible restaurant purchases with no annual fee, and there's no cap on total rewards.

It can't match the Business Essentials Plus card's 5% return, but there's no annual fee to recoup. A business would need to spend about $14,750 annually on dining for the 5% rate to make up for the $295 fee versus the Triple Cash card's no-annual-fee 3% return. Therefore, if you're looking for simple cash back but have more moderate restaurant spending, the Triple Cash is a stronger fit.

To learn more, read our full review of the U.S. Bank Triple Cash.

The Marriott Bonvoy Business Amex is a good fit for businesses that frequently entertain clients, host events at Marriott properties or incur dining expenses while traveling. It earns 4 points per dollar spent on eligible restaurant purchases worldwide, which represents a 3% return at TPG's November 2026 valuations. Since it doesn't impose a spending cap on its restaurant rewards, businesses can earn consistently throughout the year.

The card becomes especially valuable for businesses that regularly stay with Marriott and can put both its hotel benefits and Bonvoy rewards to use.

Of course, loyalty to one hotel brand won't work for everyone. Businesses that prioritize more flexible redemptions may prefer a card that includes Marriott as a transfer partner rather than choosing a cobranded card specifically.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bonvoy Business Amex.

Apply now: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card

The right business card option depends on more than earning rates. You'll also need to account for how much your business spends, whether you prefer cash back or travel rewards and whether you're willing to pay an annual fee.

Start with the net value, not the largest number in the table. The Amex Business Gold and Business Essentials Plus only deliver their highest dining returns when restaurant purchases rank among the business's top eligible categories. But cards that earn lower rates of return on dining might be a better value once you factor in annual fees and spending caps.

In addition to considering the type of rewards best for your business, think about what else these cards offer. Secondary benefits like travel protections, cellphone insurance, lounge access or elite status might make up for a lower earning rate on meals when you consider the whole package.

A large welcome offer can improve a card's first-year value, but it shouldn't outweigh its long-term fit. Compare ongoing rewards after the annual fee, along with the protections, credits and other benefits your business will realistically use. That said, when two or more cards are equally strong long-term fits, a welcome bonus can be a useful tiebreaker. Especially since some credit cards currently offer welcome bonuses of 100,000 points or more.

Lastly, confirm your spending will count toward elevated earning rates if the bonus rate affects which card you pay with. Dining bonuses depend on how the merchant categorizes the purchase, and not all food vendors are considered a restaurant. For example, a hotel cafe may code as travel, while a bar might code as nightlife or entertainment.

The Amex Business Gold offers the highest potential dining return based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, but its earning rate alone likely doesn't settle the decision. Spending caps, annual fees, redemption flexibility and other card benefits will also factor into which card delivers the most value for your business.

Businesses with large, predictable restaurant expenses will come out ahead by choosing premium cards, even after budgeting for an annual fee. When your dining spending is more moderate or inconsistent, though, a no-annual-fee card may produce the same net value with less monitoring. Don't pay for an earnings rate your business won't regularly trigger.

#6299. Delta Air Lines CEO Vows To Fight Heathrow Move That Separates It From Virgin Atlantic

Delta Air Lines is fighting Heathrow Airport’s decision to move it away from Virgin Atlantic, warning that separating the partners will hurt passengers and undermine years of investment. I understand why Delta is upset. But whether that should entitle it to remain in Terminal 3 is a more complicated question.

Heathrow plans to move Delta from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028, while Virgin Atlantic remains in Terminal 3. The decision would split an operation the two airlines have spent years integrating.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian issued an unusually pointed public statement on November 2, calling the decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.” He argued that sharing Terminal 3 supports convenient connections and a consistent premium experience. Delta intends to challenge the move, saying it “will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision.”

“Heathrow Airport Limited’s decision to relocate Delta’s operation to Terminal 4, away from our partner Virgin Atlantic, is short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers. For more than a decade, our airlines have served millions of customers through our co-located operation in Terminal 3, offering travelers convenient connections, premium amenities and access to an expanded global network.

“Delta and Virgin Atlantic provide UK consumers with a valuable competitive alternative across the Atlantic. Separating our operation undermines years of investment and disregards the tightly integrated customer benefits that we offer in our co-located terminal. We are committed to preserving the seamless travel experience for which Delta and Virgin Atlantic are known and will pursue all available remedies to correct this decision. We urge Heathrow Airport Limited to reconsider their decision in favor of a more prudent and thoughtful outcome that puts travelers first and allows competition to flourish at Heathrow.”

Terminal assignments can sound like an obscure airport planning issue until you are the passenger trying to make a connection.

A traveler arriving on Delta and continuing on Virgin Atlantic would face a terminal transfer that is unnecessary today. The same applies in reverse. Unfortunately, terminal transfers are not easy at LHR and moving between terminals introduces another step and more opportunity for something to go wrong.

For someone simply flying Delta to London and heading into the city, the effect may be less consequential. But Delta and Virgin sell their partnership as an integrated travel experience. Separating their airport operations makes that promise harder to deliver.

There is also the premium experience. Eligible Delta passengers currently benefit from Virgin Atlantic’s Terminal 3 facilities, including its Clubhouse. Those facilities are part of what makes the partnership attractive, especially when choosing between similarly priced business class tickets.

If the move happens, I would assume that a Delta flight departing from Terminal 4 will not include access to Virgin’s Terminal 3 facilities, at least in any practical capacity. However as I mentioned in my earlier story, integrating with Air France/KLM in Terminal 4 makes a lot of sense (far more connecting itineraries) and the lounge is not bad at all.

Still, replacing something that already works well requires money and effort. I can understand why Delta would prefer not to start over.

Heathrow’s decision follows a three-year terminal review. The airport says the changes will improve its use of existing capacity and operational resilience, while creating room for growth.

Heathrow also says airlines representing 81% of its passengers support the outcome (that is a share of passenger traffic represented by supportive airlines, not a survey showing that 81% of travelers approve).

Delta is not the only carrier being asked to move. The wider reshuffle also affects Finnair, Japan Airlines, LATAM, and China Southern.

An airport cannot necessarily give every airline its preferred location. Keeping one partnership together may mean imposing constraints or additional costs elsewhere. Delta’s investment deserves consideration, but it should not automatically settle how Heathrow should allocate scarce terminal space.

Bastian also presents the shared terminal as supporting competition across the Atlantic. I accept that a more cumbersome ground experience could make Delta and Virgin less attractive to some travelers. A passenger comparing connections may reasonably prefer an itinerary that avoids a terminal transfer.

But claims that the move will weaken competition or drive up fares need more support than the fact that Delta dislikes it. Heathrow is changing where Delta operates, rather than announcing that it must stop serving London or taking slots away. Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult. That deserves a substantive answer but there’s undeniable logic in the shuffling.

Delta has good reason to challenge a Heathrow move that would separate it from Virgin Atlantic. Sharing Terminal 3 offers practical benefits, and I understand Bastian’s anger. But Heathrow must manage the airport as a whole. I would be more persuaded by a clear account of what this reshuffle improves and why those gains outweigh the disruption.

For now, this is a dispute over a planned 2028 change..itt does not mean your next Delta flight has moved to Terminal 4. I hope the eventual outcome preserves as much of the current passenger experience as possible, but I’m still not convinced Delta is being unfairly picked on by LHR and I am convinced that whether Delta wins or loses this battle, its passengers will enjoy a great ground product at Heathrow for many years to come.
