Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Not to defend Delta, but why would anyone connect from DL onto AF/KL at LHR. It just adds complextity and cost versus flying DL to AMS/CDG and connecting from there. I doubt they have anything to gain by being co-located with AF/KL rather than VS. Also T4 is worse than the T2/T3 complex for ground transport or self-connecting options.

Is terminal 4 underutilized or are they shifting the problem of crowding from T3 to T4? With LHR ruling out the prospect of new slots at LHR in 2028 when Heathrow’s Management says this move will lead to gains the question they haven’t answered is gains for who, for which airline.

If this move is really about alleviating congestion in T3 then go for it. But if this move is part of a broader plan that will see Delta capacity at T3 replaced by another carrier then Delta has every right to throw a fit.

T4 is operating significantly under capacity and since BA needs to move additional capacity into T3 to relieve T5, it has to be one of the larger T3 tenants who moves out.

Delta doesn’t adult very well and tends to react particularly poorly when told no. Not everyone is going to come out a winner and they just need to deal with the fact that this is a loss for them.

A better solution would be to move all SkyTeam out of Terminal 3 into Terminal 4, move all OneWorld and its partners into Terminals 5 and 3 and distribute the non-aligned between Terminals 2 and 3 as space allows. Terminal 4 is much more modern than Terminal 3 so there should be little complaint on that one.

I tend to agree and the current two-level Qatar lounge would make a great new Clubhouse. LHR should do this and just help VS/DL pay for it…

Yep. This was the obvious move by LHR if that’s your end game. End of the day this will be about compensating DL/VS for the move to T4. But VS(/DL) gets no brownie points for renovating the current Clubhouse in a transparent attempt to forestall this. LHR told VS/DL that this was the likely outcome – if VS(/DL) wanted to waste their money playing a game of chicken, that’s on them.

Are there really that many people connecting in LHR to Asia on Virgin?

While the clubhouse is nice I wasn’t overly wowed by it. And since flights are day time west, it’s not as important having a lounge meal like eastbound when you’re trying to maximize sleep. The Air France lounge in T4 looks nice enough anyways. I think the biggest loss for anyone flying D1 is the arrivals lounge, especially if you’re heading straight into the office.

Maybe Delta should have listened to their pilots a few years ago and stopped outsourcing so much of their international flying to partners…

” Delta’s strongest argument is the concrete one: it has built a useful shared operation with Virgin, and Heathrow is proposing to make that operation more difficult.”

Heathrow is proposing to level the playing field between the two major US-UK Joint Ventures at the airport. Virgin had the chance to move, as well. It’s not as though Delta doesn’t have the cash to build a reasonable ground experience at T4. LHR isn’t even anything close to a transfer hub for DL. Those hubs are AMS and CDG — CDG, an airport where DL/AF customers have to change terminals and clear security between terminals. what a concept for Delta.

I get why Delta is upset but it doesn’t seem very persuasive to be mad about “connections” when LHR isn’t much of a connecting airport for their Joint Venture. But as usual… Delta and Virgin Atlanta love to cry foul when asked to do what AA/BA do today…

#6298. In Luxor, Ancient Egypt feels newly alive

The water is cold and clear. Half-hidden amid the palm-tufted grounds of the Mortuary Temple of Seti I, this sacred sunken lake on Luxor's west bank was once the domain of ancient Egyptian priests. More than 3,000 years later, women from nearby villages still come, hoping its waters will serve as a fertility aid or a balm for their sick children, says my guide Ahmed Hassan, who was born and raised on this side of the Nile. It's one of the area's many miracles, he adds: No one knows where the water comes from, but it hasn't run dry since those priests of antiquity first bathed here. Hedging my bets, I submerge my hands.

It can be difficult to know what to believe in this transcendent stretch of Upper Egypt, 410 miles south of Cairo, where the Nile exudes a life force of its own; the mountains cradle secret treasures; and the light, particularly at golden hour, plays tricks, almost convincing you that you have traveled back in time. The line between the real and the mystical feels flimsy, whether you are considering the scale of the approximately 1,000-ton, 65-foot-tall colossus of Ramses II, inexplicably carved from a single piece of granite and lying prostrate at the king's statuesque funerary temple, the Ramesseum; or observing the unnerving precision of the hieroglyphs in the tomb of Ramses V and VI, in the Valley of the Kings, that has proved immune to the ravages of time.

Formerly ancient Thebes, Luxor—whose name comes from the Arabic Al-Uqsur (The Palaces)—served as Egypt's capital during the New Kingdom, from circa 1550 BCE to 1070 BCE. On the west bank of the Nile, sugarcane and banana plantations lead to a limestone canyon topped by Al-Qurn, or The Horn, a natural peak shaped like a pyramid. The rulers of the New Kingdom decided that this would be the ideal spot to protect their richly decorated tombs from grave robbers—a failed exercise, since every tomb in the Valley of the Kings was looted in antiquity, bar that of now legendary boy king Tutankhamen.

“There are many sites that have an impressive amount of ‘stuff,’ but what you have in Luxor is truly monumental,” Mennat-Allah El Dorry, from the American University in Cairo's department of sociology, Egyptology, and anthropology, tells me. “You have Karnak and Luxor temples on the east bank, and the mortuary temples on the west, as well as Valley of the Kings. It is such a dense area.”

I take her recommendations, balancing the quiet of the lesser-visited, only partially restored Mortuary Temple of Seti I and the Ramesseum with the many-splendored tombs at the Valley of the Kings, where voyeuristic crowds swell to see the diminutive mummy of Tutankhamen languishing 26 feet below ground. By contrast, the tomb of Ramses V and VI close by is deserted. A toothless, djellaba-wearing guard smiles conspiratorially before letting me behind the barrier. He takes my phone and assumes the practiced ease of a fashion photographer directing his next magazine cover: “Come closer; go there; look over your shoulder.”

Much of Luxor feels like it hasn't changed in centuries. At sunset the sails of felucca boats trace a timeless scene on the Nile's surface. Amid the clip-clop of horse-drawn carriages, the call to prayer tumbles from minarets and the sky settles into strips of apricot and lavender.

Matching the restraint of Arax is the stripped-back Marsam Hotel and discreet yet stately Habu Hotel, the latter just feet away from the Medinet Habu Temple. But Hotel Al Moudira sits at the opposite end of the spectrum. Founded by Italian Lebanese artist Zeina Aboukheir in 2001, and originally designed by famed Egyptian architect Olivier Sednaoui, the hotel revels in its maximalism: a whimsical interplay of domes and arches embellished with terra-cotta plaster, frescoes, and antiques. In 2022, Aboukheir sold the hotel to its new owner, Florian Amereller, but she still guides its creative direction, most recently in the design of six new villas. I stay in one of the five rooms in the salmon pink Villa Casbah, where hand-painted silhouettes of gazelles trip skittishly across the walls.

Chef Gioconda Scott at The Moudira Farm Kitchen

Under its new ownership the now five-star Al Moudira has expanded to include a huge swath of surrounding farmland. It's here, in an open kitchen engulfed in greenery, that I find British Spanish chef Gioconda Scott in the midst of a busy lunch service. In 2025 she launched The Moudira Farm Kitchen, where she transforms the fresh produce grown on-site into an unfussy, seasonal menu inspired by the Mediterranean. “This is simple cooking,” says Scott, who populates her kitchen with young chefs from the local tourism college. “Every element has to be good. If you don't have a good olive oil or a good tomato, there's no hiding.”

The restaurant itself is filled with products made by artisans on the farm. Crockery, rendered in a range of earthy tones, was crafted by potters whom guests can join for classes. I can hear the distant clack of the loom that wove the jaunty turquoise tablecloth, while, in other corners, artisans carve alabaster, blow glass, and upholster furniture.

The same crafts inhabit the decks of Al Moudira's new, 180-foot Nile Canopus, a nostalgia-infused nod to historic travel along this evocative waterway. Open-air decks with safari-tent-style coverings, a cozy library, and rooms fitted with brass beds and bespoke teak and rattan furniture are designed to evoke the age of Amelia Edwards, author of the seminal 1877 travelogue A Thousand Miles Up the Nile.

There has been a proliferation of new dahabeahs on the Nile, which offer more intimate, personalized experiences than do the hulking, 50-cabin motorboats that also ply these waters. Laden with modern conveniences, today's dahabeahs are admittedly no longer sprightly enough to be harried along by wind and sail; instead they are pushed and pulled by dinky-looking tugboats. On the inside they are increasingly elaborate. Karine Hassoun called on Egyptian painters, professors, and artisans for her eight-cabin dahabeah, Nile Divine, a celebration of contemporary Egyptian craft. In the nine-cabin Oro, a dark wood exterior pays tribute to the dahabeahs of old but with a dramatic brass wall in the reception area, a plunge pool extending out over the deck, a full-fledged bar up top, and suites with private terraces and hot tubs. Oberoi Hotels and Resorts will join the fray later this year with two seven-suite dahabeahs featuring interiors by Karim Mekhtigian, founder of Alchemy Design Studio, while Waldorf Astoria Hotels and Resorts' new, 29-suite Nile cruiser will bring to the water all the elements of its land-based hotels, including its Peacock Alley brasserie.

Change is underway on land too. I see the cranes hovering over the east bank, pinpointing where a Four Seasons Hotel, due to open in 2027, is rapidly taking shape. The much-loved Winter Palace—archaeologist Howard Carter's base during his 1922 Tutankhamen tomb discovery and where Agatha Christie was inspired to write parts of Death on the Nile—recently closed for a renovation and will reopen as a Mandarin Oriental in July 2027, exactly 120 years after its official inauguration, hopefully with original features and charm fully intact.

That's only weeks before next year's solar eclipse: On August 2, Luxor will witness the moon masking the sun for its maximum duration, a total of 6 minutes and 22 seconds. Just enough time for that line between the real and the mystical to grow even flimsier.

A few feet from Habu Temple, recommended for its deeply etched hieroglyphs and particularly well-preserved colors, is a property with its own historic pedigree: the unassuming, 17-room Habu Hotel was one of the first hotels to open on Luxor’s West Bank in the 1920s. It has been given a smart revamp, its public areas now filled with antiques, including stately granite busts and wooden statues from the 1800s. Sundowners on the hotel’s charming rooftop terrace bring you close enough to the temple’s chiseled interior that you can admire its exterior engravings from the comfort of your lounge chair.

A day spent tirelessly exploring Luxor’s sites is best ended in the spa at Hilton Luxor Resort and Spa, where treatment rooms look directly over the Nile and the infinity pool is one of the best spots in the city to catch Luxor’s famous sunsets. This is an ultra-convenient base if you want easy access to the historic sites on Luxor’s East Bank—Karnak Temple, in particular, is within walking distance. A private breakfast on a felucca offers a fresh perspective of the Nile, especially if you time it to coincide with hot-air balloons rising majestically over the Valley of the Kings.

For a stripped-back stay that’ll make you feel like an Egyptologist of old, head to Marsam Hotel, which started life as the excavation house for the University of Chicago, before being converted into a hotel in 1939. There’s (very intentionally) no swimming pool or TVs; the 29 pared-back rooms and five suites are designed for guests who are serious about exploring the many sites that surround this historic hotel. Whether or not you spend the night, make time for lunch at Marsam’s farm-to-table restaurant, where the menu changes daily and you’ll be serenaded by the resident donkeys, camels and horses.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6297. 15 of the Coolest Marathon Courses Around the Globe, From the Arctic Circle to the Great Wall of China

The TCS New York City Marathon is consistently one of the best days of the year in the city—it's emotional, it's inspiring, and it shows off the best of humanity. If you're a runner or a spectator who got the itch for more this past weekend, you're in luck: There are tons of incredible courses around the world, and while they may not traverse NYC's five boroughs, they will take you to world wonders, through safari lands, and across borders.

As someone who regularly travels for halfs, I spend a lot of my time researching and bookmarking races. For me, running through a new place one of the best ways to get to know a destination—you get the lay of the land, see what the community is like, and notice things you might not see from a car or public transportation. And as destination races grow in popularity, the courses offered are getting even more spectacular. The races on this list—halfs, fulls, 10Ks, and more—prove it. Below, I’ve rounded up 15 of the most spectacular races happening in the next year or so, all of which are well worth traveling for.

Date: March 13, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 10K, 3.5K

What to know: If you haven't run a Rock ‘n’ Roll marathon yet, you're missing out on a good time. As the name suggests, these music-centric runs make for an extremely lively course—bands and DJs fill the roads and the after party. Locations change each year, and in 2027, the series is going to Taitung on Taiwan's east coast; runners will move between the mountains and the Pacific Ocean on a flat, smooth route. After the race, be sure to check out the area's night markets, hot springs, and endless good eats.

Where to stay: Luxury hotels near the starting line include the Sheraton Taitung Hotel, which has an outdoor swimming pool, and Formosan Naruwan Hotel, with a spa and saltwater pool.

Date: April 25, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, 21-miler, 11-miler, 12K, 5K

What to know: With a cliffside, oceanview course running from Big Sur to Carmel along California’s iconic Highway 1, it doesn’t get much more scenic than this. It’s a Boston qualifier race and has a six-hour time limit, along with several course length options, making it a good one to run with a group, even if your ideal mileage differs.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at a few different properties in Monterey, closer to the finish line. Of course, there is no shortage of luxury hotels in the area—Alila Ventana Big Sur, Post Ranch Inn, and Carmel Beach Hotel are a few Traveler favorites.

Date: April 4, 2027Registration: The 2027 lottery entry has taken place; check back in May for the 2028 race; charity bibs are still availableDistances included: Half-marathon

What to know: As the name suggests, the course runs past several London landmarks, including Big Ben, the Tower of London, the London Eye, and Somerset House. It’s a lively course—musical performances, DJs, dancers, and themed cheer stations can be expected—and even better, it's a flat one, with 238 feet of total elevation gain.

Where to stay: In 2026, Blue Orchid Hospitality and the Clermont Hotel Group offered discounts for race weekend stays at properties like The Wellington Hotel, The Tower Hotel, and Thistle Trafalgar. We’ll update that list once 2027 partners are announced. For luxury stays near the starting line, consider Raffles London at the OWO or the Corinthia London.

Date: April 04, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half marathon, 10K

What to know: Okay, I'll get the cons over with first (for most, I'd presume): This is a cold and snowy course. Once you've got that fact out of the way, you can weigh the very unique pros. This Finnish Lapland course kicks off in Santa Claus Village square (!) in Rovaniemi, starting exactly on the line of the Arctic Circle. It's put together as part of a five-day running program with log cabin lodging, each with a private sauna, as well as activities like husky sledding, Northern Lights excursions, and an Ice Pool Experience. It all wraps up at a trophy dinner with—wait for it—Santa Claus himself. This is peak whimsy, friends.

Where to stay: Lodging is included in the tour package.

Date: May 15, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 8.5K

What to know: This race lets you run along one of the seven wonders of the world. It’s a strenuous, hilly course, but if the views alone don’t keep you going, the residents in local villages cheering you on along the route just might.

Of note, to register, you must sign up for a tour package; the starting price is $790 and includes race entry plus two nights of accommodations. It’s sponsored by Albatross Adventure Marathons, which also puts on The Big Five Marathon (more details below) and the Iceland Volcano Marathon, among other adventurous runs.

Where to stay: Hotels must be booked along with the packages. For a relaxing post-race stay, check into the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, with its award-winning spa (after a massage, consider the tea meditation too) and standout dining options, from Italian to dim sum.

Date: May 16, 2027Registration: Open now and quite affordable—the most expensive distance is €39 ($44)Distances included: Half-marathon, 10K, 5K (paved course); 17K, 8K (trail)

What to know: Set in Tossa de Mar, a beautiful, historic seaside town on Spain’s Costa Brava, these runs are all about the coastal views. Of course, that does mean a challenging, hilly course for all but the 5K, which boasts a flat route in the town’s center. Of note, the maximum time is on the shorter end: 2 hours 35 minutes for the half, 1 hour 15 for the 10K, and 45 minutes for the 5K.

Where to stay: Zel Costa Brava, about a 10-minute drive from the starting line, was mentioned in our list of the Best Places to Go in Spain and Portugal in 2026. It has a funicular to take guests down to the beach, a huge pool with plenty of lounge chairs to kick back on, and a spa with a thermal circuit, ideal for soothing sore legs.

Date: June 11-12, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 5K

What to know: Running around America's first national park, near sites like the Grand Prismatic Spring, is bound to be a highlight for any outdoor-loving runner. While not inside the bounds of the park, the views from the Custer Gallatin National Forest and the Hebgen Lake Ranger District are still impressive. The half marathon starts bright and early at 6 a.m. and has a four-hour course limit. There are five aid stations along the way, and 552 feet of elevation (of note, there are some technical, rocky sections to contend with).

Where to stay: The Lazy Duck Inn is the most convenient choice, given it's location near the start and finish line. To pad out the rest of your trip, check out our guide to where to stay in and near Yellowstone.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon

What to know: The name says it all: You might just see the big five while you run! The course takes runners through the South African Savannah on the Entabeni Game Reserve. It is a smaller race, with a maximum of 300 participants, in a moderate climate (expected to be in the 60s to 70s this year) along a sand and gravel trail. Past participants rave about this one, calling it “The ONLY marathon I have wanted to run twice!” and “the best adventure ever.” Like the Great Wall course, registration requires selecting a tour package, starting at $3,560 for the seven-day package, which includes accommodation, meals, game drives, bush walks, and more.

Where to stay: At the end of any package, you’ll be transferred to Johannesburg International Airport. Give yourself a night to decompress at the Park Hyatt Johannesburg, where peacocks roam the grounds, rooms overlook serene gardens, and Sunday brunch comes with a side of live music.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 10K, 5K, kids race

What to know: The Tromsø, Norway, race begins at 8:30 p.m.—but thanks to the midnight sun the event is named after, it’s still light out. One of the northernmost races in the world, with a course surrounded by mountains and fjords, it boasted 9,000 runners from an impressive 88 countries last year. Of note, the maximum time limit is 5 hours and 30 minutes for the marathon and 3 hours and 30 minutes for the half.

Where to stay: Right in Tromsø, St. Elisabeth makes for a lovely stay, especially if you take advantage of the spa’s thermal bath, pool, and saunas. A bit further out (45 minutes or so), the Yggdrasiltunet Farm Hotel offers an even more blissful setting for a post-race escape with its wood-fired barrel sauna, guided ice bathing, hot tub overlooking the sea, and yoga classes.

Date: June 20, 2027Registration: Open now (half marathon is already sold out; sign up for 2028 notifications on the website)Distances included: Half marathon, 10K

What to know: The race website dubs this “the most beautiful run on the planet,” and honestly, that might not be so hyperbolic. Running through Canada's first national park sounds like a dream, especially when the course passes by the Vermilion Lakes, Legacy Trail, and Bow Valley Parkway, with wildlife likely to be spotted along the way. It's not a particularly hilly course, with a total elevation gain of 418 feet, but do note the elevation, which maxes out at 4,620 feet.

Where to stay: The official host partner is Banff Lodging Company, which operates 16 hotels across Banff, Canmore, and Lake Louise, including Hotel Canoe & Suites and Otter Hotel. Guests can receive a 15% discount on these rates. Afterward, consider a wellness-centric stay at the stunning Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise.

Date: July 03, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon, 10.55k

What to know: Designed for adventure-seekers, this Northern Iceland race explores one of Earth's geological hot spots—you’ll run along the rim of two volcanic craters and over black lava rock, with steaming geysers taking your mind off the miles ahead.

Unless you’re an Icelandic resident, you’ll need to book the six-day tour package, which is around $3,100 and includes accommodation, transportation, meals, a celebratory post-race dinner, and some activities, with add-ons like whale-watching and waterfall chasing available too. Of note, race entrance is not included in that fee ($350 for the half and full, and $223 for the quarter marathon).

Where to stay: Our resident Iceland expert and contributing writer Erika Owen highly recommends one of the tour lodging options, Fosshotel Glacier Lagoon, saying that it “embodies the best of Iceland: seclusion, surrounding nature, and beds topped with Icelandic wool blankets.” On your way out of town, consider a stay at The Retreat at Blue Lagoon; beyond the must-dip-in thermal baths, the tasting menu at Michelin-starred Moss is well worth a splurge.

Date: July 18, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half-marathon, 5K, The Pairing (both!)

What to know: A 13.1-mile route through Napa and Sonoma’s wine country, this course is surrounded by farms, vineyards, and ranches—yes, there are gently rolling hills, but it’s not an overly challenging course. The real prize for the 3,000-ish participants is at the finish line: At the post-race wine festival, top local vineyards reward you with wine tastings, and your goodie bag includes a commemorative wine glass.

Where to stay: Several hotels partner with the race to offer discounted stays, including the Westin Verasa Napa Hotel, notable for its Hyperice Recover & Recharge Kit available at the front desk. (Heads up for other future runs: Hyperice and Normatec products can be found at most Westins across the US! I swear by the Normatecs and Hypervolt for post-race recovery.) Just across the street from the starting line sits Carneros Resort and Spa, a seven-time Readers’ Choice Award winner; down the street is Stanly Ranch, Auberge Collection, a resort with a gorgeous outdoor pool that’s exactly where I’d want to park myself post-race.

Date: October 15–17, 2027Registration: Opens January 1, 2027Distances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler, kids races

What to know: This is one course that’s absolutely on my running bucket list, and one I hope to tackle in 2027 (which happens to be the event's 50th anniversary!). It’s the only US race I’ve found that crosses borders: After starting in downtown Detroit, runners cross over the Ambassador Bridge into Windsor, Ontario, before returning to the US through the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel (yep, an underwater mile!). Uniquely, this means you will have to carry your passport during the marathon and international half.

Where to stay: The AC Hotel Detroit at the Bonstelle is minutes from the start line, and well-situated to other places of interest (Little Caesar’s Arena, Fox Theater, the Detroit Institute of Arts). For a post-race treat, stop by Warda Pâtisserie. JW Marriott Detroit Water Square, opening in February 2027 near the Riverwalk, is sure to be a lovely place to stay too.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, 10K, 5K

What to know: History buffs will love this course in Greece, which, according to legend, follows the original marathon route Pheidippides ran way back in 490 B.C. when he brought news of victory from the battlefield of Marathon (it’s also the course used in the 2004 Olympics). The marathon course stays open for eight hours and passes by landmarks like the Athens Concert Hall, Eleftherias Park, the Presidential Palace, and the National Garden. There are packages available if you want transportation, accommodations, and tour options baked into your visit; they’re not required for entry, but individual registration tends to sell out first, so plan accordingly.

Where to stay: The race starts in the town of Marathon, northeast of central Athens. For a stay close to the finish line with an excellent spa and both indoor and outdoor swimming pools, consider Hotel Grande Bretagne, a Luxury Collection Hotel. A bit further south, the seaside One&Only Aesthesis offers a touch of coastal glamour, plus a Guerlain spa.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler

What to know: The course begins in downtown Tulsa, weaving through neighborhoods and the University of Tulsa campus. Along the way, you'll encounter lots of support from the community, with block parties hosted along the course to cheer runners on. Of note, this is a Boston Qualifier, and race day temperatures tend to sit around the 50s.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at several partner hotels, including Brut Hotel, a charming boutique hotel a short drive from the start line with an outdoor pool, rooftop bar, and spa. I’m eyeing the Olympian Massage, designed to “relieve tension and restore mobility by utilizing deep tissue and sports massage techniques.”

#6296. Delta CEO Calls Heathrow Move ‘Short-Sighted’

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is pushing back against a planned terminal move at London Heathrow, calling the airport’s decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.”

In comments posted Monday on LinkedIn and published by Delta, Bastian objected to Heathrow’s decision to relocate the airline from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4. The move, planned for 2028, would separate Delta from joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic, which would remain in Terminal 3.

Bastian said the airlines’ shared operation has served millions of passengers for more than a decade, providing connections, premium amenities and access to their combined networks. He argued that splitting the carriers would undermine years of investment and the benefits of operating from the same terminal.

Delta will “pursue all available remedies to correct this decision,” he said, urging Heathrow to reconsider. Bastian did not outline specific legal or regulatory steps.

Virgin Atlantic has also challenged the plan. CEO Corneel Koster said separating the two airlines would complicate journeys, weaken competition and reduce passenger choice. The carrier is considering its options to contest the relocation, Sky News reported.

Heathrow says the changes will help ease congestion and make better use of its terminals. The airport began notifying airlines of the outcome of its terminal occupancy review on Oct. 27.

A Heathrow spokesperson told Sky News that the plan followed consultation with airline customers and would improve the passenger experience, strengthen operational resilience and provide room for growth.

Delta is one of five airlines slated to change terminals. Finnair and Japan Airlines would also move from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4, while LATAM would relocate from Terminal 3 to Terminal 2. China Southern would move from Terminal 4 to Terminal 5.

Delta consolidated its Heathrow operation in Terminal 3 in September 2016 to operate alongside Virgin Atlantic. In announcing that move, Delta cited easier connections and last-minute flight changes, along with access to Virgin Atlantic’s premium facilities for eligible passengers.

#6295. Flying Blue Delays 50% SAF XP Price Hike After Admitting “We Didn’t Handle The Rollout Well”

Flying Blue has postponed an abrupt devaluation to the elite status credit members earn through sustainable aviation fuel and charitable contributions. I remain skeptical of the underlying scheme, but program chief Tiffany Funk deserves credit for acknowledging the botched rollout, listening to members, and giving them time to adjust.

Air France-KLM Flying Blue initially changed its earning rates on November 2, 2026, without advance notice. For cash contributions toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the cost increased from €10 per XP to €15 per XP, a 50% increase.

XP, or Experience Points, determine Flying Blue elite status. Members who had incorporated these contributions into their qualification plans suddenly faced a more expensive path to their goal.

Now, as One Mile At A Time also reports, Flying Blue has postponed the changes until December 1, 2026. The previous earning rates return effective November 4, and contributions made since November 2 will also receive credit at the prior rates.

Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, addressed the reprieve:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I appreciate the candor. Funk acknowledges that Flying Blue handled the rollout poorly and offers a practical correction. Members now have a transition period, including protection for contributions made during the initial rollout.

To be candid, I consider this arrangement a greenwashing revenue-generating measure. Awarding elite status credit for an environmental contribution is a convenient way to monetize the pursuit of status while wrapping the transaction in a sustainability message, a win-win for both Flying Blue and frequent travelers but probably not for the environment.

We don’t have to litigate that here and I readily acknowledge SAF can play a role in reducing aviation’s lifecycle emissions, but purchasing a contribution does not make a passenger’s flight emissions disappear. And I suspect the additional XP is the deciding factor for many members who participate, not altruism for Mother Earth.

Flying Blue certainly understands the appeal. Someone approaching a qualification deadline may find paying for a contribution far more convenient than taking another flight. But my skepticism about the arrangement does not diminish the importance of treating participating members fairly. Flying Blue offered an opportunity, and members planned around it. Their reliance was entirely foreseeable.

Flying Blue owes no one a permanent opportunity to acquire additional XP at a particular rate. It can decide that the existing formula is too generous or that it wants a different balance between flying and other qualification methods. Members can then decide whether the revised offer is worthwhile.

My larger objection, as with most devaluations, concerns candid communication and advance notice. Tell us what is changing. Give us time to adjust plans made under the existing rules. Please spare us the suggestion that a reduction in benefits is an “enhancement” inspired by member feedback.

Funk avoids that familiar gaslighting here. She does not claim members asked to pay more for their XP. She acknowledges that feedback exposed a problem with the rollout and explains what Flying Blue will do about it.

That is a much more credible use of member feedback.

Consider someone who booked travel expecting to earn a certain number of XP from flights and make up the remainder through SAF contributions. An overnight change can upset that calculation after the flights have already been purchased.

That member is not necessarily demanding that the rules remain unchanged forever. The objection is that a plan made in good faith has become more expensive without warning.

The additional time gives members an opportunity to complete contributions at the previous rate or reconsider their qualification strategy. Crediting contributions made since November 2 at the old rate also avoids penalizing those who happened to transact during the botched rollout.

Neither measure eliminates the devaluation. Both make its introduction fairer.

I commend Funk for listening and adjusting. Management can respond to criticism without abandoning the underlying business decision. Here, a relatively straightforward concession makes loyal customers  feel heard rather than taken for granted.

I remain skeptical of Flying Blue’s SAF contribution scheme, and the higher cost per XP will make it less attractive. Heck, I remain skeptical of status in general as a proud free agent for two years running. But the program has corrected the avoidable failure of introducing that change without clear communication or notice.

Funk acknowledged what went wrong and gave members time to prepare. Flying Blue is entitled to revise its earning rates. Members who planned around those rates deserve a reasonable transition, and they now have one. That is a welcome response…I never thought Funk would make the program more generous as other loyalty programs cut and devalue, but measured and clear changes with advance notice to members are all anyone can ask for.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

There’s a difference between not owing permanence in the terms of a loyalty scheme and constantly tinkering with stuff in ways that are disadvantageous to members.

Devaluing twice in the space of 1.5 year and doubling redemption rates in the process while reducing short-haul XP earnings and using opaque formulae for partner redemption (I just got quoted 48k miles for 1.5 hour in ‘business class’ with an airline which doesn’t even offer that cabin on the route in question!) are all telltale signs of a programme that just shouldn’t be trusted.

#6294. Getting to Know New York Through Its Sandwiches

“By the end of our time together, I will be asking you again: ‘So, what is a sandwich?’”

An expert-led tour that starts by questioning its own object of inquiry is unconventional. But then, so is our guide. Ben Gollan, known to his Instagram followers as A Man and His Sandwich, has spent the last nine years reviewing sandwiches across New York City. Gollan moved here from Australia in 2016, after nearly a decade as a government lawyer. For about as long, he has run an Airbnb Experience that turns a food crawl into a two-hour pilgrimage to the city’s best sandwich slingers.

It was a pastrami sandwich at Harry & Ida’s, a former deli in the East Village, that turned Gollan into a professional sandwich hound. “It was a fourth-generation Jewish deli that broke every rule of pastrami sandwiches: it was thick-cut and fabulous,” he says as we dash across Bowery. We’re scuttling over from a coffee shop in Cooper Square that served as our meeting point and into the East Village—a neighborhood of contrasts that still manages to connect New York's past and present. There are 12 of us in total, mostly locals, a couple of newer transplants, and just one traveler. “It’s usually mostly visitors, so this is different,” he says.

It’s a great introduction to the city. After all, New York runs on sandwiches, and there’s no shortage of great ones, whether it’s a classic Italian deli sub you’re after or a grab-and-go banh mi. They’re economical, versatile, delicious and, as is the point of Gollan’s tour, telegraph the city’s greatest personality trait—its diversity. So is there such a thing as a New York sandwich? “Not really,” he says, "but the chopped cheese, born in East Harlem, might come closest.”

The Bono at Via Della Scrofa, a small family-owned joint that wouldn't look out of place on the streets of Rome

“We start here because it’s closest to what we think of as a traditional sandwich,” says Gollan, before filling us in on the origins of what is the modern-day sandwich. It involves John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who, in the 18th century, gave his title to the now-ubiquitous food. Gollan loves to talk and think about sandwiches as much as he eats them. “Although I've learned never to trust history, especially when rendered by colonizers,” he muses. “Do we really think it took us till the 1700s to invent the sandwich?”

Named after a Roman street, Via Della Scrofa is the kind of bottega or alimentari you might find in Rome, with a tiny counter selling tiny espressos and focaccia, as well as imported groceries from Italy. “It's small family-owned joints like this that make New York what it is,” says Gollan. While the rest of the group gets to try the Porcodeddena panini (made with porchetta), I’m getting a Bono: grilled eggplants sweetened with sun-dried tomatoes, with arugula and buffalo mozzarella, in a warm roll that’s toasty on the outside and soft and warm on the inside. The bread is perfect—it’s a rosetta (or michetta), a traditional Roman bread roll. I wash it down with a Crodino, a popular non-alcoholic bitter aperitif from Italy.

Around us, the Lower East Side Arts & Culture Open House, an annual event, had taken over the street, adding personality to our time with its bands, pop-up stalls, and lively crowds. Gollan regales us with stories of owner Giovanni Bartocci, describing him as a real character with “a man bun, suspenders, tattoos, and naturally, a Harley," and I look around hoping he'll show up. I ask Gollan why he isn’t eating with us. “I never want to tire of these sandwiches, and if I keep eating them, I will.” The wind picks up and blows over the canvases at an art stall, but the band is undeterred, playing “New York, New York.”

A spicy Pakistani rendition of the chopped cheese at Nishaan

The writer and her chopped cheese sandwich, the chapli kebab replaced with Impossible Meat.

Order: A chopped cheese, but make it desi

An 11-minute walk up 1st Avenue and a few blocks later, we spot our next sandwich spot. A cobalt-blue sign reads Nishaan; bags of rice are piled high along its exterior; and a long line snakes out of what I can only assume is a tiny space inside. Nishaan began as a pop-up at the weekly open-air food festival Smorgasburg and went on to win season 18 of The Great Food Truck Race. While there are other dishes on the menu (elote chaat, mango lassi), it’s Nishaan’s twist on that great New York City bodega staple, the chopped cheese, that many are after: a spice-laden chapli kebab, chopped up on a griddle with peppers and onions, then enhanced with a zingy cilantro sauce and tamarind chutney. When it opened in August 2025, it was one of the most talked-about new restaurants in New York City, which has emerged as a hub for a new generation of Pakistani eateries. “New York belongs to everyone, and so does the sandwich,” proclaims Gollan.

In a city that runs on pastrami, vegetarians like me don’t faze Gollan; he orders me a version with Impossible Meat. We tuck ourselves out of the wind and into an alley and dig in. I can’t stop eating, making a mess as I go along. “Half the fun of a sandwich is the experience of eating it,” Gollan adds.

Regulars love the pho sandwiches at Sunny and Annie’s—sandwiches stuffed to the brim with pho ingredients, minus the broth.

Sunny and Annie’s is a 24/7, 365-day-a-year kind of neighborhood classic with 92 items on its sandwich menu.

“We’re taking a detour,” says Gollan, frantically looking around him. It’s the day of the Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade, and the crowds around us are building, as are the dogs in costume—cheese boards, UPS drivers, and, suitably for the occasion, hot dogs. We ditch the idea of cutting through the park and work our way around the revelers.

Our destination? Sunny and Annie’s, a 24/7, 365-days-a-year kind of neighborhood classic that has been open since 1997. There’s no front door here, because there’s always someone around. Inside, past the candy, chips, and dish detergent, we’re greeted by what must be the most extensive sandwich menu I’ve ever encountered, all written out on brightly colored sheets of paper stuck to the glass counter. There are 92 handheld options in total, some named after politicians and celebrities, like the Jackie Chan—bulgogi, cilantro, avocado, lettuce, jalapeños, and onions, served on a roll or hero. There’s also a chicken cutlet sandwich called the Australian. It’s not named after Gollan.

This is not a place to linger, so we keep it moving. Outside, the crowds have thickened, and Gollan instructs us to head to a neighborhood bar called ABC Beer Co., which often features at the end of his tours. As someone who has spent many a night in an East Village bar, I’m disappointed I’ve never been here before. It’s spacious, has a backyard, and is equally welcoming to couples on dates and families with little ones.

The writer's sandwich tour ended at ABC Beer Co, a hybrid beer bar and store with a particular focus on NYC breweries.

Gollan appears with our pho sandwiches, wrapped in spinach tortillas. They smell like pho, taste like pho; only the avocado throws me off.

Some of us get ciders and wine, and the conversation winds back to where we started: So, what really is a sandwich? “I want this to get contentious: bang the tables, let’s have a food fight," Gollan says, egging us on. Hot dogs? Quesadillas? What about a hamburger? A pizza folded in half? Does it have to have a carb? What about a lettuce wrap instead of bread? Gollan briefs us on a famous 2006 Massachusetts lawsuit—White City Shopping Center vs. Panera Bread—which legally answered an age-old culinary debate: Is a burrito a sandwich? The judge ruled that a burrito is, in fact, not a sandwich, clearing the way for the Mexican fast-casual joint to open in the vicinity of Panera Bread. “A sandwich court case is my Roman Empire," he says. “When this question goes to the Supreme Court, I will be there.”

The point of this tour—and the posed question—Gollan says, was never to walk away with an answer, but to open our minds and palates. So, what are Ben Gollan’s own rules for a sandwich, I have to ask. He lists the following:

And then he adds: “Take those rules and throw them in the bin.” And with that, class is dismissed.

The NYC Sandwich Tour can be booked directly on the A Man and His Sandwich website, as well as on Airbnb. Tours run every day of the week, with the exception of Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Ben Gollan, who proudly calls himself the Chief Sandwich Officer, often leads the experiences himself, but he also has co-hosts to help guide fellow sandwich enthusiasts on these two-hour outings. Along the way, guests sample three standout sandwiches—from the classic to the “slightly unhinged”—before finishing up at a bar to settle the debate over what really counts as a sandwich. While my tour focused on the East Village, Gollan also leads sandwich tours around Williamsburg. And word on the street is that he has his eye on opening a sandwich shop of his own one day.

#6293. Avelo Airlines Cancels All 6 International Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Avelo Airlines cut all of its international routes from its network this year, as the airline redeploys its aircraft on domestic routes instead. The airline is a Texas-based ultra-low-cost carrier that has evolved from Xtra Airways and Casino Express Airlines. The carrier, which has a growing number of flights on the US East Coast, has had terrible luck with international services.

Indeed, one just lasted a matter of weeks. All international flights operated by the airline were terminated in January of this year. Many of these routes faced no direct competition.

Being a budget carrier, Avelo offers a basic economy service with extra ancillary services like checked baggage, meals onboard or seat selection coming for a fee. The airline has focused on serving secondary airports, or routes that face no competition. As such, the airline tried its hand in international flying. However, this chapter was ultimately short-lived.

Of its six international routes, three of these were served from Bradley International Airport (BDL), which serves Hartford, Connecticut. A sole international route operated from Wilmington International Airport (ILM) in North Carolina, and the remaining two services were from Raleigh–Durham International Airport (RDU). Their destinations were popular tourist hotspots in the Caribbean.

Avelo's decision to cancel all international services came as part of a major restructuring of the airline's network. It refocused on a back-to-basics domestic strategy after financial losses and fleet changes.

Avelo began operating two international services from Hartford in November 2024, with the airline connecting the city to Cancun International Airport (CUN) and Montego Bay (MBJ). This was quickly followed by a link to the Dominican Republic in February 2025. These were the airline's first regular scheduled international services.

Raleigh joined the pack in February of the same year, with two international services operating to Montego Bay and Punta Cana. These operated for almost a year, before the airline's ultimate termination of all international flying.

Wilmington (ILM) saw its sole international link to Punta Cana go live in December. However, after just a number of short weeks, the airline pulled its aircraft from the route, citing weaker-than-expected demand, and Wilmington lost its sole international route.

Seasonal and year round frequencies are trimmed, forcing travelers to reroute through neighboring airports for connections.

Data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, clearly identifies the painfully low load factors that Avelo faced when operating international flights. Airlines aim for a minimum 80% load factor, which provides enough income to allow the flight to operate at a profit.

Since the airline first launched into international flying, load factors only steadily increased to around 79% in June 2025 before dipping again on the other side of the busy summer travel period. After Avelo's swift exit from international flying, the carrier is now focused on scaling up a number of core domestic bases and has no immediate plans to return to the international skies.

#6292. But Our Flag Was Still There

Imagine a time when Americans could be arrested by soldiers and imprisoned without the opportunity to challenge their detention before a judge. When a former congressman could be tried by a military commission for a political speech, then banished from the country. When newspaper offices could be occupied by troops and publication stopped. Imagine an editor imprisoned in the very fortress his grandfather had immortalized in a song about American freedom.

O say, can you see By the dawn’s early light

I woke up this morning thinking about the question at the beginning of our national anthem.

After an election, we tend to look for answers. This morning, I find myself more interested in what we can still see.

I see a country in which people cast ballots and those ballots have consequences. A country in which officeholders can be challenged and voters can change the direction of government. I see people who care enough to argue, sometimes bitterly, about the future of a place they still believe is worth fighting for.

That is an exhausting way to govern ourselves, but what a remarkable inheritance!

What so proudly we hailed At the twilight’s last gleaming

The president in those opening examples was Abraham Lincoln.

His administration’s restrictions on civil liberties are part of our history, even if they sit uncomfortably alongside the achievements for which we rightly honor him.

Beginning in 1861, Lincoln authorized the suspension of habeas corpus, the means by which a detainee can ask a court to examine the legality of detention. The Constitution permits suspension in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it. Whether the president could exercise that authority without Congress was fiercely contested. The practical consequence was that people could be held by military authorities without the ordinary judicial protection against unlawful imprisonment.

In September 1862, his proclamation, circulated by the War Department as General Orders No. 141, subjected people discouraging enlistment or engaging in broadly described disloyal practices aiding the rebellion to military trial. It also suspended habeas corpus for those detained by military authority.

These were sweeping powers, with consequences far beyond the battlefield.

Whose broad stripes and bright stars Through the perilous fight

In 1863, a former Ohio congressman was arrested after delivering an antiwar speech, tried by a military commission, and convicted. Lincoln changed his punishment from imprisonment to banishment into Confederate territory.

Another critic, a Baltimore newspaper editor, had been arrested in 1861 and confined at Fort McHenry. His grandfather was Francis Scott Key. Think about that for a moment. The grandson of the man who wrote the words we sing about the land of the free became a political prisoner inside the fort associated with those words.

He was a Southern sympathizer. The former congressman’s politics were deeply objectionable in their defense of a slaveholding order. But we do not need to admire either man’s cause to take seriously the government’s treatment of him. Constitutional protections have little substance if they depend on our approval of the person invoking them.

O’er the ramparts we watched Were so gallantly streaming

General Ambrose Burnside ordered the suppression of the Chicago Times in 1863. Lincoln intervened to have that order revoked. That correction belongs in the account as much as the original abuse.

But in 1864, after the New York World and Journal of Commerce published a forged presidential proclamation, Lincoln himself ordered military action against the papers, including seizure of their printing establishments and the arrest of their editors and publishers.

The forgery was serious. So was the use of military power against newspapers.

All of this happened while the country was fighting a rebellion rooted in slavery, with its survival genuinely in doubt. That context is essential to understanding Lincoln’s decisions. Even so, it does not place those decisions beyond scrutiny and reminds us today there is nothing new under the sun.

I can regard Lincoln as a great president and still recoil at some of the powers exercised under his administration. An honest affection for America must leave room for that.

And the rockets’ red glare The bombs bursting in air

Our anthem was born of an actual bombardment. The danger was physical, and the outcome could not yet be known.

We sometimes speak of our own political moment as though we alone have discovered uncertainty. Every alarming development becomes unprecedented. Every election becomes the final opportunity to save the country.

Some warnings deserve our attention. Rights can erode, and institutions can fail. History offers plenty of evidence for the absolute necessity vigilance.

This country has been torn apart by civil war. It has tolerated profound injustice while congratulating itself on liberty. It has denied the protection of its promises to people who had every right to claim them.

And Americans have challenged those failures…often at great personal cost and against a majority quite comfortable with the way things were.

The work has never been easy, and progress has never been secure. The end of slavery did not prevent the injustices that followed. A constitutional promise could exist for generations before people received anything approaching its protection.

But the promise gave people something to demand. It still does.

Gave proof through the night That our flag was still there

I won’t comment on the outcome itself, but I have great hope after an election like this. The system is working. Imperfectly, unevenly, and with people understandably dissatisfied by its results. Yet democracy remains alive. Voters can register disapproval and impose consequences. Political power remains something that must answer to the public.

One election cannot certify the health of an entire republic. It can, however, demonstrate that the mechanisms of accountability still operate. I think we should allow ourselves to recognize that today, across political lines.

I spend much of my life traveling beyond our borders. That has made me more conscious of how much I value the ability to criticize my government openly and expect another opportunity to vote. Neither should be taken for granted.

We have built something very special here. Its failures are real, and so is its capacity for correction.

Repairing what is broken will require patient work long after the election coverage ends. Some damage will take years to undo. Some losses cannot be restored to the people who suffered them.

Still, Americans before us have undertaken that work under circumstances far more desperate than ours. We can honor them by continuing it.

This morning, I feel grateful that the country remains ours to shape. Grateful that disappointment can find expression at a ballot box. And I’m hopeful that we retain enough humility to recognize our mistakes and enough resolve to address them.

The anthem ends with a question. After all this time, it remains a question worth asking ourselves.

O say, does that star-spangled banner yet wave O’er the land of the free and the home of the brave

If you have yet to take a solo trip, there are many reasons why you really should. Solo travel helps you build confidence and new skills. It also provides time to reflect, recharge and reconnect with yourself — so you can return home the best version of yourself for the people who rely on you day-to-day.

I know it can be daunting to embark on your first big trip alone. But never fear, intrepid soloist. I've rounded up the top solo travel mistakes so that you can avoid them to ensure your trip goes smoothly.

Related: Travel mistakes that could ruin your next trip

One of the perks of solo travel is that you get to decide where to stay and what to do, so put some thought into it. This will ensure you have the best trip possible.

A good starting point is to check the State Department travel advisory for your destination, which will help you understand any safety concerns and identify neighborhoods you may want to avoid. It's also a good idea to enroll your trip in STEP, so you'll be alerted to things like natural disasters and security threats.

Safety isn't the only thing to consider. Are you looking for a quiet, relaxing getaway or a bustling neighborhood with endless things to do? Would you rather stay close to the action or save money by staying in a less popular area? Choose your accommodations accordingly.

Don't make the mistake I made on my first solo trip and not plan any activities. Spontaneity sounded fun, but I found making decisions on my own much harder than expected. You don't need to have your entire itinerary planned out to the minute, but doing some planning before you travel will reduce your stress during the trip.

Plus, many popular tourist attractions and trendy restaurants fill up quickly — and waiting in long lines is even less fun with no one to talk to. Do your research, and if needed, make a reservation or book a timed-entry ticket ahead of time.

Sometimes, the difference between traveling solo and with others really shines through in the little things...like using an airport bathroom.

You can't simply ask a companion to hold your luggage while you run to the restroom or figure out how to operate a metro ticket machine; you must keep track of it at all times. So think twice about packing that extra-large checked bag or hauling a not-so-ergonomic shoulder duffel on an international trip, as you will have to take it with you literally everywhere.

I personally prefer a backpack and small rolling carryon, which I can easily maneuver through crowded airports and over cobblestoned streets — without reaching my destination with a backache. Plus, it's big enough to accommodate sufficient clothing for a week (or more). My carryon is expandable, so if I buy too many souvenirs, I can unzip the extender and check it on the way home.

Related: How to pack your carryon right and avoid checking a bag

Connecting with new people is one of the many joys of solo travel, but that doesn't mean you should completely let your guard down. You may run into pickpockets, con artists and worse on your journey, and as a solo traveler, you're more likely to be targeted.

One simple step to reduce your risk is by not broadcasting your solo status. Err on the side of caution when chatting with new friends — and if they start getting nosy, tell them you're meeting up with friends later.

One way to prevent hotel staff from knowing your single status is opting for mobile check-in so that you can bypass the front desk completely. Or, you can ask the concierge for an extra key and allude that someone will be joining you shortly. And when catching a ride to or from your accommodation, it's a good idea to be picked up or dropped off down the street from your hotel.

Related: Solo travel safety tips every traveler should know

You only want to be incognito to the locals.

Let your actual friends and family know your travel plans: flight numbers, where you'll be staying on which dates, contact info for your tour operator, etc. You'll be glad you did if you hit a snag and need help rebooking on the fly. You can go a step further by sending them a copy of your passport or ID, in case you lose your documents while traveling.

You'll probably want to stay in contact with loved ones through text messages, phone calls or social media posts every so often. But you can also share your location continuously with apps like Find My, which can help ease their minds as well as give you an added layer of security. That way, both you and your loved ones can enjoy your trip stress-free.

Some things are must-haves no matter how many people you're traveling with, but they become even more critical when you're on your own — because if you forget something, you can't just reach into a companion's suitcase.

For instance, do you have a backup plan in case your phone dies while you're navigating a new city or road-tripping through an unfamiliar country? You can't simply borrow someone else's phone, so a charged power bank or old-fashioned map can come in clutch.

The same goes if you wind up at a store that doesn't accept your credit card. Always pack a couple of backup cards (preferably ones that don't charge foreign transaction fees) and keep some cash on hand.

Similarly, if you catch a cold on your flight or get food poisoning during a solo trip, there's no one else to run to a drugstore. And if you hurt yourself while out hiking alone, it may take a while for help to arrive. Prepare yourself for anything with a travel-ready first-aid kit.

Related: Travel essentials that can save your trip when things go wrong

One of the downsides of solo travel is that it can start to feel lonely, especially on longer trips. Making new friends is a great way to combat loneliness, as well as learn more about local culture and/or meet likeminded travelers.

If striking up a conversation with a stranger sounds more stressful than fun, you're not alone. Thankfully, there are plenty of ways for even the shyest travelers to make connections, including cruises and small-group tours designed specifically for solo travelers.

Female Travel Buddies is one of many Facebook groups ideal for those flying solo: Members post open invitations for fellow travelers in the same area to join you for brunch, sightseeing or a show. If this type of thing interests you, consider joining a handful of groups a few months ahead of your trip to get familiar with the members and learn how they work.

Related: 6 tips for meeting people when traveling solo

Just because you're traveling alone doesn't mean you can't take photos along the way — but capturing memories can be trickier by yourself.

The good news is you don't have to be limited by the length of your arm. Be sure to pack a selfie stick, mini tripod with remote shutter or selfie monitor screen. You'll find it well worth the investment, as having the right tools will make it far easier to snap the perfect selfie. (Just remember: safety first, especially when hiking, taking selfies near cliff edges, etc.!)

If, like me, you feel a little awkward or uncomfortable taking selfies alone, the best advice I can give you is to do it anyway. The more you do it, the more comfortable you'll get and the better your photos will turn out.

Solo travel doesn't have to be daunting. Follow these tips to embark on your first solo trip with confidence and ensure it goes smoothly, and before you know it, you'll be a seasoned solo traveler.

#6290. There's a New Luxury Sleeper Train Route Coming to the French Riviera Next Spring

As someone who travels a lot for work, I would give anything to swap a flight for a train—even if that means spending eight hours on the rails.

Thankfully, it's easy to travel Europe by train at nearly any price point. And although I am a big fan of modern high-speed routes, the most romantic way to see the continent is certainly aboard one of Belmond's gorgeous luxury trains, which travel to destinations such as the British countryside, the Amalfi Coast, and the Scottish Highlands.

But in 2027, my bucket-list Belmond journey is a glamorous new addition to its already impressive collection of itineraries: the French Riviera.

The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express offers three cabin types: Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites.

On May 10, 2027, the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is launching a new route from Paris to Monaco, traveling to Monte Carlo for the first time in its history.

The journey, which will become a regular addition to the train's annual schedule, will take passengers through some of the most spectacular scenery along the French Riviera before arriving in the glamorous principality.

The new route will take travelers to Monte Carlo for the first time in the train's history.

The experience begins in Paris, where passengers will board the train's distinctive midnight blue carriages before settling into their accommodation for the night. There are several options to choose from, including the classic Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites, each drawing inspiration from the train's Art Deco heritage.

For those looking to really splash out, there's also L'Observatoire, an exclusive carriage created in collaboration with French artist JR. Designed as a private sanctuary on the rails, it comes complete with a bedroom, an en-suite bathroom featuring a freestanding bathtub, a spacious living area, a library, and even a secret tearoom.

As evening approaches, guests can enjoy dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord and L'Oriental, before heading to the famous Bar Car 3674 for cocktails and live piano music.

But perhaps the most exciting part of the new journey comes the following morning. After waking up to breakfast served in their cabins, passengers will be treated to sweeping views of the Mediterranean as the train makes its way along the Côte d'Azur. The route passes the red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and travels through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice. The train will then continue towards Monaco before arriving at Monaco-Monte-Carlo station.

Breakfast served aboard the Venice-Simplon Orient Express.

Monte Carlo also has a surprising connection to the train's history. In 1977, two original train carriages were purchased at an auction in the principality, helping set in motion the project that would eventually become the luxury train we know today.

“Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival,” says Pascal Deyrolle, Belmond's Europe area managing director for trains. “There's also something rather special about coming back to Monte Carlo, given the role it played in the train's history.”

The new journey is part of Belmond's expanding collection of European rail experiences, alongside the second year of its “Villeggiatura by Train” itinerary, which connects the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express with Belmond hotels in Italy.

Of course, a journey this luxurious comes with a price tag to match. Tickets for the new Paris-to-Monte-Carlo route start from €4,870 (approximately $5,450) per person, based on two people sharing a Historic Cabin. The fare includes the overnight journey, all meals with sommelier-selected wines, unlimited soft drinks, transfers, and 24-hour steward service.

A version of this article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6289. On Location: How Coastal Newfoundland Set the Scene for Netflix's No. 1 Series ‘Below’

A mysterious sea creature is captivating audiences on Netflix as the Josh Hartnett-led series Below remains the No. 1 show in Netflix’s global rankings. The six-episode thriller paints an eerie image of small-town life in Newfoundland, and viewers are intrigued by the mystique of the striking Canadian backdrop.

Despite the fictional giant squid terrorizing Snook’s Arm, the show pulls on elements of reality, from climate change affecting the Atlantic Canadian sea life to the government-run resettling of remote fishing towns, which started in 1954 and continues to this day. It’s that history that drew production designer Emmanuel Fréchette into the project.

“When I found out that more than 300 towns in Newfoundland had been resettled, I was amazed,” he tells Traveler. “The script is very interesting, mixing that reality with the mundane life in Newfoundland—and this creature!” After all, creator Jesse McKeown (The Umbrella Academy) had frequented the region for years, inspired to bring an authentic depiction of its culture to the screen.

That started behind the scenes as the cast and crew engaged in Newfoundland and Labrador’s most famous tradition. Visitors, who they called CFAs (or Come from Aways—this is also where Broadway hit musical draws its name), get “screeched in” by kissing a cod to become honorary citizens. So they all went to St. John’s Christian’s Pub to pucker up. “The guy there is such a great character, and he has a routine and speech that’s very entertaining," Fréchette says.

When it came to filming locations, the remote regions posed practical challenges, so the majority of the sets were built by production, a joy for Fréchette, who was trained as an architect. “I was stunned by the humble architecture, built by boat owners and builders,” he says of the homes’ low ceilings. “The structures are very endearing and make you think of a boat, so I wanted to follow that thread.”

That’s also what helped root the fantastical storyline into reality. “This was vernacular architecture—architecture without architects—just following the needs of the people out of survival, and I found that so beautiful,” he says. “So I really tried to mimic what I was seeing all around me that survived the decades.”

And it’s clearly had an effect on audiences. According to data provided by Booking.com, not only have searches for the province’s capital of St. John’s risen 16.9% by Americans on the platform compared to last year, but the coastal town of Twillingate, home to the floating icebergs, has skyrocketed 123.7%.

Here, Fréchette shares the filming locations from the popular Netflix series Below.

The show is set in the actual resettled town of Snook’s Arm, which had a population of 10 when it was approved for resettlement in 2017, according to the CBC. But its remote location would have been difficult to film in with such a big crew, so Brigus South—a town with a population of about 700 at last count in 2021—stood in.

“We picked that place because it had a connection with the water,” Fréchette says of the inlet going deep into the land. “Lots of the characters are dragged into the water, so it was great to have this presence for the eeriness.”

But to get the cozy town ready for its close-up took work, as the crew designed and built about 80% of what appears in the series, including the fish plant, Fishermen’s Hall, and wharf. The Penneys home was an existing home they covered, and the church was also a house that they retrofitted, adding the bell tower.

When Fréchette was scouting locations, he stayed in a hostel by the sea in Twillingate, about 275 miles northwest of the capital. “We’d be having a coffee with the window open, and suddenly we were freezing,” he recalls of a sudden drop in temperature from 68 degrees Fahrenheit to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s when they’d look up and see an iceberg floating their way. “It lowers the temperature all around the bay—it’s such an amazing phenomenon.”

As it turns out, the Atlantic town sits along Iceberg Alley, where from late April through July, the remnants of broken glaciers glide down the coast. Many of the shots of Calvin (Hartnett) harvesting icebergs were actual footage from these massive blocks of ice naturally floating along.

The capital served as the home base for the cast and crew, who were spread out across hotels and home rentals during filming. But its Ocean Sciences Centre, about 30 minutes north of downtown, found the spotlight as one of the most striking structures in the series, the marine research center where Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) worked.

While Fréchette admits it took some work to convince the operating facility to shoot there, he’s excited it worked out because “it really adds production value and is a great location.” After all, the circular wooden structure reflects that government building architect of the 1960s and early 1970s, “at a time we were dreaming and imagining things beyond what was possible to build today.” Reminiscent of designs by Canadian architects like Arthur Erikson, he adds that “it was ambitious, but it had a vision—and is fantastic!”

About 20 miles north of St. John’s at the top of the Avalon Peninsula sits Pouch Cove, a town of about 2,000 residents. The art director told Fréchette about the Pouch Cove Heritage Society, a historical building that was closed since they were fundraising to preserve it, so one weekend, they went up to visit. “The floor was sunken in and it was structurally unsafe,” he says.

The show’s head carpenter and engineer got to work, fixing it up, temporarily transforming it into the interior of Below’s Fisherman’s Hall, while permanently restoring it for the community. “It was a win-win because they were happy to get the money from the location, but also the work we did on it was helpful for them.”

When Calvin returns to his abandoned childhood town of Little Pot Rock, that dilapidated setting was an actual resettled town, about a 30-minute drive down from Pouch Cove on a dirt road that the production had to grade in order to shoot there.

“It was quite tricky, but just stunning—really wild and rugged,” Fréchette says, calling it “the most amazing location.” All that was there was one tiny house, about 12 by 20 feet, but it never showed up on camera. Instead, the production custom built all of the Budgell family’s dwellings. But the area can be visited as part of a 4.3-mile hike along the East Coast Trail.

The fishing village of Bay Bulls is home to North America’s largest Atlantic puffin colony, as well as a prime whale watching destination. But for Below, it was all about the functional purpose of its Pennecon Marine Base. Though it never shows up on screen, its industrial harbor was essential in order to dock the boat used as the research vessel since it had a draft (depth) of nearly 10 feet, and they needed an appropriate spot that the cast and crew could board. Also shot here were the exterior scenes of the submersible, which was hung from the boat by a crane and lifted onto the dock.

Pittman’s fish farm played an integral part of the plot, as Calvin confirmed that the sea creature was real—but it turns out the location was landlocked. “It was very complicated to do this on the sea because we’d have to deal with tides and storms, so we decided to cheat it on a lake in Brigus,” he says of the town that’s actually about 60 miles northwest from Brigus South. There was no actual fish farm there, so they custom-built the floating dock and cabin.

While the outside of Linda’s Bar was filmed using a retrofitted Brigus South home, the interior was actually the Rising Tide Convenience shop in the town of Harbour Main, about 33 miles southwest of St. John’s. The local business, best known for its homemade ice cream, “looked great inside, so we dressed it up,” Fréchette says, taking extra care to ensure the exterior entrance they built flowed seamlessly between cuts. As for Noah (Kaleb Horn)’s on-screen screech-in? That was a prop, but an actual frozen fish to ensure the fish kiss was genuine.
