#6288. United Airlines First Class Steak And Eggs: Great Steak, But Where Were The Eggs?

United Airlines served me excellent cubed steak for breakfast on a recent flight from Chicago to Houston. The problem with its steak and eggs dish? The missing eggs.

For this week’s Meal of the Week, I want to highlight a breakfast that I would happily order again, even though one part of it was very disappointing. On a recent flight from Chicago O’Hare (ORD) to Houston (IAH), I selected the steak and eggs, described on the menu as:

Steak and eggs with home fries and chimichurri sauce

The tray was nicely presented, with sliced steak topped with chimichurri, potatoes, and what I expected would be an egg soufflé.

The steak was excellent for airplane red meat. The chimichurri worked very well with the beef, and this was the highlight of the meal.

Unfortunately, instead of the egg soufflé I expected, I received something much closer to bread pudding…in fact, it was the same bread pudding I had out of Chicago a couple months ago. There may have been egg binding it together, but it had virtually no discernible egg texture or flavor. It was like eating bread.

You can see the bread cubes in the photo. This was not simply a soufflé that turned out a little firmer than expected. Bread dominated the portion that was supposed to provide the eggs in my steak and eggs.

That was disappointing, especially because the steak was so good and because I try to limit my carbs. I hope United can address this with its catering out of Chicago, as I’ve seen other reports of the same problem (this wasn’t a one-off). An actual egg component would make this a much more satisfying breakfast and match the menu…

The accompaniments were better. The chocolate croissant was served warm and was excellent. Between that and the bread pudding, I certainly had enough bread on the tray…

The fruit was ripe, and the Chobani vanilla Greek yogurt was decent. I would prefer a no-sugar-added Greek yogurt, but at least this one provided 10 grams of protein.

The coffee was strong, which was also appreciated. I also requested orange juice, though I must confess that was more to add color to the tray for the photo. I did not drink it.

I would order United’s steak and eggs again. The steak with chimichurri was excellent, and the warm chocolate croissant was great. But United needs to fix the egg issue out of ORD. There is a good breakfast here. It just needs the eggs its name promises.

#6287. Delta Plans Another Austin Route

Delta is expanding its Austin, Texas, network with a new daily route set to launch next spring.

The carrier will begin flights between Austin and Northwest Arkansas National Airport, which serves Fayetteville and the surrounding region, on March 7, 2027. SkyWest will operate the route under the Delta Connection brand using an Embraer E175.

Service from Northwest Arkansas to Austin begins March 8. Tickets are now on sale.

Flights will depart Austin at 8:59 p.m. and arrive in Northwest Arkansas at 10:49 p.m. The return flight will leave at 6 a.m. and arrive in Austin at 7:50 a.m. All times are local.

“Connecting Central Texas and Northwest Arkansas with new nonstop service brings two dynamic, growing regions closer together while giving our customers even more choice and convenience,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement.

Guitart described the addition as another example of the airline’s investment in Austin.

Delta has been building its Austin operation, with plans to offer more than 70 peak-day departures to approximately 30 destinations by summer 2027. That expansion includes new service to Paris and San Diego, a second daily flight to San Jose, California, and year-round service to Cancun, Mexico.

#6286. Why the Algerian Sahara Should Be Your Next Off-Grid Adventure

I woke up in the small hours of the night. Orion’s Belt was directly above where I lay on a thin roll-up mattress, zipped into a canvas sleeping bag. The hunter’s three luminous studs stood out in a canopy awash with stars from horizon to horizon, the Milky Way a glittery paint stroke across the scene. Aside from an occasional shuffle or snuffle from my fellow campers, the night was draped in a thick blanket of stress-shrinking quiet. It’d been days since I had cell reception. I could practically hear my nervous system thanking me.

A breathtaking canopy of stars illuminates the vast Algerian Sahara.

You don’t need to sleep al fresco while camping in the Sahara Desert—I could crawl back inside my own pop-up dome tent at any time—but I’d certainly recommend it. It was a highlight of my trip to Algeria’s tranche of this continent-spanning desert.

I was in the Sahara on a nine-day tour with Explore Worldwide, a UK-based small-group tour company, which began running trips to Algeria earlier this year, partly as a reaction to the country’s new, albeit cautious, encouragement of tourism. I wanted to find out what that development looked like on the ground and experience the desert region that hopes to attract new visitors.

Algeria is one of our Best Places to Go in Africa in 2026. Find our full guide here.

Africa’s largest country is hard to miss on a map, but all but one of the 10 well-traveled people in my group (mostly British and 60-years-plus) were first-timers in Algeria. Traditionally, the economy here has been driven by the oil and gas sector, and the development of tourism has been of little interest to the government. This has led to a fraction of the arriving tourists received by other North African countries such as Morocco or Egypt; roughly a third of its visitors are members of the diaspora coming to visit and stay with family. But recently, a push to diversify the economy has led to the launch of an ambitious “master plan” to increase arrivals four-fold by 2030, with a special focus on desert tourism.

Although the majority of projects (such as much-needed new hotels) remain in-progress, the government has introduced visas on arrival for people spending the majority of their time in the Sahara—an option taken by nearly 39,000 visitors since 2023, contributing to an uptick in arrivals. I took advantage of the scheme myself. After an hour or so in the capital Algiers’ Houari Boumediene International Airport—queuing, waiting, and nervously watching an official wander around with my passport—I paid my fee in cash ($150 for 10 days), my passport was stamped, and I was warmly welcomed to Algeria.

Algiers' iconic Casbah is the most ancient quarter of the city—and well worth exploring for its winding alleys and traditional Ottoman-style architecture.

The trip kicked off with an Algiers city tour, giving us a brief but necessary taste of the country’s culture and history before we flew into the desert. I arrived early for a little solo exploration, allowing me to wander the cool, peaceful paths of the lush Hamma Botanical Garden, and enjoy a bowl of rechta (thin noodles with chicken in a clear broth) in the intimate lounge of El Walima Restaurant.

With our tour guide Wassim Messgo, we walked through the narrow lanes of the Casbah—the UNESCO-listed historic center—past a smattering of souvenir stalls, and visited the hard-hitting National Museum of the Mujahid—dedicated to the bloody war for independence from France between 1954 and 1962. I could’ve spent longer in Algiers and want to return to see other cities in the north. Messgo recommended Constantine: “You get Roman ruins in other parts of the region,” he said, “but not in a city like this.”

But my focus for this trip was the Sahara.

The Algerian government has introduced visas on arrival for people spending the majority of their time in the Sahara.

Algiers to Djanet—a little oasis town in Algeria’s southeast near the Libya and Niger borders—is a two-hour flight, usually scheduled in the middle of the night (to avoid desert winds during the day, so I was told). On arrival, I was reminded of Algeria’s high levels of security, partly due to fluctuating tensions with neighboring countries, particularly Morocco at present. Our passports were collected and our names ticked off against a list that linked us with our guide: Aissa Khirani, a Djanet native who’s spent the past 20 years leading tours locally and across Africa. Khirani told me that guides have to submit their plans to the military, including the identities of guests and staff, along with car registration numbers.

In addition to being a military hub, Djanet is the tourism gateway to this swathe of the Sahara. Our flight was perhaps half tourists—but for the five days we were in the desert, we encountered only six other vehicles. This was a benefit of traveling with a guide who knew his way around, while having a flexible itinerary so we could avoid other travelers—and account for unexpected weather events.

Djanet is a little oasis town in Algeria’s southeast near the Libya and Niger borders, and a gateway to the Sahara.

As we drove around the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau over the following five days, the landscape varied with surprising frequency—Mars-like rocky flats; sandy canyons edged by colossal rock formations; sweeping seas of peachy dunes with crisp ridgelines and wind-rippled faces. Camels, many belonging to Touareg nomads, grazed on sparse patches of vegetation. Caves and overhangs here have protected at least 15,000 examples of rock art, some thought to be 10,000 years old, depicting people hunting or dancing, giraffes, cattle, and jars possibly for carrying water as the region dried up.

We eased into desert life with two nights at something close to a glamping site—shared with a couple of other guests—which had tents you could stand up in, thick mattresses, even charging units. For the following three nights, we camped among the dunes and at the base of hulking rockfaces that resembled elephant skin. Our mobile set-up consisted of basic tents, a dining table by the campfire, and a “bathroom”—a chair with a cut-out seat in a canvas cubicle.

Camping at the base of the hulking rockfaces of the Algerian Sahara

Tents come with comfortable mattresses, extra seating, even charging units

“To be honest, I don't want Algeria to be like Morocco or Tunisia or Egypt,” Khirani told me, as we drove out of Djanet in a convoy of four Toyota four-wheel-drives, echoing sentiments Messgo had also shared. Both guides spoke about how relaxed Algeria currently feels for visitors; when I visited Djanet’s market, for example, we’d been greeted but otherwise left alone to browse the stalls of jewelry and fabrics.

As for the desert, Khirani continued, it still feels remote. “The desert to me means peace of mind,” he said. “It’s a sensation like emptiness, but with it a kind of happiness that you cannot describe.” He hopes to protect that experience, while encouraging tourism “in a smart way.”

The shifting shades and surfaces of the desert dunes

Caves and overhangs in the region have protected at least 15,000 examples of rock art, some thought to be 10,000 years old.

While I had precious moments of solitude—sitting on a dune at sunrise, submerged in quietness as the sand turned cool beige to warm caramel—many of my favorite memories are of people: Hemaya baking bread in the sand under hot coals; driver Ali Lazghem playing the same four songs on repeat and letting other drivers know exactly how he felt when they stalled at the top of a dune he was powering up; the whole team excited to see a locally famous and yet unnamed rock formation that features on the cover of Lonely Planet’s latest Algeria guide for the first time.

Back in Djanet, at the end of our off-grid adventure, I was finally able to shower again. I knew one wash wouldn’t be enough to fully de-grit my hair—at that stage, almost solid with desert debris—and that I’d be tapping out orange sand from my shoes for days. But that’s the thing about time in the desert. It tends to stick with you, in more ways than one.

I traveled with Explore Worldwide on their nine-day Algeria’s Sahara Desert Adventure tour, which begins and ends in the capital Algiers. Prices start at $2,410 (excluding international flights, which are typically via hubs such as Paris or London). The package includes accommodation, most meals and activities, including a day-tour of Algiers and five nights camping in the Sahara Desert; don’t expect guides to keep strictly to the itinerary, but you’ll certainly spend plenty of time in scenic parts of the Sahara, see several examples of rock art, and be treated to warm hospitality and tasty food throughout. If you want to explore the northern cities too, you can do Explore’s two-week Ancient Algeria and the Sahara Desert tour. In Algiers, the comfortable El Aurassi is considered one of the best hotels, though service and style fall short of a standard five-star experience. For a visa on arrival, tour operators will provide the required authorization letter—otherwise you can apply for a visa from your nearest Algerian embassy. Bring dollars to exchange for Algerian dinars when you arrive (ATMs are unreliable), as cards aren’t commonly accepted. Exporting dinars is prohibited. Also note that it’s illegal to carry binoculars and drones into Algeria.

#6285. What Is the UNESCO Tentative List, and How Do You Get on It?

With a total of 27 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the United States is peppered full of sites of wonder. There's the Statue of Liberty, the patinated icon that has served as the first face millions of immigrants saw once they reached the country's shores and the San Antonio Missions in Texas which were first constructed the 18th century. Beyond manmade wonders, UNESCO has also recognized natural sites such as the Florida Everglades and the Grand Canyon. There's no shortage of modern marvels and breathtaking landscapes to behold in the US, which leads us to ask, how does a destination gain recognition as a UNESCO World Heritage Site? The process begins with the UNESCO Tentative List, which puts the best of the best up for consideration.

The Tentative List, as the name suggests, comprises natural and cultural properties that a country considers to have the potential to be recognized as World Heritage. It is not a confirmation that a site has been selected for inscription, only the first step towards a formal nomination, which is drawn up subsequently in the process. To qualify for World Heritage status, a property must demonstrate Outstanding Universal Value (OUV), meaning its cultural or natural significance ought to be considered exceptional from an international perspective. A site’s inclusion on the Tentative List places it in the position to be examined further for its potential OUV. This process enables a stronger foundation of vetting for the final nominations that a country draws up.

Even if a site included in a Tentative List is not nominated during one evaluatory round, there’s always a chance in the future that it may be added back to the list and considered for a nomination. The list is updated at any time per the country’s discretion, but each included site must undergo a separate nomination and evaluation process before qualifying for the World Heritage List. Once a site is inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage, it is removed from the Tentative List.

At the heart of UNESCO’s World Heritage process is the concept of Outstanding Universal Value (OUV). In simple terms, this means a place must be significant beyond its own country, and its cultural or natural importance must be exceptional enough to matter to people around the world, including future generations. A site must demonstrate this value against at least one of UNESCO’s 10 selection criteria, whether for its contribution to human history and culture, its geological features, its ecological processes or its biodiversity.

The cultural criteria include sites that represent exceptional examples of human creativity, demonstrate an important exchange of human values, bear testimony to cultural traditions or civilizations, or illustrate significant stages in human history. They also cover traditional settlements and landscapes, as well as properties associated with events, living traditions, beliefs, and works of outstanding universal significance.

The natural criteria consider exceptional natural beauty, significant stages in the Earth’s geological history, ongoing ecological and biological processes, and habitats important for conserving biodiversity.

Meeting one or more criteria is not enough on its own. A proposed property must also satisfy the relevant conditions of authenticity and integrity, alongside requirements for protection and management. Its inclusion must make a case for why its significance is exceptional in a global context, including through comparisons with similar properties.

It’s important to note that UNESCO’s 10 criteria are regularly revised to reflect the evolving understanding of World Heritage.

Countries identify properties they consider to have potential OUV and may eventually nominate for World Heritage status. UNESCO encourages them to involve a broad range of stakeholders in preparing their Tentative Lists, including site managers, local communities, government bodies, and non-governmental organizations. The process is led by each country, so the extent and nature of consultation can vary.

Currently, the US has 17 sites on their Tentative List, with nominations dating from 2008 and 2017. The US has submitted both cultural and natural sites for consideration with locales raning from the country's Pacific territories to Alabama. Below are the current contenders on the Tentative List, according to the National Park Service.

The country must still decide whether to proceed with a formal nomination and prepare the documentation required to demonstrate the property’s OUV. This includes establishing how the site meets the relevant selection criteria, documenting its authenticity and integrity, outlining the measures in place to protect it, and presenting a management framework. The nomination must also explain how the property compares with other sites of similar significance.

The country, not UNESCO, decides which properties to nominate for World Heritage status. Once a site on the Tentative List is formally nominated, independent advisory bodies assess its significance and conservation measures. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee then makes the final decision on whether to inscribe it on the World Heritage List.

#6284. 10 Classic Airliners That Needed A Third Person In The Cockpit

Swissair | Wikimedia Commons | Simple Flying

A third seat in an airliner’s cockpit can tell you a surprising amount about the machine itself. On some jets the person occupying it was often a flight engineer, responsible for monitoring and managing systems that modern flight crews now take for granted . On others, the job became so closely tied to the aircraft that the engineer’s station was almost as recognizable as the engines or the silhouette.

The flight engineer’s place in the cockpit did not disappear overnight, and the aircraft that carried one were far from interchangeable. Some made the role part of everyday long-haul operations; others pushed it into unusual territory. This countdown features ten classic airliners that were designed or operated with three crew members in the cockpit. The selection is based on that crew configuration, rather than requiring every aircraft to use the same title or staffing arrangement for its third crew member. The aircraft are ranked by their historical influence, fleet size, and the lasting place the third cockpit position held in their identity.

The Douglas DC-6 first flew on June 29, 1946, and entered airline service with American Airlines and United Airlines in 1947. More than 700 examples were eventually built, making it one of the most successful large piston-powered airliners of the postwar era. Its four Pratt & Whitney R-2800 radial engines, pressurized cabin, and long-range capability helped airlines expand their domestic and international networks. NASA's aviation history covers the aircraft's introduction and commercial impact.

The DC-6's cockpit required a minimum crew of three: a pilot, copilot, and flight engineer. The engineer monitored the four engines and managed the aircraft's systems, taking on responsibilities that would otherwise have added to the pilots' workload. Delta initially operated the aircraft with two pilots, but federal regulations soon required a third cockpit crew member. The Delta Flight Museum documents that change, and the aircraft's operating manual specifies the minimum three-person crew.

The DC-6 ranks tenth because it represents the postwar expansion of the traditional three-person cockpit. Its combination of four complex piston engines and long-distance operations made the flight engineer an important part of airline operations, setting the stage for the larger piston airliners and early jets that followed.

The Douglas DC-8 first flew on May 30, 1958, and entered commercial service with Delta Air Lines on September 18, 1959. One of the first American jetliners designed for long-range passenger operations, it combined four underwing engines with a pressurized cabin and the speed needed to transform transcontinental and international travel. Douglas eventually built 556 examples, including the stretched Super 60 series. The FAA's historical chronology records the aircraft's development and entry into service, while Boeing's historical archive preserves its first-flight history.

The DC-8 retained a three-person flight deck, with a captain, first officer, and flight engineer. Seated behind the pilots, the engineer monitored the four engines and managed systems including fuel, electrical power, hydraulics, and pressurization. The aircraft's type certificate specified a minimum crew of three, making the engineer an integral part of its approved operating configuration.

The DC-8 ranks ninth because it brought the traditional flight engineer's station into the first generation of successful American jetliners. Its long passenger and cargo career also showed how enduring that arrangement would be: even as jet technology advanced, the third cockpit position remained standard throughout the DC-8's production life.

The DC-8, a rival to the Boeing 707, defied the odds and continued flying cargo missions well into the 2020s, outlasting its competitor by decades.

The Lockheed Constellation first flew on January 9, 1943, initially as a military aircraft, before entering commercial service with TWA in 1946. Its pressurized cabin, long-range capability, and distinctive triple-tail design made it one of the defining airliners of the postwar period. Later versions, particularly the Super Constellation, introduced improved engines and greater operating range. The Smithsonian's Lockheed Constellation collection record documents the aircraft's development and its first flight.

The Constellation also helped establish the flight engineer as an important member of the long-distance airline crew. Operating four large piston engines while monitoring fuel distribution, electrical systems, and other aircraft functions demanded considerable technical knowledge. A dedicated engineer's station allowed these responsibilities to be separated from the pilots' flying duties, particularly during lengthy oceanic operations. The Airline History Museum's Constellation archive provides additional aircraft history and restoration information.

The Constellation ranks eighth because it helped establish the traditional three-person cockpit as a practical arrangement for long-range commercial aircraft. Its engineer's position represented a growing specialization within airline flight crews.

The Tupolev Tu-154 first flew on October 4, 1968, and entered Aeroflot service in February 1972. More than 1,000 were eventually built, making it a standard Soviet and later Russian medium-haul airliner. Its designers wanted a relatively lean flight crew of captain, first officer, and flight engineer, at a time when other Soviet airliners routinely carried four or five people up front. The Tu-154B-2 could be flown by three crew members, because Hungary's Malév judged larger crews economically unacceptable. Simple Flying notes that the Tu-154 filled nearly the same role in the Eastern Bloc that the 727 played in the West.

Navigation requirements meant that many Tu-154 operations retained a dedicated navigator in addition to the engineer. The navigator and flight engineer occupied separate workstations, illustrating how cockpit staffing differed between Soviet and Western aviation. The German Federal Bureau of Aircraft Accident Investigation's report on the 2002 Überlingen collision documents the positions of the Tu-154M's navigator and engineer. Crew arrangements varied by operator and version.

The Tu-154 ranks seventh because it demonstrates that the three-person cockpit was not a universal solution. Its long production life and continued use of additional specialists highlight the different approaches to cockpit staffing that existed during the jet age.

BA Concorde first flew on March 2, 1969, and began scheduled passenger service in January 1976 with British Airways and Air France. Its flight crew consisted of a captain, first officer and flight engineer. Cruising at approximately 1,350 mph (2,170 km/h) and reaching altitudes of around 60,000 feet (18,300 m), it presented technical challenges unlike those of an ordinary subsonic airliner.

The engineer occupied a dedicated station behind the pilots, monitoring fuel, electrical, hydraulic, air-conditioning, and engine systems. Fuel management was particularly important because fuel was transferred between tanks to control the aircraft's center of gravity as it accelerated and decelerated. Warren Hazelby, a former Lockheed L-1011 flight engineer who later worked on Concorde, described the aircraft's complexity in a CNN interview about his experience operating the supersonic jet.

Concorde ranks sixth because it demonstrates how essential the flight engineer could remain even in a technologically advanced aircraft. Only 20 were built, including development aircraft, but the third crew member remained part of its commercial operation until retirement in 2003.

How the L-1011-500 pioneered long-haul thin routes, using innovative design and extended range to fill a unique aviation niche.

The Lockheed L-1011 TriStar first flew on November 16, 1970, and entered service with Eastern Air Lines in April 1972. Lockheed built 250 examples, and the aircraft became known for its advanced flight-control technology and relatively quiet operation. Despite having an advanced autopilot capable of automatic landings, the TriStar retained a three-person cockpit. Lockheed's own historical account of the L-1011 describes its advanced automatic flight-control system and the technical ambitions behind the aircraft.

The flight engineer monitored the aircraft's complex mechanical and electrical systems, including fuel, hydraulics, and engine performance. The importance of crew coordination became particularly evident during Eastern Air Lines Flight 401 in December 1972. While the crew investigated a landing-gear indicator problem, attention shifted away from monitoring the aircraft's flight path. The FAA's account of the Flight 401 accident explains how the crew became distracted while troubleshooting the indicator and failed to monitor the aircraft's flight path. The accident helped shape later thinking about crew resource management. The TriStar's engines brought their own challenges, as the Rolls-Royce RB211 program experienced major development difficulties that delayed the aircraft's introduction.

The TriStar ranks fifth because it demonstrated that sophisticated automation did not immediately make the flight engineer redundant. Even one of the most advanced airliners of its generation continued to rely on a dedicated systems specialist.

The McDonnell Douglas DC-10 first flew on August 29, 1970, and entered service with American Airlines on August 5, 1971. Its flight deck was designed for three people: a captain, copilot, and flight engineer. The engineer occupied a dedicated panel behind the pilots, monitoring systems that included fuel, electrical power, hydraulics, and engine performance. The DC-10 was developed as a widebody trijet, with two engines mounted beneath the wings and a third installed at the base of the vertical tail. This arrangement provided the capacity and range airlines wanted while meeting the long-haul regulatory environment of the period.

The flight engineer's responsibilities included monitoring fuel distribution, electrical buses, and hydraulic systems, as well as helping identify abnormal conditions. According to Boeing, the later MD-10 conversion introduced a modern glass cockpit, allowing the removal of the flight engineer's position.

The DC-10 ranks fourth because it illustrates both the importance and eventual disappearance of the flight engineer's position. The DC-10's passenger career gradually ended as more efficient widebody aircraft replaced it, although freighter operations continued for decades. Its long service history makes it one of the clearest examples of the transition from traditional three-person flight decks to modern two-pilot cockpits.

The Boeing 727 first flew on February 9, 1963, and entered service with Eastern Air Lines on February 1, 1964. It became the first commercial jetliner to pass 1,000 sales, with production eventually reaching 1,832 aircraft before ending in 1984. The type required a three-person flight deck, with the engineer seated sideways behind the pilots. Its distinctive arrangement of three rear-mounted engines allowed Boeing to deliver the performance airlines wanted without placing engines beneath the wings. The aircraft's integrated rear airstair and sophisticated high-lift system also made it attractive for operations at airports with limited ground facilities and relatively short runways.

The 727's third engine emerged from a compromise among United Airlines, American and Eastern. United wanted strong performance at hot-and-high airports such as Denver, while Eastern needed an aircraft suitable for overwater operations. Many smaller airports offered runways of just 4,500 feet (1,372 m), which the 727's triple-slotted flaps helped it handle. Its systems remained complex enough to require a dedicated engineer, who monitored engine instruments and the fuel, electrical, and hydraulic systems. Boeing's historical aircraft collection provides further information about the aircraft's development and its remarkable production run.

The 727 ranks third because its flight-engineer era stretched across decades of everyday flying. It became a familiar sight at airports around the world, and its long freighter career kept the third cockpit seat in use well after newer passenger jets had moved toward two-pilot operations. FedEx retired its final 727s in 2013, marking the end of a particularly important chapter in the company's freighter fleet. For many airline pilots and engineers, the 727 remained one of the defining aircraft of the traditional three-person cockpit.

Discover how a retired Boeing 727 became a home and how planes worldwide are finding second lives as restaurants and hotels.

The Boeing 707 opened the jet age for most travelers. Developed from the Boeing 367-80 prototype, the first production 707-120 flew on December 20, 1957, and FAA certification followed on September 18, 1958. Pan Am began regular service on October 26, 1958, with a transatlantic flight from New York to Paris. Boeing eventually delivered more than 1,000 aircraft across the 707 family, including the smaller 720. The aircraft's four turbojet engines and long-range capabilities made it one of the most influential commercial transports ever built. Its cockpit was designed around a captain, first officer, and flight engineer, establishing a layout that would become familiar throughout the first generation of jet airliners.

The engineer's workstation was particularly important during the 707's early years. The aircraft's systems required continuous monitoring, including fuel management, electrical power, hydraulics, and pressurization. The engineer also assisted the pilots during engine start and monitored the four engines throughout the flight. Pan Am's Clipper America helped establish the aircraft's international reputation, and the 707 quickly became a symbol of the new era of commercial aviation. Its military derivatives extended the design's life considerably, with aircraft such as the E-3 Sentry continuing to use flight engineers long after most passenger airlines had moved to newer designs. The Pan Am Historical Foundation's account of the airline's first 747 also provides useful context for the transition from the early jet age to the widebody era.

The 707 ranks second because it helped establish the standard for the first generation of long-range jetliners. The 727, 747, and DC-10 that followed inherited the same three-person philosophy, and the 707 proved that jet aircraft could operate profitably on major international routes. Its influence extended far beyond passenger service, with military derivatives continuing to fly for decades. The 707's engineer station became a familiar feature of the early jet age, making it one of the most historically significant aircraft on this list.

The Boeing 747 made its first flight on February 9, 1969, with Brien Wygle as copilot and Jess Wallick as flight engineer. Pan Am launched passenger service on January 22, 1970, on a New York–London flight. The Boeing 747-100 was designed to carry approximately 366 to 452 passengers, depending on configuration, and its introduction transformed the economics of long-distance air travel. Behind the pilots, the engineer faced sideways toward a large collection of panels. The aircraft's size and complexity demanded continuous attention to fuel pumps, electrical buses, pressurization, hydraulics, and air conditioning, tasks that two pilots would have struggled to manage alongside their flying responsibilities. Boeing's official 747 history documents the first flight, the aircraft's development, and the beginning of passenger service.

The flight engineer's role on the 747 was particularly recognizable because of the dedicated sideways-facing station. Boeing's early jumbo jets contained numerous switches, lights, and gauges, and the engineer monitored systems that extended throughout the aircraft. Typical duties included operating fuel pumps, managing fuel transfer, monitoring electrical systems, and coordinating the use of backup systems when required. The position remained a standard feature on the 747-100, Boeing 747-200 and Boeing 747-300, but the introduction of the Boeing 747-400 in 1989 changed the arrangement. Its Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System, together with more advanced digital displays, allowed the aircraft to operate with two pilots instead of three. The Pan Am Museum Foundation's history of the jumbo jet provides additional background on the aircraft's introduction and its impact on international travel.

The classic 747 earns the top spot because it fused scale, symbolism, and the traditional flight engineer's role. Boeing built more than 1,500 747s across the aircraft's production history, and the engineer's sideways seat became the best-known example of the third crew position. The jumbo jet represented the peak of the traditional widebody cockpit, but it also demonstrated how quickly that arrangement could become outdated. Automation, digital displays, and integrated warning and monitoring systems eventually allowed newer aircraft to receive certification for two-pilot operations. The 747-400's introduction marked one of the clearest turning points in that transition, bringing the classic three-person cockpit era closer to its end.

#6283. Air Serbia Flight To Nowhere: A320 Forced To Return To Belgrade Over Mysterious Security Concern

An Air Serbia flight to Moscow made it as far as Lithuania before turning around and returning to Belgrade over a security concern involving one passenger. Serbian media identified that passenger as the country’s former intelligence chief, who allegedly boarded without completing security screening. He denies wrongdoing.

As flagged by One Mile At A Time, Air Serbia flight JU134 departed Belgrade for Moscow on November 3, 2026, but turned back over southern Lithuania. According to Serbian media, the Airbus A320 left at 6:48 PM and returned shortly before 10:00 PM. Passengers spent more than three hours flying only to end up where they started.

Air Serbia confirmed that airport authorities requested additional security checks concerning one passenger. The airline said it returned in accordance with the instructions it received, but did not publicly identify that passenger.

The passenger in question has since been identified as Aleksandar Vulin, Serbia’s former intelligence chief. It appears that someone helped him board without completing the required screening and that the airport’s corporate security director ordered the return after reviewing surveillance footage.

Vulin insists he completed the required checks, was carrying no prohibited items, and was being targeted for political reasons (his pro-Russian party lost in a snap election last month). He said his trip concerned negotiations over Serbia’s gas arrangement with Russia.

Passengers and their luggage underwent additional screening in Belgrade. The flight eventually continued to Moscow with a replacement crew, arriving about seven hours late.

If the reports are accurate, the obvious question is how someone was allowed to board without completing the required checks. Political prominence should not provide an exemption from an aviation security procedure, though I understand how easy it is to open an employee access door for a VIP).

But Vulin disputes that account, and the airline’s statement establishes only that authorities requested additional screening. That leaves important questions about what happened before departure and what prompted the return. Vulin was allowed to continue on the delayed flight to Moscow.

Belgrade’s Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office has requested an investigation into the circumstances, including whether procedures were followed, who authorized the aircraft’s return, and what security assessment supported that decision.

That inquiry is appropriate. If someone bypassed screening, there should be accountability for how it happened. If the checks were properly completed, authorities need to explain why an aircraft full of passengers was brought back.

This is all may be Serbian domestic politics…

An alleged screening lapse involving a former intelligence chief turned a routine Air Serbia flight into a lengthy journey back to its starting point. The aircraft eventually reached Moscow, but the competing accounts of what happened remain unresolved.

I hope the investigation establishes whether someone received preferential treatment or whether there is another explanation for this extraordinary return. Either way, the passengers arrived very late into Moscow.

Good news for travelers who prefer vacation rentals over luxury hotels: Chase is giving select cardholders thousands of new ways to put their travel benefits to use.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, The Edit by Chase Travel℠ will include more than 10,000 curated vacation homes in addition to its existing collection of luxury hotels and resorts.

That means eligible Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees), Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees) and J.P. Morgan Reserve® cardholders will soon be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward vacation home stays — and potentially enjoy additional perks as part of their stay (minimum four-night stay required).

The information for the J.P. Morgan Reserve card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you're unfamiliar, The Edit by Chase Travel is a curated collection of luxury hotels and resorts that offers eligible cardholders additional perks when booking through the Chase Travel portal (minimum two-night stay required).

Currently featuring more than 1,500 hotels and resorts, the collection will expand to include more than 10,000 vacation homes beginning Jan. 1.

The homes will be curated by Plum Guide, a luxury vacation rental platform that evaluates properties using "more than 150 criteria related to comfort, design and location".

This builds on Chase Travel's partnership with Plum Guide, announced in April 2026, which brought luxury vacation rentals to more Chase cardholders through the travel portal.

With the latest expansion, eligible Reserve cardholders will have access to a curated collection of vacation homes through The Edit, complete with premium benefits.

Cardholders will also have the flexibility to redeem Chase Ultimate Rewards points toward these stays through Chase Travel.

Additionally, Sapphire Reserve and Reserve Business cardholders will have access to Reserve Travel Designers, who can help match travelers with vacation homes and provide personalized concierge assistance before, during and after their stays.

Related: I’ve been using the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business for a year — here’s why I’m keeping it

One of the biggest draws of booking a hotel through The Edit is the additional perks that come with a qualifying stay (minimum two-night stay required).

Depending on the property, these can include complimentary breakfast for two, a $100 property credit, room upgrades when available and early check-in and late checkout.

Vacation home bookings through The Edit will come with a different set of benefits.

There's an important catch, however: Vacation home stays must be at least four nights to qualify for these The Edit benefits. Some benefits are subject to availability and may vary by property.

Eligible cardholders will also be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward qualifying vacation home bookings.

As a refresher, here's how those credits break down:

Beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business will offer four statement credits of up to $250 each for The Edit stays that can be used throughout the year. That's up from two statement credits of up to $250 each available on the card in 2026.

Keep in mind that while a two-night prepaid booking may qualify for the statement credit, vacation home stays must be at least four nights to receive the additional The Edit benefits.

Also, be aware that while you can redeem Ultimate Rewards points for eligible bookings, stays paid entirely with points do not qualify for The Edit statement credits under Chase's current terms. If you want to use the statement credit, you'll need to make an eligible prepaid purchase with your card.

Related: How to stack Sapphire Reserve credits for up to $500 off

The addition of more than 10,000 vacation homes to The Edit is welcome news for eligible Chase cardholders, particularly those who prefer the space and flexibility of a vacation rental over a traditional luxury hotel.

It also gives cardholders more options for using their annual The Edit statement credits, while offering perks such as a $150 in-stay credit and early check-in and late checkout when available.

Just keep the minimum-stay requirements in mind, and compare prices before booking to make sure you're getting the best value.

#6281. American Airlines Dropped Trump’s Name From West Palm Beach Gate Screens Ahead Of Midterm Elections

American Airlines quietly removed the Trump reference from its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The timing will invite speculation, but the simpler destination label is an improvement regardless of what prompted the change, which does not appear politically-motivated to me.

JonNYC reports that American has changed its destination displays from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

That reverses a change introduced after Palm Beach International Airport was renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport earlier this year.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ?

The change is likely not connected to this week’s election and occurred in August as part of a planned transition. The IATA code for the airport is still DJT after the July 9, 2026 change from PBI.

The original change was peculiar because American generally identifies destinations by city, adding airport names when useful to distinguish between airports serving the same destination.

American does not ordinarily add the presidential names associated with airports serving places like Little Rock (Bill Clinton) or Grand Rapids (Gerald Ford). The West Palm Beach label stood out. Then again, as I indicated above, other airports did not change their IATA code.

There is a very practical reason to distinguish New York JFK from New York LaGuardia or Washington Reagan (National) from Washington Dulles. Leading with presidential initials on a flight to West Palm Beach offers less obvious help to passengers.

There was no possibility of similar confusion when flying into West Palm Beach.

Of course people will notice that this reversal surfaced around the midterm elections, but as I mentioned this goes back to August. Even so, it is an irresistible invitation to speculate about corporate America adjusting to a changed political environment, which was becoming clear even over the summer.

But I think it’s safe to say that American’s leadership did not order a “political” retreat, no matter what some MAGA world may be suggesting this morning. This was more likely all part of the transition plan.

I would be equally cautious about declaring that the original wording was personally ordered by executives seeking favor with the administration, though that could well be the choice as well. It was an unusual choice. The reasoning behind it remains a separate question.

Still, American created an unnecessary distraction by departing from a straightforward city label in the first place. Once a company makes a conspicuous change involving a political figure, undoing it will inevitably attract attention too…especially now.

American Airlines has restored the West Palm Beach destination label on its gate monitors, removing the presidential reference it added earlier this year.

The timing will generate political interpretations. Without more information, I would leave those as speculation and it appears wholly unrelated. The practical result is easier to assess: passengers once again see the name of the place they are flying to. That works for me. Now it’s time to move DJT back to PBI…there was certainly no need for that change either, though that ship (plane?) has sailed.

#6280. Frontier Shakes Up Leadership Team

Frontier is reshuffling its leadership team, hiring a new chief operating officer, and announcing the departures of two senior executives.

Michael Delehant will join the carrier as executive vice president and chief operating officer on Nov. 30. He will oversee all airline operations and report to CEO Jimmy Dempsey, Frontier said Monday.

Delehant most recently served as group managing director at Wizz Air, overseeing operational and commercial activities. He previously held senior positions at Vueling, including chief strategy and network officer, and worked in several leadership roles at Southwest.

Dempsey said Delehant’s experience would be “instrumental as we continue growing our airline and executing against our strategic priorities.”

The appointment comes as Trevor Stedke, senior vice president of operations, and Alex Clerc, senior vice president of customers, prepare to leave Frontier on Nov. 13. The airline did not give a reason for their departures in its announcement.

“I want to express my sincere gratitude to Trevor and Alex for their dedication and contributions to Frontier,” Dempsey said.

Frontier also promoted James Fenner to senior vice president and chief revenue officer. His responsibilities include pricing and revenue management, loyalty, and network planning.

Fenner has spent more than a decade at the airline, most recently serving as vice president of revenue and loyalty.

Bobby Schroeter will move into the role of senior vice president and chief marketing officer, overseeing the airline’s brand and customer experience. Both Fenner and Schroeter will report directly to Dempsey.

The changes follow Frontier’s third-quarter results, which showed a $104 million net loss, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Excluding special items, the carrier reported a $40 million profit on record revenue of $1.36 billion.

#6279. How to Sing Karaoke Every Night, in Every Borough of New York City

In 1968, Daisuke Inoue decided he was going to be in two places at once. A musician who played in a backup band working Kobe’s nightlife circuit, Inoue soundtracked the evenings of soulful salarymen whom he befriended. With drums as his instrument of choice because “all you have to do is hit them,” he turned those relationships into business, arranging entertainment for their other engagements. As the legend goes, he couldn’t make it out to a gig he had booked at an insurance company’s trade show, so he invented the next best thing. Combining a standard eight-track tape player used in car stereos, a microphone, an amplifier, and a 100-yen coin slot, he placed his ghost in the machine, which he fashioned into the Juke 8. Inoue’s device—the progenitor to the modern-day karaoke machine—was a success.

A more rigorous history might question whether Inoue really invented the first such machine or whether that credit belongs to electronics manufacturer Shigeichi Negishi’s Sparko Box a decade earlier. But the meteoric takeoff of karaoke has soared far past its humble—and slightly murky—origins. A portmanteau of the Japanese words kara, meaning empty, and oke, meaning orchestra, karaoke evokes both loneliness and collective belonging. Nearly 60 years on, we still root for the little machine that could—and all the brave singers who bare their heart through age-revealing ballads and club classics.

An impassioned rendition of Celine Dion’s “It's All Coming Back to Me Now” transpires at Beats Karaoke Cafe in Williamsburg

Perhaps nowhere is karaoke’s full breadth more on display than in New York City, where, on one side, you’ve got lounges complete with floor-to-ceiling video walls and speakers with built-in auto-tune capabilities and, on the other, decades-old dives whose performers are as much an institution as the establishment.

A karaoke spot is the one place where post-prom dates, wedding parties, and career performers alike gather to spend their time and money on gloriously subpar entertainment, entirely without irony. When you’re the one behind the mic, it becomes something mythic—a reprieve from the passive consumption dominating much of the city’s nightlife. Tally up the past year’s most recent headlines, and you’d get the impression that we’re becoming less fun—we’re having less sex, drinking less alcohol, going to fewer parties, and hosting fewer of our own. The karaoke bar might be one of the last, thriving places in New York where we wait half an hour to openly embarrass ourselves, and for that it’s well worth our nights out.

With the hundreds of sing-along nights and 30-plus specialized bars in New York City listed on trackers like Karaoke Crowd, there was no way we’d be able to cover them all. So we visited one place a day for a week, crisscrossing the boroughs for a taste of the city’s diversity. We commenced our week in Koreatown, where some-dozen private rooms are conveniently concentrated on a single street, and continued our spree at an Irish pub on the Upper East Side, where shouting for sport and song are one in the same. We hit up a Staten Island dive of devoted locals and a year-old Astoria restaurant where, once the Tagalog ballads have begun, you must push the plate away and join in. These watering holes, old and new, are living proof of the many shapes karaoke takes and the unifying joy of belting it out together, even when so much else threatens to divide us.

A singer takes the stage at Iggy’s on the Upper East Side to perform Billy Joel and Elton John’s “Piano Man”

We began the week where many end it, on the dense corridor of West 32nd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues. Along this stretch of Koreatown, karaoke bars, podiatrists, escape rooms, and coworking spaces stack atop one another. Our crawl started at Gagopa, whose BYOB policy is a favorite among the large-group partiers and Midtown corporate crowd for fast-tracking camaraderie. The bar eluded us at first, not for a lack of signage but for its location on the fourth story of its building, and the search more or less provided a template for our crawl: a ride up an elevator the size of an airplane lavatory and head-scratching decor. At Gagopa’s sister bar, 32 Karaoke, this last item consists of Polaroids of visiting groups on the walls—the very karaoke canon that, once you’ve stepped through its doors, you become part of.

Anticipatory staircases aside, no amount of symbolic literacy can prepare you for a K-town elevator panel. Despite its abundance of labeled buttons, deciphering them only makes things more confusing. To reach Space Karaoke Bar and Lounge, for instance, you have to avoid accidentally ending up at Space Ping Pong, one of two Space sports bars, or the Space golf simulator. Take it as a sign to stop trying to make sense of things and just embrace the ride.

Across the street, Chorus Karaoke Lounge has a clubbier feel, with a purple-and-blue-lit bar. To the left is a hallway of private rooms, lined with porthole window portraits of Madonna, Morrissey, Elvis, and all the other greats. On the evening we visited, only one karaoke room at the end of the white hallway was occupied—by a lone singer crooning to himself. It may well have been a strict weekly ritual, the first step in a vocal warm-up regimen. “I sing, therefore I am,” read a sign near its entrance as we left, a reminder that although thinking may be proof of existence, song is proof of life. —Skyli Alvarez & Kat Chen

Pianist Mark Benjamin, left, accompanies performers at Sid Gold's Request Room on 26th Street, which has additional locations in Detroit, Nashville, and Washington, DC

In the liminal space between Chelsea and Flatiron, Sid Gold’s Request Room is a bit of an outlier. Sandwiched between an empty office space and halal buffet, its old-timey façade simply reads “piano” and “karaoke.” Both await you in the spacious piano lounge, tucked behind a pair of velvet curtains at the back of the cocktail bar.

We arrived around 9 p.m. and slid into one of the alcoved booths closest to the stage, a small black platform beside the bar centerpiece: a Baldwin baby grand. As we settled in, a singer, backdropped by pianist Mark Benjamin’s harmonies, wrapped up his performance to a crowd of now four; he then came to take our order. Fortunately, others trickled in: tourists and their New Yorker friends; Tuesday-night regulars; a dog named Henry. Many, as we learn, were here for Benjamin's performance—and succor.

As we came to find out later on in the week, karaoke works better in numbers, but Sid Gold’s makes the case for a small yet mighty group. A particularly moody evocation of Chris Isaak’s “Wicked Game,” prefaced by the singer’s memories of angst-ridden high school years, drew out lower-than-low notes. In what could only be described as a shouty but otherwise cheery cover of “Back to Black,” each verse’s forceful delivery was more unpredictable than the last. At some point Benjamin called upon someone named Eric, who kicked off his flip-flops to sing “Part of Your World,” a method for getting into character (one can only assume) that would be frowned upon everywhere else but here.

If you think you can evade the stage, Benjamin will make sure you get on up there. He’ll harmonize and improvise riffs even if he’s never heard the song (or wants you to think this); pause to match your pace; and convince you that it was made for you to sing. —S.A.

I was immediately given the cousin treatment when I passed the threshold of Barkada Social Club. In case there was any ambiguity about the cultural identity of this Astoria restaurant and bar, let it be known I walked into Bruno Mars’s “Risk It All,” with plates of lumpia and kwek kwek covering the tables. It was a good night to come—Barkada NYC, a separate but similarly named LGBTQ+ Filipinx community group, hosts its monthly Kikay Konek karaoke event here. Joey, a queer-affirming physical therapist by day and programming coordinator with Barkada NYC, was my gregarious host for the night. When I asked them about encountering struggles with finding kindred souls, they gave me a considerate look before breaking out into a smile and saying, “I honestly can’t relate.” This came as no surprise as I watched them record the “Toxic” floor routine for BNYC’s Instagram before rushing off to plan next month’s programming, discuss bringing BYNC to the Bronx, finalize plans for a hike three weekends away, and introduce me to their boyfriend. It takes a social whirlwind like that to bring together a collective of members from across all five boroughs, plus exotic reaches like Tenafly, New Jersey. The crowd is in constant flux, peeling off and joining in depending on what the song queue has in store. The one exception to the rule is when someone requests Jesse Zaragoza’s “Bakit Pa,” a sweeping Tagalog ballad from the ’90s about unrequited love that brings everybody rushing to the fore. “It’s like our national anthem,” Joey says. —K.C.

Tim sings at Steiny's Pub in Staten Island

At Sid Gold's, patrons are more than ready to be called up for a harmonized performance

At the site of the former Mayfair Bar and Grill, a favorite among St. George’s queer patrons in the 1950s and ’60s, Steiny’s Pub was once a low-key gay bar turned sports joint that now exists somewhere between the two. It’s fitting for a borough that’s often the butt of the joke, cloaked in its perceived suburban isolation, though an eight-minute walk from the Staten Island Ferry makes it surprisingly less difficult to reach from Manhattan than one might assume. We passed a small group of local 30-somethings smoking near the entrance and, once inside the dive, encountered a lively emcee who goes by the DJ name Nazz Raidience. We’re quickly singled out for not being regulars and handed a Sharpie and clipboard to add to a queue that Nazz only loosely followed.

As co-owner John Michael works behind the bar, a few seated patrons watch tennis and baseball while others belt it out to their backs. The L-shaped booth seating next to the DJ setup operates as the stage. Most who perform adhere to genre: bar patron Dia’s heavy metal numbers by Kittie are complete with death growls, Connor does Eminem with breakdancing and triple-threat delivery, and others insist on 1980s ballads. Nazz shepherds the queue at an auctioneer’s pace, sometimes joining in and always poking fun, calling upon you to spin the prize wheel that could lead to a free drink or 10 push-ups. Although they host karaoke nights across the city, Steiny’s is their favorite for the many different worlds it attracts, and they'll convince you to stay for the ferry sailors who, post-shift, are said to come singing around 2 a.m. When it became clear to us this would not be the night, we left without sea chanteys in our hearts but with a better understanding of the appeal of the city’s least-populated borough. —S.A.

Performing karaoke cosplaying as Shadow the Hedgehog, hands full with impulse purchases from Comic Con’s artist alley, is my penance. I had postponed this visit for too long, leaving me with no option but to come as I was. Bronx Beer Hall is nestled within a larger food hall in the historic Italian neighborhood of Arthur Avenue (please, try the veal). By the time Friday karaoke night is in full swing, all of the surrounding businesses are fully closed. From the outside the telltale sign that anything is happening is the ambient trail of music. Channel an ’80s B-movie slasher victim, and follow the noise into the darkness. Upon emerging into the light, you’ll see a hallway lined with T-shirts printed with lines like “Call it gravy, not sauce!” or “I’m not a gynecologist, but I’ll take a look.” As for the music selection, it’s what you’d expect from a generationally eclectic crowd. There’s tender performances of Bon Jovi and Air Supply following the crowd-rousing momentum of “NUEVAYoL” by a man wearing a snapback with what was certainly a record-breaking number Yankees logos embroidered on the design. Every three songs the DJ would queue up 50 Cent’s “In Da Club” to announce yet another birthday, and BBH turned out to be just the kind of place where an unrelated 24-year-old and 40-year-old blow out their candles together. Being Shadow the Hedgehog did not go unnoticed either. Our millennial bartender who grew up playing the original Sonic games requested “Live and Learn,” the main theme song of Sonic Adventure 2. As I took in the lyrics for the first time on the TV screen, I lived and I learned. —K.C.

The karaoke room at Iggy’s becomes rowdier as the night progresses

This Irish karaoke bar was our first reporting excursion, and it established a curious precedent. Between its Upper East Side location, Gaelic rafters, and portraits of 27 Club musicians, the place seemed tailor-made for Xennial dads. We assumed butt rock was inevitable and hedged our bets on at least one rendition of Hinder’s “Lips of an Angel.”

My hunch came from Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, specifically her theories of homosociality: the nonsexual bonds between people of the same sex. Spend enough time at karaoke, and you’ll notice that “Lips of an Angel” is almost always performed as a duet between two men. For the uninitiated, the song imagines a phone call between a singer and an ex he still quietly yearns for, wishing she were there instead of the “girl” in the next room. Sure enough, two friends took up the mantle. Maybe it was simply a fun song to sing; maybe karaoke offered a safe conduit for expressing something else. We encountered the song at every subsequent karaoke night, always sung by two people of the same sex.

While some bars use online queues for song requests, attendees go analog at Iggy’s

As a week of karaoke draws to a close, you will come to find specific crowds come in waves. First come those who learned to love performance in youth-theater productions, usually in duos or trios, and take their sing-alongs seriously. Then there are the harder-to-place groups: coworkers, reunited friends, or couples using karaoke as a social buffer. Next come the balladeers and lone yearners, eager to broadcast exactly how they’re feeling, followed by the humble soloists who know they’re good and have nothing to prove. Finally, the rowdy late-night crowd of after-partiers spills in, at worst hogging the mic and at best uniting an entire room.

In our five hours at Iggy’s, the former theater kids delivered truly spectacular covers of “Defying Gravity,” the Irishmen shouted Irish pub songs, and the soloists flirted by way of song choice. Three dollars grant you one song that you select from an impressively up-to-date binder and scrawl onto a piece of paper, then the waiting game begins. “We just met in the photo booth” is how one performer introduced a B-side from The Cure, an effort to woo over a stranger who he knew shared at least one common interest. Karaoke gives singers permission to say what they otherwise cannot or will not admit, though the message is rarely subtle. —S.A. & K.C.

Though Seventh Heaven's evenings often begin with film screenings, watch parties, and other community events, they always end in karaoke

During a week when we spent every other waking hour thinking about karaoke-ing, we sometimes looked past dives and private rooms for other ambitious reinventions, like on a boat; in a taxicab en route to the airport; or in an East Williamsburg apartment turned karaoke rental. Still, it’s ultimately the most obvious spots that draw the crowds. Take Williamsburg’s Beats Karaoke Cafe, an eight-minute walk from the Bedford Avenue station, with a rustic bar on the first floor, leading to a hall of private rooms that continue downstairs. We eventually wound our way into film production coordinator Natalie’s group of eight, who told us this was their go-to whenever they “want to add a little divorced dad rock to the night,” and we had caught them testing out new material. Still, they made their way through classics like The Cranberries’ “Zombie” and “Time of My Life,” while also executing many Dirty Dancing lifts.

Farther along the L train, it was only appropriate that we ended up at a bar named Seventh Heaven. We were among the youngest crowd by far, at least in taste. Karaoke-goers swarmed the stage and fluently rattled off the romaji lyrics of “A Cruel Angel’s Thesis,” the theme song to ’90s anime Neon Genesis Evangelion. This bar gets its crowd, with a cocktail menu filled with allusions to the fandom, like the Apothecary’s Negroni fashioned after popular light novel series The Apothecary Diaries, or my own drink, the Boy’s Love G&T, which is named after the popular fiction genre that focuses on the romance between male characters. Turns out, there are plenty of effusive ex–theater kids who understand the assignment.

The DJ cued up our request, “Viva la Vida.” From the vantage point of the stage, the outstretched hands of the crowd looked not unlike the Eugène Delacroix painting of the Revolution of 1848, which Coldplay used as cover art their 2008 album Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends. A notably resigned wedding party lingered at the back of the audience, while city newcomers hailing from nearby venue House of Yes gleefully accepted our mic to unleash a few verses. The karaoke-goers had in the very least not given up on tonight. —S.A. & K.C.

#6278. Boeing's Renton Factory Must Stagger The 737 MAX 10 With Smaller Jets, But Everett Can Run Nose-To-Tail

Boeing rolled the first 737 MAX 10 out of its new North Line at the Everett facility on October 26, and media attention naturally focused on the historic location shift. Destined for launch customer WestJet, this is the first time a 737 variant has been assembled outside of Boeing’s historic Renton plant since 1970. This change in build location makes sense because the longest variant in the 737 family has outgrown the layout of the factory that birthed it.

The motivation for establishing the North Line isn't simply to increase monthly hull count. The 143 feet, 8 inches (43.8 meters) fuselage of the 737 MAX 10 is not best suited to fit inside Renton’s compact assembly bays. To build the MAX 10 in Renton, Boeing had to stagger the elongated airframe between smaller variants like the MAX 8 to prevent structural overlap between adjacent stations. Now, by repurposing space in Everett’s massive widebody plant, Boeing has finally provided its largest narrowbody with an assembly line tailored to its length.

Boeing’s Renton factory has been the manufacturing heart of the 737 program for decades, but its boundaries were drawn around significantly shorter airframes. Covering roughly 1.1 million sq feet (102,000 m²) of total floor space, Renton’s three active assembly lines operate within tight architectural confines bounded by Lake Washington and local rail lines. When managing standard 737 MAX 8 aircraft, measuring 129 feet, 6 inches (39.5 meters) long, the moving assembly lines operate with minimal spatial clearance between stations.

The introduction of the 737 MAX 10 disrupted this tightly calibrated footprint. Stretched 14 feet, 2 inches (4.3 m) longer than the baseline MAX 8, the MAX 10’s nose and tail sections intrude into overhead crane pathways and the working envelopes of adjacent stations when positioned directly in sequence. To avoid costly structural collisions during station transitions, Renton line managers must manually stagger the build sequence so a longer MAX 10 is always preceded and followed by shorter MAX 7 or MAX 8 airframes.

This requirement creates scheduling friction across Renton’s 12,000-person workforce. Staggering limits production flexibility, as line operators cannot build MAX 10s based solely on order-book priority. According to Boeing, there are 1,555 firm orders for the MAX 10, about 31% of the total 737 MAX backlog, so Renton’s layout threatened to become a permanent operational bottleneck for Boeing’s most important commercial variant.

Something had to be done about Renton’s layout constraints, so Boeing began a $1 billion capital project to establish the 737 MAX North Line inside its flagship Everett facility. Occupying high-bay space in Building 40-22, vacated following the consolidation of 787 Dreamliner assembly to South Carolina, the new line provides approximately 20% more usable floor area per station compared to Renton. This means the 737 MAX 10 can move continuously in a true nose-to-tail orientation and does not need those staggered buffers.

Supported by an initial workforce of roughly 1,000 employees, about half of whom were reassigned directly from Renton to transfer specialized narrowbody assembly expertise, the North Line operates with modernized tooling, according to Barron's. The added clearance permits automated overhead crane systems and mobile scaffolding rigs to work around the MAX 10’s extended fuselage without interfering with adjacent work centers. Crucially, the dedicated layout increases total 737 manufacturing capacity by 25% across Boeing's Puget Sound industrial network, Lynwood Times reported.

However, uncoupling the MAX 10 from Renton's spatial constraints is not the end of the story for Boeing. Of course, the North Line provides the needed floor space for smooth assembly, but bringing these aircraft to market is a completely different reality for Boeing, and just adding floor space does not guarantee success in this area.

The opening of a second 737 assembly line in Everett represents more than just additional manufacturing space.

Achieving rollout on October 26 was a major milestone, but it does not mean customer deliveries are imminent. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) granted amended type certification for the 737 MAX 10 flight platform just a few days earlier on October 20, 2026. It was excellent news for Boeing, confirming that the MAX 10’s aerodynamic design, flight controls, and safety systems meet airworthiness standards, though it is only the first stage of regulatory clearance and many more stages remain.

Before WestJet or any subsequent customer can take delivery of an Everett-built MAX 10, Boeing must secure a separate amendment to its FAA Production Certificate. Everett is an entirely new production line for the 737 program, so FAA inspectors must audit every station, tool calibration log, and quality management process inside the North Line. The agency will need to independently verify that the Everett facility builds aircraft with the same structural consistency as Renton, which is a huge undertaking for Boeing.

During this initial low-rate production phase, the North Line moved the first airframes through assembly stations at a deliberately slow pace, according to Assembly Magazine. The extended flow time allows quality engineers to validate assembly steps alongside FAA observers. Consequently, initial WestJet deliveries will remain paused until the production certificate amendment is formally issued, making the short-term backlog relief more of a future expectation than an immediate result.

Everett solves Boeing's internal floor space limitations, but the pace of total 737 production remains tied to Tier-1 supplier health. As Boeing leadership confirmed, the main constraint on narrowbody output is an ongoing shortage of wing subassemblies. The complex wing structures, featuring advanced-technology winglets and dedicated trailing-edge flap mechanisms designed to handle the MAX 10’s higher takeoff weight, are arriving at assembly plants well behind schedule.

Even with a vastly improved production environment, an airframe cannot progress past early structural joining stations without its wing sets, so wing availability sets the pacing clock for both Renton and Everett. In response, Boeing revised its master production ramp. The target rate of 47 aircraft per month has been revised slightly, and Boeing now expects to reach and hold the 47-per-month milestone in 2027, before attempting a further push toward 52 jets per month later that year, according to Fortune.

The controlled ramp rate is designed to prevent traveled work, or moving unfinished airframes to downstream stations without completing preliminary assemblies. Holding the North Line at a steady, measured pace means Boeing is protecting manufacturing stability while supplier factories bring wing deliveries back into alignment.

The move will also free up capacity in Renton as Boeing looks to scale up MAX 8 and MAX 9 production.

The strategic commitment to build a $1 billion dedicated line in Everett is backed directly by market demand. At the top of the 737 MAX family, the MAX 10 carries 185 to 210 passengers in a standard two-class layout, with a maximum capacity of 230 seats. With a range of 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 km), the variant competes directly with Airbus’ dominant A321neo, offering airlines low seat-mile costs on high-density domestic and transcontinental trunk routes.

With 1,555 firm orders logged from global operators including United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, WestJet, and Ryanair, the MAX 10 is seeing a wave of popularity worldwide. Even Lufthansa has opted for the type, bringing the 737 back into the fleet after 10 years of pure Airbus narrowbody focus in the mainline fleet. Airlines have structured long-term fleet renewals around the high-capacity variant to replace aging 757-200s and older 737-900ERs. Failing to deliver the MAX 10 efficiently risked pushing these key customer accounts to convert options into competing European narrowbodies.

With Everett’s North Line dedicated to the MAX 10 alongside high-density MAX 8 runs, Boeing has clearly divided industrial labor. Renton can focus its three moving lines on high-volume MAX 8 and MAX 9 builds, while Everett takes on the complex, elongated MAX 10 airframes. As a result, Boeing has the industrial headroom needed to fulfill its multi-year backlog and finally get its production lines moving at record speed once again.

The rollout of the first 737 MAX 10 from Everett is really a significant milestone for more reasons than just the beginning of a new era for the 737 family. It also ushers in a permanent structural transformation in Boeing’s manufacturing footprint. What began in 1970 as a single-factory narrowbody setup in Renton has evolved into a multi-facility production network spanning Puget Sound. Boeing recognized that floor space, rather than worker effort, was limiting MAX 10 efficiency, so it positioned its commercial airplane division to push higher manufacturing rates with greater structural precision.

Over the coming years, the co-existence of Renton and Everett will redefine Boeing’s production dynamics. Renton remains the high-volume engine of the 737 program, while Everett provides the spatial flex capacity needed for specialized, high-capacity airframes. Once the FAA approves Everett’s production certificate and supplier wing deliveries stabilize, Boeing will possess an industrial system capable of supporting its long-term target of 52 aircraft per month.

Ultimately, the Everett North Line shows that modern aircraft manufacturing is as much about factory geometry as it is about aerodynamics. Giving the 737 MAX 10 the floor space it needs to move nose-to-tail, Boeing has cleared a path to deliver its largest narrowbody variant to global customers.
