#6210. Lufthansa Realizes 28 Business Class Seats Isn’t Enough For Boeing 787

In recent times, Lufthansa has started taking delivery of factory fresh Boeing 787s, featuring the carrier’s all-new Allegris cabins. Management at the airline has reportedly decided that the configuration of these planes isn’t quite right for many routes, so now it’s planning some updates.

That’s a sensible change, but it always just feels like Lufthansa is a step behind when it comes to acting logically and catching onto trends, no?

Lufthansa currently has a fleet of 20 Boeing 787-9s. Four of these were acquired secondhand (they were former Hainan Airlines jets), while 16 are brand new, and feature Allegris interiors. Not only that, but Lufthansa has at least another 22 of these planes on order, which will be delivered in the coming years.

In the long run, the Dreamliner is supposed to be the carrier’s primary long haul aircraft based in Frankfurt, complementing the Boeing 747-8s and Boeing 777-9s. Meanwhile Munich (MUC) is primarily getting Airbus A350s (including the A350-900 and A350-1000).

Lufthansa’s 787s are configured with 287 seats, including 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Keep in mind that three of those seats aren’t even certified yet (but should be certified before the end of 2026), so actual business class capacity is currently just 25 seats.

Anyway, even with all seats certified, Lufthansa Group management has decided that the capacity doesn’t actually match demand on many routes, with CEO Carsten Spohr indicating that the airline is working on installing more business class and premium economy seats on upcoming Dreamliners.

Reportedly nothing has been finalized yet, as this is still in negotiations with suppliers, but the idea remains that the current configuration doesn’t offer enough premium seats.

Given the eventual size of Lufthansa’s Dreamliner fleet, it would also be reasonable to think the airline may have two configurations in the long run, to reflect the demand of different destinations. For example, one would assume that the potential customer demand profile would be different to New York (JFK) than to Columbus (CMH), both of which are going to be Dreamliner routes in the coming months.

I know ragging on Lufthansa is just too easy, from its challenging labor relations, to its botched Allegris rollout, and more. However, I can’t help but feel like the airline is a little behind on trends.

I mean, for how long have we been talking about the surge in premium travel demand? American is taking delivery of 787-9s with 51 business class seats, United is taking delivery of 787-9s with 64 business class seats, and British Airways is reconfiguring 787-9s with eight first class seats and 38 business class seats.

So Lufthansa just taking delivery of dozens of factory fresh 787s with just 28 business class seats seems a little off, especially since Lufthansa only recently started adding these planes to its fleet.

I get that demand differs between markets, and the 787 is actually supposed to be the less premium plane in the fleet, in the long run (with the Boeing 747s and 777Xs being the most premium Frankfurt-based planes), but still, 28 seats just doesn’t seem like a lot by any metric. Heck, the Airbus A330s that are slowly being retired have 42 business class seats, and that’s an overall smaller plane.

Of course the whole Lufthansa Allegris and SWISS Senses situation is just sort of messy, from the 3.5-seat first class cabin that makes no sense, to the need to install a weight on SWISS A330s to balance out the weight of first class, to the new Allegris seats delaying entry into service for planes by years, despite it not actually being that cutting edge at this point.

Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr has indicated that the airline is considering a new configuration for many upcoming Boeing 787s. Management has decided that 28 business class seats and 28 premium economy seats isn’t sufficient, which strikes me as a rather obvious, when you look at trends. Heck, these Dreamliners are partly replacing planes with 50% more business class seats.

I’m curious to see what Lufthansa eventually settles on for a premium Dreamliner configuration, because I agree, 28 business class seats isn’t a lot!

What do you make of Lufthansa reconsidering its 787 layout?

The whole Allegris philosophy was a gamble on one very specific aspect: segmenting customers with different seat types. The allegris business class seat is a very inefficient seat. It is essentially the same concept as united’s Polaris, except with more seat pitch, and every second row, just one middle seat instead of two. Lufthansa thought they could segment their business class customers, upsell certain seats (especially the throne seats, the long bed and the mini-first class at the bulkhead) and make up for the lost revenue of having such an inefficient layout and shrinking the size of the cabin (to maintain a large economy class cabin). But this gamble failed, because Lufthansa didn’t realise that by upcharging so many business class passengers even to simply select a window seat put a bad taste in many people’s mouths. Look at BA, AF and KL. all business class seats in their cabins are created more or less equal with the exception of the bulkheads. Furthermore, Frankfurt is a business heavy market, but has less point-to-point business traffic, and a lot of connecting traffic. It is easy for travellers who are not star-alliance loyal to simply connect elsewhere, or fly united across the Atlantic. Lufthansa wanted to create a segmented business class cabin, but instead created a business class “lite” and charged for extras after that. And now they’re stuck with a VERY expensive, delayed seat, which occupies way too much space on their aircraft, and as such they have had to make huge compromises like shrinking the first and business class cabins. They will seriously lose out in the long term.

#6207. United’s Premium Boeing 787s With New Cabins: Which Routes Do They Fly?

We recently saw United Airlines introduce its long awaited new Boeing 787-9s, featuring all-new cabins, which are being branded as United Elevate. This represents the evolution of the carrier’s long haul experience, including all-new Polaris business class seats.

Of course one common question is which routes actually feature these new planes. So in this post, I’d like to go over that — which planes have the new cabins, and which routes do they fly? The airline is flying these planes on an increasing number of routes out of two hubs, so there are more opportunities to try this product.

Prior to 2026, United already had over 80 Boeing 787 Dreamliners in its fleet, split between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 variants. However, United is now taking delivery of another 71 Boeing 787-9s, which recently started to be delivered (in addition to 56 Boeing 787-10s, which will be delivered as of 2028).

What’s exciting about these planes is that they feature an all-new passenger experience, and are in an ultra premium configuration. The planes feature just 222 seats, compared to the 257 seats you’ll find on all the previous 787-9s.

If you want to actually fly a United Boeing 787-9 with the new United Elevate interiors, what are your best odds of getting on one of these? The good news is that they’re consistently scheduled on certain routes.

As it currently stands, United has 16 of these 787s in its fleet, with several more expected to be delivered in the coming months. United plans to have 33 of these jets by 2028, so the airline is taking delivery of an average of around one of these per month (though the pace has been even faster in the first several months).

When you go to book a ticket, the best way to tell if a flight is operated by the new plane is whether you see “Polaris Studio available” listed under the United Polaris fare options (assuming those seats are for sale). Otherwise there are no obvious indicators, other than looking at the seat map.

We recently saw the IATA winter season kick off, and with that, we’re seeing the plane based out of both Houston (IAH) and San Francisco (SFO).

You’ll currently find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of San Francisco:

You’ll then find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of Houston:

Let me emphasize that schedules are always subject to change (especially when Boeing delivery delays are a potential factor), and the above is just how things currently stand. I’m also not including flights between San Francisco and Houston, which sometimes see the plane so that it can be rotated between hubs, but obviously that route doesn’t feature the true Polaris soft product.

In recent months, we’ve seen United start to take delivery of its brand new Boeing 787-9s, featuring a more premium layout, plus new cabins. These are exciting planes for passengers, as they feature a much improved onboard experience. They’re also great in terms of upgrade and award availability, given the number of premium seats.

If you want to fly United’s new 787s, you’ll currently find them flying out of Houston and San Francisco. Out of Houston, they’re primarily flying to London, Sao Paulo, Sydney, and Tokyo, while out of San Francisco, they’re primarily flying to London and Singapore. It’s great to see the pace at which United is taking delivery of these planes.

I look forward to trying the new interiors, though I’m hoping to wait until these planes have Starlink installed, since I think that really completes the experience.

What do you make of United’s new Boeing 787-9s, and the routes they’re flying?

#6206. Wyndham Is Giving Members Free Hotel Status Upgrades—Some Can Claim 3,000 Points Instead

You have to register, and the gift depends on your current status, where you live, and whether you’re already enrolled in Wyndham’s Insider subscription.

I don’t get excited about Wyndham status, but free status and free points are good things. If you don’t have hotel status today, having something could be an avenue to match somewhere else. So it could be worth a couple of clicks, even more so if you have a Wyndham stay coming up.

Claim the status upgrade by December 30, 2026. It lasts through December 31, 2026, and Wyndham says to allow 24–48 hours for it to take effect. (Do it on December 30 and it may activate and expire simultaneously – yay!) New members can join and claim Gold. Note that you can’t use the promotional status to match to Caesars Rewards.

The upgraded earning rate is determined by your status at checkout. A stay ending January 1 won’t earn the holiday status bonus.

Wyndham normally requires 5 qualifying nights for Gold, 15 for Platinum, and 40 for Diamond. The benefits are modest:

Preferred room choice means a better location or view within the room category you booked. Early check-in and late checkout are subject to availability, generally up to two hours before or after the hotel’s stated time. Diamond suite upgrades depend on availability at check-in.

As I explained when I looked at Wyndham’s instructions to hotels, you should ask for the preferred room and checkout benefits. And there’s no program-wide elite breakfast or lounge benefit. At a hotel earning the usual 10 base points per dollar, moving from Platinum to Diamond adds just 50 points on $100 of eligible spending. That’s 35 cents at a valuation of 0.7 cents per point.

Eligible Diamonds need to claim their 3,000 points by December 31, 2026.

Members who become Diamond through this holiday upgrade don’t qualify for the points gift. Neither do members with a competitor status match unless they’ve completed the required 10 qualifying nights within 90 days of receiving that matched status.

Wyndham’s messaging on this says 3,000 points are enough for a discounted night at any participating hotel. That doesn’t actually match their current award chart.

Following the September 15 devaluation, standard free nights cost 5,000, 15,000, 30,000 or 45,000 points per bedroom. The points plus cash price at a 45,000-point hotel starts at 4,500 points plus the cash portion.

Ultimately Wyndham has lost much of what made it interesting to me: Vacasa redemptions are gone, the easy credit card route to Caesars Diamond ended, and the top award price rose 50%.

Wyndham Rewards Insider normally costs $95 per year and automatically renews. It offers hotel discounts, extra points, and access to deals on flights, cruises, rental cars, activities and entertainment, along with a concierge.

The advertised 50% increase in earning applies to the elite bonus. A Diamond’s bonus rises from 20% to 30%, so ordinary earning at a 10-point-per-dollar hotel goes from 12 to 13 points per dollar or 8.3% more points. And the hotel discount isn’t a promise of the lowest price. Wyndham acknowledges that another rate available to non-Insiders can be cheaper. Buying Platinum could make sense for someone who isn’t, can’t status match, but still plans a bunch of Wyndham stays upcoming.

The holiday upgrade can be combined with Wyndham’s current 4X points promotion. Register before booking, book direct by January 15, 2027, and complete eligible paid stays by January 19. The holiday status itself ends December 31. The multiplier applies to base points, with a cap of 15,000 promotional bonus points. At the normal 10-point base rate, a non-Insider Diamond earns 40 points per dollar from the base earning and promotion, plus 2 elite bonus points (not four times their usual 12). Insiders can earn another 5,000 points after two qualifying nights, either together or across two stays. That bonus doesn’t stack with the separate Wyndham cardholder bonus. Premier cardholders can earn 10,000 instead. For an upcoming stay, claim your status first and register for the points promotion before making the reservation since a booking made before promotion registration doesn’t qualify. I get asked some version of the same question all the time: what’s the best travel credit card to actually keep in your wallet?

For me, the answer has changed over time. As my travel habits have evolved, so has the mix of cards I rely on. Some help me earn points quickly, others offset travel costs with built-in credits, and a few simply make traveling more comfortable.

While getting outsize value from a travel credit card often means paying an annual fee, I've found that the right perks can more than justify the cost. And one of the cards I'm looking to add to my wallet next doesn't charge an annual fee at all.

These are the travel credit cards I keep coming back to — and in some cases, the ones I'm planning to add next — based on their earning potential, flexibility and benefits I actually find useful.

I chose these cards based on the value they can provide travelers. In particular, I considered:

I've also included cards for different types of travelers, from beginners and those seeking premium perks to airline and hotel loyalists and travelers who don't want to pay an annual fee.

Purchases that qualify for the $300 annual travel credit will not earn points.

*Welcome offer value is an estimated value based on TPG's November 2026 valuations and is not provided by the issuer.

The newest premium travel card in my wallet is the Chase Sapphire Reserve, and after just a few months, it's already become one of my favorites.

While the $795 annual fee is steep, I've been getting plenty of use out of the card's travel perks. One of my favorite benefits so far has been the up to $500 in annual credits for The Edit, Chase’s curated hotel booking platform (issued as two credits of up to $250 per calendar year for stays of two nights or more).

I recently used one of those credits for a luxury stay at At Six in Stockholm, where I also enjoyed some of the other perks when you book with The Edit, such as complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit. The hotel's impressive breakfast spread was a particular highlight, and I was able to use the property credit to cover a couple of dine-in meals.

Lounge access has also been a major benefit. I frequently fly through Dulles International Airport (IAD) when visiting family on the East Coast, and the Etihad Lounge, which is part of the Chase Sapphire Lounge network, has become one of my go-to spots to relax before a flight.

I've also booked other hotel stays through Chase Travel, where the card earns 8 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. Between the hotel benefits, lounge access and $300 annual travel credit, I've found plenty of ways to put the Reserve to work in a short period of time.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve: Earn 100,000 valuable points

The Sapphire Preferred was the first travel card in my wallet — and that goes for a lot of us here at TPG. It’s also the card I recommend most often to beginners or casual travelers who want flexible points without a sky-high annual fee.

With beginner-friendly perks like a $100 annual hotel credit and strong travel protections, it delivers real value without overwhelming complexity.

The card also makes it easy to get quick, upfront value. After earning the welcome offer and maximizing bonus categories — like 3 points per dollar spent on dining and 2 points per dollar spent on travel purchased outside the Chase Travel portal — I was able to build a sizable stash of points within a few months.

I ultimately redeemed those points for a trip through four European countries, which felt like a pretty great return for my first year with the card.

I'm also particularly excited about the card's newer earning category for vacation rentals. As someone who's stayed in more than 60 Airbnbs, I love that I can now earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation home rentals, including Airbnb bookings.

It’s the travel card I recommend over and over again to friends and family because of its ease of use, strong earning potential and outsize value relative to its modest $95 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Preferred.

Related: 6 ways to maximize the Chase Sapphire Preferred as a beginner

Best for: Straightforward premium rewards

Another top contender in the premium space — and one that’s firmly earned a place in my wallet — is the Capital One Venture X Rewards Card. For me, its biggest selling point is how easy it is to get value from the card without having to overthink my spending.

Part of the reason I added the card was to diversify my points and miles beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards. Up until recently, I’d been almost exclusively earning Chase points, but as I’ve gotten deeper into the points and miles world, I’ve realized how valuable it is to have access to multiple transferable currencies and transfer partners.

At the same time, the Venture X fits naturally into my everyday spending habits. Cardholders earn a flat 2 miles per dollar on nearly every purchase, which removes the need to track bonus categories or optimize every swipe. It’s become my go-to catch-all card and the one I reach for whenever a purchase doesn’t neatly fit into a bonus category on another card.

I've also gotten great use out of its travel benefits. I recently used the card's $300 annual Capital One Travel credit toward a three-night stay at the DoubleTree by Hilton London Marble Arch, bringing the cost down from $1,096 to $796. I also appreciate being able to relax in Capital One Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges when I travel.

For me, the Venture X works because it combines straightforward everyday earning with travel benefits I actually use, making its $395 annual fee easier to justify.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Related: 5 reasons why I’m applying for the Capital One Venture X

For travelers who regularly fly a single airline — especially those based near one of that carrier’s hubs — a cobranded airline card can make a lot of sense.

That’s been true for me with United, but I think the same general strategy applies to frequent Delta and American Airlines flyers as well. If you consistently fly one carrier, the right airline card can make your travel experience cheaper, smoother and more comfortable through perks like travel credits, free checked bags and priority boarding.

Despite its $350 annual fee, the United Quest offers several easy-to-use benefits that help offset the cost. The $200 annual United travel credit, for instance, has helped offset flights home to visit family. And the two free checked bags for me and a travel companion have already saved me a significant amount in baggage fees.

The card also offers award flight discounts, anniversary bonus miles, priority boarding and improved award availability, which make the card feel like a keeper for the long term.

That said, I do wish it included lounge access — especially at this price point.

Still, the Quest has made flying United more affordable and convenient for me, which is exactly what I want from an airline credit card.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

Not every worthwhile travel rewards card needs to charge an annual fee. The Freedom Unlimited is one I'm interested in adding to my wallet because it could fill an important gap in my Chase strategy without adding another annual fee.

On its own, the Freedom Unlimited earns cash-back rewards. But when you pair it with an eligible Ultimate Rewards-earning card like the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, you can combine your rewards and potentially get more value by redeeming them for travel or transferring them to Chase's airline and hotel partners.

That's particularly appealing to me because I'm working toward building the Chase Trifecta, a strategy that combines multiple Chase cards to maximize earnings across different types of purchases.

With no annual fee, the Freedom Unlimited could give me another way to earn rewards on everyday spending while letting my Sapphire cards handle travel purchases and unlock more valuable redemption options.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

Related: The best beginner Chase card combo for travel rewards

Best for: Hilton perks without the premium price tag

The Hilton Surpass is the newest addition to my wallet — and my first hotel credit card.

For years, I've prioritized flexible rewards over hotel-specific points because I didn't want to commit to a single hotel program. But as I've started traveling more and spending more nights in hotels, I realized I was leaving some valuable perks on the table.

After comparing several hotel cards, I ultimately chose the Hilton Surpass because it struck the right balance between cost and benefits. One of the biggest draws for me is automatic Hilton Honors Gold status, which gives me meaningful hotel perks without requiring me to earn status through stays.

I'm also a fan of the card's up to $200 in Hilton statement credits each calendar year, issued as up to $50 each quarter. And Hilton's large footprint means I'm much more likely to find a property where I can actually put those benefits to use when I travel.

For me, the Surpass is a relatively approachable way to test-drive hotel loyalty while getting useful benefits from the start. As I spend more nights with Hilton, I'll be able to see whether a hotel card deserves a permanent place in my travel strategy.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Surpass.

Related: How I chose my first hotel credit card — and the 4 cards I considered

Choosing the right travel credit card ultimately comes down to how you travel, where you spend your money and which perks you'll actually use.

For beginners, the Chase Sapphire Preferred remains one of the strongest entry points thanks to its balance of value, flexibility and simplicity. Frequent travelers looking for a more premium experience — especially when it comes to lounge access and travel perks — may get more value from the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Meanwhile, the Capital One Venture X is a great fit for travelers who want premium benefits without overcomplicating their rewards strategy, and the United Quest offers a strong value proposition for frequent United flyers who prioritize convenience and United-specific perks.

For travelers who don't want to add another annual fee, the Chase Freedom Unlimited can be a useful complement to a Sapphire card, particularly if you're building a Chase trifecta. And for travelers who want hotel-specific perks, the Hilton Surpass offers a relatively accessible entry point to hotel loyalty with automatic Hilton Gold status and useful Hilton credits.

You certainly don't need all six cards on this list to get good value from travel rewards. But whether you're looking for your first travel card or considering adding another to your wallet, I'd start by thinking about which benefits you'd use most often — and whether they're worth the annual fee.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

#6202. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6200. Passenger Forced To Pay ‘Employee Retention Fee’ For JFK Airport Self-Checkout Machines

A traveler buying a $21.99 book at New York JFK used self-checkout but was still forced to pay an employee retention surcharge. Hudson’s Bryant Park Market in terminal 5 added the mandatory 3% fee, then sales tax on the fee. Does the machine’s employee wellness program cover maintenance on the cooling fan, or maybe paid time off to install Windows updates? The passenger bought John U. Bacon’s The Gales of November: The Untold Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald, and shared the self-checkout receipt. A 3% surcharge has been applied to your purchase. This charge is for employee and retention programs and is not a gratuity. Mandatory employee fee at bookstore when I used self checkout.by u/alternativo- in EndTipping The tax on the surcharge annoyed the shopper, too. But New York calculates sales tax on the full taxable purchase price. And the surcharge is just a hidden part of the price. I’ve written about airports allowing surcharges as an end-run around their own pricing rules. The Port Authority of New York New Jersey is clear on this. Its regulation generally caps prices at 15% above comparable street prices, but expressly allows an additional employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%. The regulation also excludes the employee fee from gross receipts under agreements where the Port Authority collects a share of concession revenue. I covered the same 3% employee benefit and retention charge at a Newark self-checkout last year. The Port Authority tells merchants to add the fee, and incentivize them to do it – moving part of the price into fees means they get to keep more of the money. Philadelphia authorized a similar 3% add-on while retaining its street price cap. There it was expressly a way to let merchants charge passengers more and circumvent the cap. Minneapolis prefers a 4.5% hospitality charge with signage explaining it wasn’t a tip and didn’t go to the people providing the hospitality. The employee fee on this book isn’t a tip, but airport machines have been demanding those, too. In Austin, I couldn’t pay for a bottle of water without entering a tip. The terminal rejected $0.00. Staff confirmed it, and the transaction only went through when I entered a penny. Earlier this year I also flagged an Austin airport self-checkout that defaulted to an 18% tip while adding a card processing surcharge. One commenter asked about the JFK airport charge, “Since I would be paying the employee retention fee, do i get a say which employees stay or go?” I’d retain the scanner, but put whomever programmed the surcharge on a performance improvement plan. The tax on the surcharge annoyed the shopper, too. But New York calculates sales tax on the full taxable purchase price. And the surcharge is just a hidden part of the price.

I’ve written about airports allowing surcharges as an end-run around their own pricing rules. The Port Authority of New York New Jersey is clear on this.

The regulation also excludes the employee fee from gross receipts under agreements where the Port Authority collects a share of concession revenue.

I covered the same 3% employee benefit and retention charge at a Newark self-checkout last year. The Port Authority tells merchants to add the fee, and incentivize them to do it – moving part of the price into fees means they get to keep more of the money.

Philadelphia authorized a similar 3% add-on while retaining its street price cap. There it was expressly a way to let merchants charge passengers more and circumvent the cap.

Minneapolis prefers a 4.5% hospitality charge with signage explaining it wasn’t a tip and didn’t go to the people providing the hospitality.

The employee fee on this book isn’t a tip, but airport machines have been demanding those, too. In Austin, I couldn’t pay for a bottle of water without entering a tip. The terminal rejected $0.00. Staff confirmed it, and the transaction only went through when I entered a penny. Earlier this year I also flagged an Austin airport self-checkout that defaulted to an 18% tip while adding a card processing surcharge.

One commenter asked about the JFK airport charge, “Since I would be paying the employee retention fee, do i get a say which employees stay or go?” I’d retain the scanner, but put whomever programmed the surcharge on a performance improvement plan.

#6198. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trumpâs trusted lawyerÂ and cable newsâs favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Boratâs ultimate get in 2006âs âBorat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,â the pranking of Americaâs mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: hisÂ corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to succeed in theirÂ mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohenâs exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.Â By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout âSubsequent Movefilmâ for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment weâre introduced to Bakalovaâs Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on parÂ with the sinking of the Titanic.Â Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, âthe happiest wife in the world,â emboldening her to join Boratâs latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Boratâs government, have not been kind to him since âCultural Learningsâ conquered America with great success â high five! â 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstanâs current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, heâs hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form â ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all â and given a new mission to smooth glorious leaderâs entry into the worldâs strongman club. How? By presenting toâVice Premier Mikhail Penceâ valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, âKazakhstanâs Minister of Culture and No.1Â porno star.â

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the filmâs release fails to ruin âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas, Â plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the filmâs full title: âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series âWho Is America?â â which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American â enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit heâd pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. âTheyâre fun!â

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, âSubsequent Moviefilmâ makes Tutarâs empowerment the centerpiece of the movieâs second half. Â Baron Cohenâs signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Wolinerâs past TV work (which includesÂ series such as âNathan for Youâ) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

Thereâs the practical matter that the character ofÂ Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that âthe problem with success, although itâs fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I âgetâ with Borat again, so itâs a kind of self-defeating form, really.â

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today.Â However, heâs right about the problem of Boratâs fame. âSubsequent Moviefilmâ confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Boratâs relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant â except for when he revealshis subjectsâ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original âBoratâ donât involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Boratâs stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in âSubsequent Moviefilm.â Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctorâs office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohenâs infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama âwith the Wuhan flu.â

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business donât tell us anything we donât already know. Instead, itâs what the context implies about Americaâs psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isnât merely in the pastorâs misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutarâs stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutarâs father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesnât disturb the status quo.

Thereâs the Texas baker who uses icing toÂ pipe the wordsÂ âJews Will Not Replace Usâ on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. Thereâs theÂ shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the âno means yesâ dress section. Thereâs the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, âWhat color is best for racist family?â says without pause or reaction, âI wouldnât go any darker than a six or a seven.â

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; sheâs also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first âBoratâ and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, sheâs a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of âSubsequent Moviefilmâ relative to the first âBoratâ sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has arenât deadly, although itâs plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the filmâs ending in ways that donât feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the âBoratâ of 2006 and the 2020 âSubsequent Moviefilmâ is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trumpâs election in 2016, to say nothing of howÂ decline and fall of basic critical thoughtÂ has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, thereâs simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If thereâs a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called âlesserâ nations.

Now it doesnât allow the audience to be so sure of itself,Â implying in the final sceneÂ that we arenât merely ugly Americans. Weâre a once glorious nationÂ being led by goons who areÂ sliding us backwardÂ into diminishment, and dangerously so. ThatÂ is nothing to laugh about.Â

âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ is currently streaming on Amazon.

#6197. American Airlines Has Reopened Its Exclusive LAX Dining Room After 6 Years—Here’s How To Get In

Last Wednesday I wrote exclusively American Airlines would reopen its Flagship Dining inside the business class lounge at LAX this week. Now it’s officially open. What was First Class Dining has been closed since March 2020, and when it returns, qualifying American business class passengers will be able to use it with their tickets, and there are other paths to entry too. That’s great news. When it was open previously it was fantastic. Flagship First Dining was a restaurant inside the Flagship Lounge. There were tables, booths, a bar and a window looking out toward the aircraft. The room had 59 seats, but when I visited there were never more than two other passengers at once. The food was excellent, too. I especially liked the miso black cod, and the pork belly came with cauliflower tempura that I still remember. American has since dropped “First” from the name. As the airline removes international first class from its Boeing 777-300ERs and replaces its three cabin Airbus A321Ts, they’ve opened the dining rooms to a much larger group instead of doing away with them. Since September 15, qualifying Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus passengers have been able to use Flagship Dining in Dallas and Miami. Los Angeles is next. Access covers qualifying American Airlines long haul international, premium transcontinental and Flagship Hawaii itineraries. That includes eligible Flagship flights between Los Angeles and New York JFK, though an ordinary domestic first class ticket doesn’t get you in. The qualifying flight must be marketed and operated by American. Business class access doesn’t include a guest. Getting into the Flagship Lounge based on AAdvantage or oneworld status doesn’t get you into the separate dining room. Eligible partner first class access continues, and there’s also a way in with miles. AAdvantage Platinum Pro members can redeem 25,000 miles and Executive Platinum members can redeem 20,000 miles for a Flagship Dining pass. It includes the member and their immediate family or up to two guests on an eligible same day American or oneworld flight, even when flying coach. It includes the Flagship Lounge, too. I’ve thought this was one of the best uses of miles when traveling as a family. American has introduced a new dining menu and a wine and chocolate pairing featuring KHK Hillside Cabernet Sauvignon and K+M chocolate, co-founded by chef Thomas Keller. The cabernet retails for about $125 a bottle. Here’s American’s photo of the pairing. The new Dallas wine list also includes Bollinger La Grande Année, which retails for around $200 a bottle. American even listed it as an ingredient in a cranberry orange spritz. That seems like an expensive way to make it harder to taste the champagne. I’d ask for it in a separate glass. And the food has improved in the broader Flagship lounges, not just in the separate dining rooms. On a recent visit to the Dallas Flagship Lounge, I found a better buffet, a staffed charcuterie station and an improved chef station. I ordered from the lounge’s menu using a QR code, and the food arrived at my table in four minutes. It was a relatively quiet Tuesday evening, but I was impressed. That menu ordering is available in Los Angeles, too. When I last wrote about the rollout, the QR codes were in the theater seating and across from the secondary beverage station. Delta still offers the more ambitious food. It now has two Delta One lounges at LAX, with table service throughout, while United’s Polaris Lounge has a sit down restaurant. I’d still put the food in American’s main Flagship Lounge behind Delta, even though the gap has narrowed. But American makes the larger Flagship Lounge available to many more passengers, including eligible elites traveling in coach. And now a regular qualifying Flagship Business fare comes with the separate dining room. United’s base Polaris fares don’t include Polaris Lounge access. Delta’s Basic Business fares will lose Delta One lounge access for travel beginning January 19, 2027. At this point Americna’s three Flagship Dining locations really close a gap and even start to offer a competitive advantage for some. The tradeoff is that First Dining was so special because almost nobody was there. Opening it to business class is a big improvement for those passengers, but it also means many more people competing for a table. American uses an electronic waitlist when the dining room is full. If you’re traveling before a busy departure period, I’d check in with the host when you first arrive. July 22, 2018 I was flying back from Sacramento to Dallas via LAX. I was CK and either got it or burned a pass for dining. Went in and thought I was the only person in there. Heard some faint talking. Positioned myself to see who was talking because I thought I recognized the voice. He hung up his call, so I made my move once I realized who it was. Former VP Joe Biden. Literally all by himself and making calls to thank people for attending an event the day before. He was not a presidential candidate (until April 2019). He was so gracious and invited me to sit with him for a bit and asked me where I was coming from and where I was going. Shared I was heading home from a 40-man golf tournament of high school friends (g.1989). I asked if it would be okay for a picture I could share with friends, he said of course. Enjoyed a brief 1:1 with future President of the United States. Btw – there was no Secret Service, he was Joe-citizen and hadn’t declared.

So the Flagship Dining at LAX is a special place in my heart.

Wow, its a wow moment for me! I like the sound of all this new details and would love to dine here. Hopefully I have enough time to sit and relax. Great job AA. See you soon!!
