#6196. Amex Platinum Card Review: Benefits & Credits That Easily Justify The Fee

While premium cards are incredibly popular nowadays, this is really a market that Amex started, with the American Express Platinum Card®. It takes some effort to maximize the card’s perks, but if you’re willing to put in the time, the value is potentially incredible.

This is my in-depth Amex Platinum Card review, so let me talk about the card’s value proposition, and the perks that make the Amex Platinum worthwhile. This is a card you should get for the rich benefits that it offers, including the lounge access, credits, and elite status, and not necessarily a card you should spend a lot of money on under normal circumstances, since there are more rewarding cards for that.

Link: Learn more about the American Express Platinum Card®

Before I get into my full Amex Platinum Card review, I want to go over the card’s key details at a glance. The card has such a long list of statement credits that it’s impossible to cover those briefly, so keep reading below to see those, as they could be worth up to thousands of dollars annually. To keep the list to non-statement credit details, here’s what you can expect:

I also put together my pros and cons of the Amex Platinum Card:

The Amex Platinum Card potentially has a huge welcome offer, though the card also has a high annual fee. So let’s cover all those details first, including card eligibility, since these are major factors cardmembers consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Platinum Card currently has the following lucrative welcome bonus offer: You may be eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $12,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer, so you’ll want to start the application, and then you’ll see what kind of an offer is available to you.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, so depending on the offer you’re eligible for, this could be worth almost $3,000 in value. That’s pretty stellar, especially for a card that offers so much ongoing value after your first year.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card in the past (so the card has a “once in a lifetime” rule). If you’ve had the card in the past you’re still eligible to be approved, you just won’t get the bonus.

Note that this is a hybrid card and not a credit card, meaning that having this card won’t count toward Amex’s limit of five credit cards per person. Make sure you consider all of Amex’s standard application restrictions before applying.

Eligibility for this card is otherwise unrelated to having any other type of card that’s not an Amex Platinum, so lots of people should be eligible for the offer.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee. Even among premium cards, this is among the highest annual fees out there, though for many people, the perks will more than offset the fee.

If you want to add authorized users to the card, you’ll pay $195 each (Rates & Fees). Fortunately there are some solid perks for authorized users, including lounge access, so some people might find that adding them is worthwhile.

As you’d expect of a premium travel card, the Amex Platinum has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees). This means you can use it abroad without racking up fees, though it’s not usually the best card for maximizing everyday spending on categories like dining.

Personally, I think the Amex Platinum Card is worth having for the benefits it offers, though it’s not a card that I think is worth spending much money on, with limited exceptions.

Some other Amex cards offer big bonus categories. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x Membership Rewards points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 of spending per calendar year, and then 1x points), which is extremely lucrative.

Unfortunately, the Amex Platinum Card isn’t as generous in that regard. However, there are still some useful bonus categories…

The best bonus category on the Amex Platinum Card is 5x points on airfare purchased directly from airlines or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 of flight purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points). This is spectacular, and it makes it the best card for airfare purchases, in my opinion.

Officially booking through online travel agencies (except amextravel.com) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice it may still sometimes code for 5x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them.

I value Membership Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, so to me, that’s the equivalent of an 8.5% return on airfare spending, which is incredible.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

The exception is Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, where prepaid reservations earn 5x points. That can be a good deal because of the perks you get, and also because you still earn points with your preferred hotel loyalty program. You can also combine this with the card’s annual hotel credit to really maximize value. I’ll talk more about that in a bit.

The above are the only bonus categories — otherwise, the Amex Platinum Card offers 1x points per dollar spent, which isn’t especially good. There are other cards offering 1.5x-2x points per dollar spent, so I would much rather put my spending on those cards, or on another card that’s best for everyday spending.

The Amex Platinum Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many. While I love Membership Rewards, I’d say that not everyone should be earning these points.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to the below airline partners and hotel partners.

The reason this represents such a good option is that you can get outsized value toward premium airfare, especially for travel in first and business class. These tickets are often super expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal with points.

For example, I frequently transfer my Amex Membership Rewards points to Air France-KLM, and then redeem 60,000 points for business class across the Atlantic. Best of all, there are sometimes transfer bonuses of up to 25-30%, which lowers my real “out of pocket” in terms of Amex points even further.

I’d note that while you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than one cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Platinum Card really shines when it comes to its credits, as the card potentially offers thousands of dollars in annual credits. As you can imagine, for some people this alone will more than justify the annual fee. The catch is that there are some hurdles to using all of these, so don’t consider most of these credits to be worth face value.

However, I’d argue that it’s quite easy to recoup your entire annual fee on these credits alone. So let’s take a look at what you need to know about these credits, and how you can maximize them. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits. This is a semi-annual credit, so you get a $300 credit in January through June, and a $300 credit in July through December.

This is actually a pretty easy perk to use — just book a prepaid hotel through Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® (no minimum stay) or The Hotel Collection (two night minimum stay) through American Express Travel®, and you can receive up to a $300 credit semi-annually. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

If you ask me, this perk alone can help recoup most of the card’s annual fee. So a major point in deciding whether this card makes sense is crunching the numbers as to whether you can get full value from this.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $400 per year in Resy credits, and enrollment is required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $100 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward dining at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants.

There are no hoops you have to jump through, so as long as you dine at an eligible Resy restaurant and pay with your card, you can receive the statement credit. Personally, I’d consider this benefit to be worth close to face value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in digital entertainment credits, with enrollment being required. This comes in the form of a $25 monthly statement credit on eligible purchases or subscriptions with any of the following:

I’d consider this to be quite valuable, since there’s an impressive variety of partners with which you can maximize this perk.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Lululemon credits, with enrollment being required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $75 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward purchases at Lululemon stores in the U.S. If you’re in the market for some athleisure wear, this is a great option.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Equinox credits, and enrollment is required. This comes in the form of up to $300 in statement credits each year on a digital or club membership at Equinox. If you’d otherwise pay for an Equinox membership, this is a great perk, while otherwise, it’s probably of limited value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a $300 credit when purchasing a SoulCycle bike. This credit can be used toward the purchase of a SoulCycle at-home bike, and it can be used for the purchase of up to 15 bikes per year.

You need to make the entire purchase of a bike in one transaction on your Amex Platinum Card in order to qualify for these savings. Suffice to say that this will be of limited value to most cardmembers.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $219 per year in CLEAR credits. When using your card to pay for a CLEAR membership, you’ll receive statement credits of up to $219 per calendar year. For those not familiar with CLEAR, this company can save you time at security, by allowing you to use your biometric data to skip the ID check.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in airline fee credits, which can be used toward airline incidentals and fees. The credit is offered every calendar year, so it follows a strict January 1 through December 31 calendar.

Every year you can designate on which airline you want to receive the credit, of the following:

You can change your airline selection in January of each year. If you don’t change your selection, then you automatically keep the same airline choice as the previous year.

Unfortunately, you can’t use your credit toward the following:

Airline tickets, upgrades, mileage points purchases, mileage points transfer fees, gift cards, duty free purchases, and award tickets are not deemed to be incidental fees.

This is particularly useful for airline ticket change fees (of which there are few nowadays), baggage fees, and other costs you may incur with an airline. Personally, this is something I have no trouble maxing out.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Oura Ring credits. This is valid if you use your card to purchase an Oura Ring through ouraring.com, and enrollment is required. I’d say this is very niche, but if you’re in the market for this product, it has the potential to be valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Uber credits. The way this is broken up, you get a $15 credit per month, and then in December, you get a total of $35 in credits. You can use this either for rides with Uber in the US, or for food with Uber Eats in the US.

To activate this benefit, you need to enter your Amex Platinum Card card number on your Uber account, and then you should see the benefit unlocked. You’ll see an amount added to your Uber Cash balance every month, and the discount will automatically be applied to the first eligible ride or food delivery.

An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $120 in statement credits each calendar year after purchasing an auto-renewing Uber One membership with the card. This is separate from the card’s $200 annual Uber Cash benefit.

An Uber One membership offers all kinds of benefits for rides with Uber and deliveries with Uber Eats, so if you use the platform with any frequency, this is pretty valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $12.95 per month in credits toward a Walmart+ membership, which covers the full membership cost. Enrollment is required. (Up to $12.95 plus applicable local sales tax. Plus Ups not eligible.) With Walmart+, you can receive free deliveries on groceries or get savings at gas stations or on video streaming.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck statement credit every four years. Simply charge the membership fee to your card, and it will be automatically reimbursed. It’s worth getting Global Entry, which has a $120 application fee compared to PreCheck’s $85, because it includes TSA PreCheck membership too.

It doesn’t matter who the fee is being paid for, as long as you charge it to your eligible card.

The Amex Platinum Card offers one of the most comprehensive lounge access benefits of any card. This is called the Global Lounge Collection, and it offers access to over 1,550 airport lounges across 140 countries for eligible cardmembers. This includes proprietary Amex lounges, as well as access to lounges run by other airlines and companies.

Before I go through the details, let me mention that Lufthansa lounge access has been cut as of October 1, 2026, which is why I’m not including it in the list, though that used to be a benefit.

Amex is well known for its Centurion Lounges, and the Amex Platinum Card can get you into these lounges. These are significantly better than what you’ll find in most U.S. airline lounges, with a solid selection of hot food and cocktails.

Currently, U.S. locations include Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, New York JFK, New York LaGuardia, Philadelphia, Phoenix, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, with more to come. There are also Centurion Lounges in Amsterdam, Hong Kong, London, and Tokyo, among other international destinations.

You can access these lounges up to three hours before your flight’s departure (if you’re connecting, then the three-hour limit doesn’t apply). Please note that you’re only eligible to bring in guests on a complimentary basis if you spend at least $75,000 per calendar year on the card.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers access to the Delta Sky Club, with some limitations. Card members can receive access within three hours of a departing or arriving flight, and must present their card, a boarding pass showing a confirmed reservation for an eligible Delta flight, and a government-issued ID.

Eligible cards issued in the United States receive 10 visits to the Delta Sky Club each year, to be used from February 1 until January 31 of the next calendar year, with all visits within a 24-hour period counting as a single visit. It’s also possible to earn an unlimited number of visits by spending $75,000 in eligible purchases on a card account in a calendar year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Priority Pass™ membership, which gives you access to lounges around the world. You can bring up to two guests into these lounges. While these aren’t the most exciting and high quality lounges, there’s no denying that this gives you access to a comprehensive collection of lounges.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to Plaza Premium Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card, and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring one guest with you at no additional cost. This is hugely valuable, as Plaza Premium has dozens of lounges around the world, which are among the highest quality contract lounges you’ll find.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to the growing network of Escape Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring in guests.

Beyond the annual credits that potentially more than justify the annual fee, as well as an incredible lounge access program, the Amex Platinum Card also offers status with three hotel loyalty programs, status with three rental car loyalty programs, access to a program that gets you valuable hotel perks, and discounts on many premium cabin airline tickets. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Hilton Gold elite status for as long as they have the card. This status is useful, and offers the following perks:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Marriott Gold status for as long as they have the card, which offers the following perks, among other things:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive Leaders Club Sterling status from Leading Hotels of the World. Leading Hotels of the World is a collection of independent, luxury properties, so this offers perks at some properties that don’t otherwise participate in major global hotel groups.

This status typically requires $5,000 in annual spending at these hotels and offers perks such as five pre-arrival upgrades per year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Your status is valid as long as you remain a cardmember; you just need to enroll. This should take the pain out of renting cars and offers the following perks:

The Amex Platinum Card offers National Emerald Club Executive status. You have to enroll to take advantage of this, and it’s valid for as long as you have your card. National is my favorite rental car company, and Executive status lets you pick out your car from the lot, and skip the counter altogether.

The Amex Platinum also offers Avis Preferred Plus status. Once you enroll, you’ll get this mid-tier status level with the rental car company and qualify for complimentary upgrades when available, a 25% points bonus, and a dedicated reservation and customer service line. You also get access to a discount code that can save you up to 25% off qualifying rentals.

With the Platinum Member Airfares program (formerly known as the International Airline Program), you can save on the cost of international first class, business class, and premium economy airfare, on around two dozen airlines. This typically provides discounts even on already discounted tickets, so is a spectacular value.

If you book paid international premium cabin travel with any frequency, this could cover the card’s annual fee over and over.

With the Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® program, you can receive extra perks for stays at over 1,900 luxury hotels around the world. These benefits include the following:

Best of all, the rate is typically in line with the best available rate. Having the Amex Platinum Card gets you access to this, and if you prepay your reservation, you even earn 5x points. You can even stack this with the card’s up to $600 annual hotel credit.

The Amex Platinum Card offers several travel insurance benefits that can add extra peace of mind. You’ll want to consult the card’s benefits guide for the exact terms and any caps and exclusions, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The card also offers an extended warranty protection benefit as well as purchase, return, and cell phone protection.

Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

What benefits do authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card get? They receive most of the same perks as primary cardmembers.

This includes all the lounge access perks, access to Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, Hilton and Marriott Gold status, Leading Hotels of the World Sterling status, access to the Amex International Airline Program, additional Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credits, and more.

The main thing that authorized users aren’t getting is incremental credits, so they’re not receiving extra airline fee credits, digital entertainment credits, Uber credits, etc.

Of course there’s never going to be any “one size fits all” answer as to whether a card makes sense, since we all value perks differently. However, speaking only for myself, I’d argue that the Amex Platinum Card is rather easy to justify.

To start, let’s just take a look at the credits. Personally, I’m able to get full value out of the $600 annual hotel credit, $400 annual Resy credit, $300 annual digital entertainment credit, $200 annual airline fee credit, and $200 annual Uber credit. That’s $1,700 in value right there, and it actually doesn’t take much effort for me to maximize that.

That also says nothing of all the other perks offered by the card, from the bonus points on airfare, to the lounge access, and more. So yeah, I’m really finding this card to be pretty great. Let me emphasize that in 2027 the hotel credit will be harder to maximize, so I’ll need to assess how much value I get out of that. But even if you drop that benefit entirely, I’m still getting $1,100 in value from the other credits.

Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves, but I think the math works out very nicely on this product. But that’s not the case for everyone. So who should skip the Amex Platinum Card?

If it won’t be easy for you to get full value out of the card’s many travel and statement credits — or even if you just don’t want to be troubled with keeping track of so many credits to prevent leaving value on the table — the Amex Platinum may not be the card for you. Credit card fatigue is a real problem!

It’s also not a great card for everyday spending, since it doesn’t earn bonus rewards on categories like dining. I’ve written a more detailed post specifically addressing the question of whether the Amex Platinum is worth it, so I recommend checking that out.

This also brings me to the next section, which is the best Amex Platinum alternatives.

There are several premium cards to choose from nowadays, so it always makes sense to look at what the competition is offering. Let’s look at a few popular alternatives to the Amex Platinum.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) is the other premium card heavy hitter, with a slightly lower annual fee of $795. I have a full post comparing the Amex Platinum and Chase Sapphire Reserve — my verdict is that both cards are worth having, but if you can only pick one, the Sapphire Reserve is better for lazy optimizers while the Amex Platinum is better for those willing to put some real work into optimizing all the card’s benefits.

Here’s an overview of the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s standout features. It’s no slouch when it comes to perks, but its list of benefits and statement credits is considerably shorter than the Amex Platinum Card’s. Specifically:

If you take full advantage of the Amex Platinum’s main statement credits for travel and dining, it has the potential to offer more value than the Chase Sapphire Reserve. But the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s earning rates are better for maximizing everyday purchases, and you might prefer having fewer “coupon book” style benefits to keep track of.

In my opinion, the Amex Gold Card (learn more) is one of the most rewarding cards out there. At $325 (Rates & Fees), its annual fee is significantly lower than the Amex Platinum Card’s, and while it doesn’t have as many benefits, it’s a better choice for everyday spending, especially if you eat out frequently.

Here are the highlights of the Amex Gold:

The Amex Gold Card can’t beat the Platinum when it comes to travel perks, but if your main goal is earning as many Amex points as possible on your spending, it could be a more useful everyday pick.

The Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another premium card with an annual fee that’s one step down from the Amex Platinum — in this case, it’s $395. I find this card to offer strong value, and it’s much simpler than the Amex Platinum Card:

The travel credit and anniversary bonus miles help justify the annual fee, and while 2x miles isn’t the highest everyday spending rate, it’s a better base than 1x points with the Amex Platinum. It’s also worth comparing Amex points with Capital One miles to see which currency you prefer before making a final decision.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee and a much longer list of credits than it used to. This isn’t a card that you should get for the return on spending it offers, but instead, it’s a card to get for all of the perks and credits that it offers.

While the $895 annual fee is obviously steep, personally I’m able to get outsized value thanks to all the credits offered, which offer significant value. And that says nothing of the bonus points on airfare, the lounge access, and more.

So even if you haven’t been able to make the math on this card work in the past, it might be time to give it another look.

#6194. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.

Delta Air Lines and American Express offer seven cobranded cards for everyone from occasional Delta flyers to frequent travelers.

Depending on the card and the offer you qualify for, you could earn up to 125,000 bonus SkyMiles.

Here’s how the current offers compare and what to consider before applying.

*Bonus value is based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer.

American Express has a few eligibility rules to keep in mind before applying for one of these cards. For starters, Amex typically only allows a person to earn one welcome bonus per card in their lifetime. That means you'll want to prioritize applying when a card offers an elevated, limited-time offer, such as the ones all but one of these cards have right now.

You also may not be eligible for a welcome bonus on a personal Delta Amex card if you have or previously had a higher-tier Delta Amex card. For example, if you have or previously had the Delta Reserve Amex, you may not be eligible for the welcome offers on the Delta Blue, Delta Gold or Delta Platinum.

Delta's business Amex cards are not subject to this same "family rule."

Amex may consider other factors when determining your eligibility, including your income, credit score and history with the issuer. Fortunately, you'll generally find out whether you're eligible for a welcome offer before accepting the card.

Delta offers four personal cards. The card that is right for you depends on how frequently you fly with Delta and how much you’re willing to pay for an annual fee.

Let’s take a look at what differentiates each of the Delta SkyMiles personal cards.

Best for: Delta loyalists or those who want Sky Club access (subject to limitations)

The Delta SkyMiles Reserve is ideal for hardcore Delta fans and frequent flyers.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

This bonus is worth up to $1,500 per our valuations.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this is an excellent time to apply. It matches the highest mileage bonus we’ve seen on the card and requires $1,000 less spending than the previous 125,000-mile offer with the lowest spending requirement.

Key benefits: Delta’s premium consumer credit card offers a range of valuable perks. For loyal Delta flyers who enjoy visiting the Sky Club, this card can pay for itself through lounge access, spending boosts and other benefits.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Plus, you'll enjoy a slew of Delta-related perks, including:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card

If you fly frequently with Delta but can’t justify the pricier Delta SkyMiles Reserve, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum is worth considering.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 90,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,080.

If you qualify for the full 90,000 miles, this is a strong offer for $3,000 in spending. We’ve seen offers with more miles or a statement credit, though they required more spending.

Key benefits: This card is a good option if you fly Delta regularly and want to earn miles on purchases and reach elite status. However, even if you aren’t pursuing status, the companion certificate alone can make the annual fee for this card worth it.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum American Express Card

Best for: Occasional Delta flyers or those test-driving a Delta card

If you want to take advantage of a welcome bonus but don’t fly Delta frequently, the Delta SkyMiles Gold is a strong option.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 80,000 bonus miles after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

TPG's valuations place this bonus at up to $960.

If you qualify for the full 80,000 miles, now is a good time to apply. However, we have seen up to 90,000 miles — as well as up to 80,000 miles plus a statement credit — offered before.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

Key benefits: This card is ideal for occasional Delta flyers seeking a few extra perks when flying with the airline.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold American Express Card

If you want an entry-level card to start earning SkyMiles and fly less frequently with Delta, then Delta SkyMiles Blue is the card for you.

Current welcome offer: Earn 10,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

According to TPG’s valuations, these miles are worth $120. The SkyMiles Blue typically doesn't receive an elevated offer, so we recommend applying whenever you're ready.

Key benefits: As a no-annual-fee card, it offers fewer benefits than the others. Still, there are some simple perks for cardmembers.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Blue.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Blue American Express Card

If you own a small business or have a side hustle through which you pay business expenses, one of these offers may be a great addition to your work wallet.

Best for: Business owners who fly Delta frequently and want lounge access

As the most expensive business card Delta offers, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business comes packed with great perks for Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,500.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this clears our usual threshold. The highest offer we’ve seen was 200,000 miles after $20,000 in spending, compared with $15,000 for this offer.

Key benefits: This card offers a range of useful perks for Delta-loyal small-business owners.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on purchases made directly with Delta.

Its suite of Delta-related benefits includes:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business American Express Card

Best for: Business owners who fly frequently with Delta

Business owners who are looking for a good mid-tier airline business card should consider the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business for its earnings potential and benefits.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

According to TPG's valuations, this offer is worth up to $1,200.

The full 100,000-mile bonus matches the highest mileage offer we’ve seen, though previous offers awarded the same bonus after $8,000 in purchases. If you already have $10,000 in eligible business spending planned and want the card now, this is a good offer. If you’re flexible on timing, we’d consider waiting for the same bonus with a lower spending requirement.

Key benefits: This is a solid mid-tier option for business owners who travel with Delta semi-frequently.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business American Express Card

Best for: Business owners who fly occasionally with Delta

The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business is ideal for smaller businesses or business owners who aren’t Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 85,000 bonus miles after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

The bonus is worth up to $1,020 when factoring in TPG's valuations.

If you qualify for all 85,000 miles, this is a good time to apply. It’s just 5,000 miles shy of the highest offer we’ve seen, which also required $6,000 in purchases. If the card already fits your business, we’d take the full offer.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

Key benefits: Even if they don't fly Delta often, small-business owners can still benefit from this card's perks.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card

With a full lineup of Delta cards, you may wonder how to pick the best offer for your needs. While it might be tempting to go with the highest offer, you should also consider its long-term value to your wallet.

The good news is that many of these offers can be a great fit, depending on your travel habits. As a round-up:

Related: Why the Delta SkyMiles Reserve card is still one of the best cards I’ve added to my wallet

Delta and American Express offer a wide range of cobranded cards, whether you fly with the airline occasionally or are a frequent Delta loyalist.

Just remember that American Express has a once-per-card, per-lifetime rule for welcome offers. If you've had a particular Delta Amex before, or, in some cases, a higher-tier personal Delta card, you may not be eligible for that card's welcome offer.

Welcome offers vary, so check the bonus you’re offered and make sure you can meet the spending requirement with purchases you already plan to make.

#6191. “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administrationâs unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agencyâs massive crackdown on immigrants.

The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

Courts have thwarted most of the administrationâs plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, theyâve threatened to prosecute election officials who donât reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

The administration hasnât explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode votersâ trust in the system.

âThe administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,â said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters âsit it outâ and âthrow their hands up.â

In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement âis not planning operations targeting polling locations,â adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of âintelligence-driven targeted enforcement.â

The DHS and the Justice Department âare laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,â the spokesperson added. âOur message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences â including criminal charges and deportation.â

Before and on Election Day, itâs typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say theyâve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committeeâs election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo FernÃ¡ndez HernÃ¡ndez, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.

Here are five issues that voting rights experts say theyâre watching as this yearâs election unfolds:

An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

Mark Earley, the countyâs supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was âfuriousâ when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the countyâs busiest early voting location last month, after heâd been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

âGiven the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,â Earley said.

Itâs against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

Nick Brown, Washingtonâs attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has âwar-gamedâ how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

âWeâve seen the tension and chaos thatâs in the air,â Brown said. He called the federal government âthe biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way itâs supposed to be.â

A DOJ spokesperson said âthe best preparation for any election official is following federal law.â

Itâs routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyomingâs primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The stateâs governor criticized these actions as âa bit aggressiveâ and âirregular.â

The Trump administrationâs multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. âIf you violate federal election law,â he warned, âI will hunt you down and prosecute you.â

This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are âlikelyâ noncitizens. The administration had obtained the stateâs public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls âspecious.â Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many werenât registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, âFederal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.â

A federal judge has rejected the DOJâs motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 votersâ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the stateâs rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJâs demands, calling them an âintimidation planâ that would interfere with legal voting.

Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were âa number of states that weâre looking at.â

In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names ânot reliable,â saying it included U.S. citizens, people who arenât registered to vote and duplicate entries. âTime and time again,â Hobbs wrote, âDHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.â

Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJâs Civil Rights Division. She said the agencyâs actions involving California and Washington were a âdisturbing use of prosecutorial authority.â

Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would âput their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.â

Voting rights advocates also worry that the governmentâs efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they wonât show up.

A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

âA voter could say, âWell, maybe I donât want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I wonât register, or maybe I wonât vote,ââ said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

States often change laws and rules related to voting.

Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters arenât sealing the inner envelope.

Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the stateâs voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasnât processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say theyâve been able to address these problems.

Every election features some issues with voting equipment.

So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines â including one from Dolly Partonâs sister in Tennessee â spawning fears that machines have been âriggedâ to switch votes.

ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadnât received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines donât signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.

Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officialsâ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said âthe fear it caused was real.â

In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISAâs help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal governmentâs absence has weakened the defenses.

âStates acting on their own just do not have the same power,â he said.

Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the presidentâs liking.

Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesnât win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

Nonetheless, the DOJâs case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

âThis is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,â said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

In response to ProPublicaâs questions, the DOJ pointed to Blancheâs statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency âdoes not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaskaâs election.â (The lawsuit calls it âvitalâ that the state not certify âany election result that may be impacted by voter confusionâ and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)

Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

âI worry tremendously about what they might do,â Brown said.

#6190. The 6 Best Airplane Bathrooms On Any Airline: The A380 Reigns Supreme

When most people think of airplane bathrooms, it’s probably not a nice image that comes to mind. Airlines have largely shrunk bathrooms on newer aircraft significantly, and at times they’re also not very well maintained.

That’s not true across the board, though. In premium cabins, we’ve seen airlines introduce some pretty amazing amenities in recent years, and that even includes awesome bathrooms.

In this post, I’d like to share what I consider to be the airlines with the best first class bathrooms (somewhat overlapping with my list of the world’s best first class airlines).

Unsurprisingly, the Airbus A380 takes center stage on this flight, as it’s an aircraft that has ushered in the most bathroom innovation. That’s because the front of the upper deck has a bit of extra space that can’t be utilized for seats, making room for some cool amenities.

With that in mind, below are my six favorite airplane bathrooms, roughly ranked…

Emirates A380 first class is one of my all-around favorite first class products, and a large part of that is the amazing A380 first class shower suites.

Emirates’ A380s have two first class shower suites at the front of the upper deck, equipped with heated floors, enough amenities to start a toiletry resale business, and most importantly, a shower.

As a first class passenger, you can schedule a shower at the beginning of your flight, and while there’s no time limit to how long you can use the shower spa, you’re limited to five minutes of water. Fortunately you can turn the water on and off without the clock “running,” so that’s more than enough water for a nice shower.

Of all the excitement I’ve experienced in the air, I don’t think anything compares to the first time I took a shower on Emirates. The airline even has shower spa attendants, who make sure the shower spas are well maintained throughout the flight.

Etihad A380 first class consists of nine “First Class Apartments,” and these passengers have access to the shower suite at the front of the cabin. Much like on Emirates, each passenger gets five minutes of water, and the shower suite is refreshed between each use.

While this is a great and refreshing feature, the shower suite definitely isn’t as spacious as on Emirates. So if you’re used to showering on Emirates, you might find that it’s a bit tight, but otherwise you’ll no doubt be delighted. Also keep in mind that there’s still The Residence on Etihad, which is a three room suite that can be reserved as an upgrade over the standard first class. This comes with a private bathroom, including shower.

Singapore Airlines A380 Suites is an incredible first class product, with only six seats in the cabin. While you won’t find a shower on Singapore Airlines’ A380s, you will find some of the most spacious bathrooms in the sky. One of the lavatories has a huge vanity, and is probably the size of 10 typical Boeing 737 MAX bathrooms. Airplane bathrooms don’t get much more luxurious than this!

Qatar Airways A380 first class has two very nice lavatories at the front of the upper deck. While there aren’t any special amenities, you’ll find that they’re incredibly spacious, and nicely decorated.

Lufthansa A380 first class features two huge lavatories at the front of the upper deck, each equipped with a bench, and most excitingly, a urinal! Lufthansa is the only airline to offer urinals on planes, so that’s pretty special… or something.

While we’re speaking of Lufthansa, I have a soft spot for Lufthansa 747-8 first class, probably at least partly because the Boeing 747-8 is my favorite plane as an avgeek. While not quite as over the top as some of the other options, Lufthansa’s 747-8 lavatories are spacious, have a bench you can extend out over the toilet, and most importantly, have a window. It’s so nice to be able to look out the window while in the lavatory.

Lastly on the topic of Lufthansa and lavatories, I do have to bring up how cool the economy lavatories on the carrier’s A340-600s were (these planes were just recently retired). They were located on the “lower deck” (in a cargo compartment), so they were probably the most unusual lavatories you could’ve recently found in commercial service. By comparison, the Lufthansa A340 first class lavatories weren’t much to get excited about at all.

All Nippon Airways A380 first class has two large, identical lavatories at the front of the upper deck. They’re huge, but there are also a couple of thoughtful design touches that I appreciate about them.

For one, ANA has a bidet function for its toilets, which is always a nice feature to have. I also appreciate how there’s a “plank” of sorts that you can extend on the ground, for situations where you want to change into pajamas without touching the regular floor of the bathroom.

On top of that, ANA does an amazing job with keeping its lavatories clean between each use, down to folding the toilet paper into perfect triangles.

Now, in fairness, there are a decent number of products with a bidet function in service, from Japan Airlines A350 first class, to Gulf Air 787 business class, to Oman Air 787 business class.

There are some pretty incredible airplane bathrooms out there. While nothing can compete with Emirates’ amazing shower suites, there are plenty of other impressive airplane bathrooms out there as well, with everything from vanities, to bidets, to urinals. As A380s increasingly get retired, unfortunately going to the bathroom on a plane is getting less pleasant!

What’s your favorite bathroom on a commercial aircraft?

#6189. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. #6188. Flagship Dining: American Expands A La Carte Lounge Dining To Business Class

Several weeks back, American announced plans to completely change the concept for its Flagship First Dining facilities, as the airline eliminates international first class. With this, we’re seeing Flagship First Dining simply rebranded as Flagship Dining, with business class passengers also getting access.

While these changes went “live” as of September 15, 2026, there’s now an additional update, as a third Flagship Dining facility has just opened, so you can now enjoy this experience in Dallas (DFW), Los Angeles (LAX), and Miami (MIA). Let’s cover all the details.

For years, American had Flagship First Dining, which are facilities inside select Flagship Lounges. The idea was that this offers an a la carte dining experience for those traveling in international or premium transcontinental first class.

American is currently in the process of eliminating “premium” first class — Boeing 777-300ERs are being reconfigured without first class, while Airbus A321XLRs (without first class) are replacing A321Ts. First class is no longer being sold on the wide bodies as of November 19, 2026, or on the narrow bodies as of March 28, 2027. So there has been a big question as to what American would do with these facilities in the future. Would they just close, or what? Well, it’s much better than that.

As of September 15, 2026, Flagship First Dining has simply become Flagship Dining, and the idea is that this is now open to all Flagship Business passengers traveling on qualifying long haul international, transcontinental, and Hawaii flights.

In other words, if you have access to a Flagship Lounge on account of your American business class ticket, you’re also eligible for Flagship Dining, on a space available basis. However, if you have Flagship Lounge access on account of elite status, or through traveling in a premium cabin on a partner airline, you wouldn’t have access to this facility.

American notes how guests interested in dining should check in with the host team inside the Flagship Lounge upon arrival. If a table is immediately available, guests will be seated at that time. If all tables are occupied, guests may be added to an electronic waitlist and will be notified when their table is ready. Tables will be offered on a first come, first served basis, and as I understand it, there’s no priority for first class passengers, Concierge Key members, etc.

I would expect that demand will greatly exceed supply, especially during peak hours. However, the same is true for the a la carte dining in United Polaris Lounges and (to a lesser extent) at some Delta One Lounges. This is really a great way for American to become more competitive with Delta and United. I’m really, really impressed, and this seems like a sincere effort to improve the premium experience.

Launching alongside the expanded dining facility access is an all-new four-course Flagship Dining menu. The airline promotes that “the seasonal offerings blend regional flavors, thoughtfully sourced ingredients and refined culinary techniques to create an elevated dining experience inspired by some of the world’s most celebrated restaurants.”

American is sharing some of the dishes that will be on offer, including a Texas pear and burrata salad…

In addition to that, American is introducing a wine and chocolate pairing, featuring KHK Wines and K+M Extravirgin Chocolate. Chef Thomas Keller, who co-founded K+M Extravirgin Chocolate with Italian olive oil producer Armando Manni, curated the pairing.

American has launched Flagship Dining, essentially a rebranding and repurposing of the Flagship First Dining facilities. This is being done because American is eliminating “premium” first class in the coming months.

This means American is now offering proper a la carte dining in its business class lounges, increasingly matching the competition. What an awesome change from American! You can find these facilities in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Miami.

What do you make of the evolved Flagship Dining concept? If you visit a Flagship Dining facility, please report back with your experience (food quality, wait times, etc.)!
