#6186. Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

Louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”

In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the big tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

They have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.

#6184. Tom Petty and The Who box sets reveal two sides of rock history

Two great box sets being released for the holiday season from Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers and The Who showcase different approaches to exploring an artist’s back catalog with strong results on both sides. “Origins 1971-1978” chronicles not just the Heartbreakers’ first two albums but also documents the journey that brought them there, while “The Who By Numbers 50th Anniversary Edition” documents the band’s seventh album in a more traditional box set presentation. Both of the releases successfully accomplish their goals and deliver a worthwhile experience for interested listeners, but follow different paths to reach their respective sonic destinations.

“It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”

In the case of the Petty box set, the records at its heart are the newly mixed and remastered editions of the first two albums: the eponymous first release and record number two, “You’re Gonna Get It!” Then there’s “Live from the Record Plant,” originally broadcast on KSAN-FM in 1977, a DVD of the band’s appearance on the BBC’s “Old Grey Whistle Test,” and finally (and most importantly for this release) a disc of unheard tracks: “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin.” (On the LP edition of the box, the latter two are separate albums, but on the CD-only version, the two are consolidated.)

Rounding out the set is a Blu-Ray with hi-res stereo, Dolby Atmos and 5.1 immersive mixes, and importantly, a full-color 46-page “fanzine” called “Heart Attack” that serves as the liner notes for this box, with photographs, essays, interviews and commentary from members of the surviving Heartbreakers. There are other editions with additional advanced artifacts like posters or simulated Polaroids — my favorite is probably the “Punk to New Wave” trading cards — but if you’re in the target market for those kinds of fun treats, you’ve probably already ordered your copy.

What’s notable about the unreleased music featured on “No Sleep Til L.A.” and “The Cut Out Bin” is that it isn’t just a simple compilation of demos and rough takes in a logical order of some kind, but instead is deliberately curated into the shape of an album. It’s intended to convey the journey Petty and the band took to get to the place where they’re going into the studio to record that first record, capturing tracks from the Mudcrutch era (Petty’s pre-Heartbreakers band that also featured future Heartbreakers Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench) as early as 1971 and then as the Heartbreakers in their early days, learning to work in the studio in L.A. and in Tulsa, where their label Shelter Records sent them to learn how to make a record instead of running the meter on a L.A. studio.

The outtake record isn’t trying to fabricate something that doesn’t exist or inject fiction into the Heartbreakers legend, but rather, to show you how the band evolved from a bunch of kids in Florida who picked up and went out to L.A. to seek their rock ‘n’ roll fortunes on a wing and a prayer into a band that would end up being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. It’s expanding the legacy, not rewriting history.

“It’s not Tom Petty good.” That’s how Adria Petty, who oversees Petty Legacy, the business concern that’s handling her late father’s catalog, told Salon as she described the standards against which decisions were made about what to include and not to include in the outtakes record. “Could this be any band? If so, it’s not in there . . . it’s gotta be something that really adds to the canon or we’re just detracting from the canon.”

And the collection absolutely burnishes the canon. It’s hard to listen to the selection of music and understand how any music business professional didn’t think this band had serious potential. There’s so many standout tracks: “Parade of Loons,” which opens the record, from the great rock ‘n’ roll tradition of writing a song from the perspective of watching the craziness unfolding around you is borderline new wave, but it also isn’t — it’s easy to understand why an industry struggling to understand the new guard needed to figure out where these new guys fit, exactly — and perusing some of the photos included in “Heart Attack” you can extend some grace on that front, because — as Adria Petty laughed, “These are not guys you want to date your daughter, you know?” But as you learn from some of the news clips included in the booklet, Petty did not want to be co-opted into anyone’s movement or limited by any genre.

“You’re Gonna Learn” is reggae-influenced at a time when that wasn’t a widely known, let alone embraced, genre in American rock, and they manage to pull it off without embarrassing themselves. “Up In Mississippi Tonight” could be an outtake from “Exile on Main Street.” There are also a couple of earnest and successful Dylan homages: “Wild Eyes” and “I Can’t Fight It.” If you’re going to borrow, borrow from the best (and from a guy you’re going to be on the road backing in 10 years).

Then there’s “Unheard Kind of Hero.” This is a song that Heartbreakers keyboardist Benmont Tench had previously mentioned as a song he saw the band perform before he was in it, and how he was astounded that a band in Gainesville, Florida, was writing original material like that. In “Heart Attack,” Tench offers, “I was following Mudcrutch around because they were so good, and they played a lot of really cool covers and they played some stuff of their own,” he remembers. And when he heard “Hero,” he asked a friend working for the band who sang it originally. When he was told it was an original, his reaction was, “OK, good lord. Because if you listen to that, whether he was 17 or 19 when he wrote it, the storytelling in it is the beginning.”

The box set is configured to bring the listener into the story, opening with the outtakes before taking you to the officially released albums, then live radio show and then, finally, the 1977 “Old Grey Whistle Test” performance. But I’d like to make the case that you should begin with the OGWT performance because it is utterly electrifying. Anglophiles are already familiar, but in case you’re not, the “Old Grey Whistle Test” is a legendary BBC music program that was the opposite to “Top of the Pops” in that its focus was on albums as opposed to hit singles. But this isn’t an OGWT where a band plays a couple of songs; this was one of their special editions where the band gets the full show. So this is a 40-minute performance by a band that was already famous and well-liked in the U.K., a status they were still fighting to achieve back home.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

They’re dressed in black (Benmont Tench rocking a red shirt underneath his suit jacket), Petty looking more like a gunslinger, Ray-Ban aviators and studded guitar strap, Stan Lynch singing harmony vocals over Petty’s shoulder, Mike Campbell dropping guitar riffs and solos without breaking a sweat, Ron Blair sharing the center mic for harmony vocals but otherwise staying low-key back against the drum riser. It’s a time machine back to 1977, with camera work more evolved than we’re used to seeing because it was a TV show about music, not a variety show that featured a band. The colors are a little over-saturated, but people who are used to watching archival rock ‘n’ roll clips won’t be phased. The most jarring element is whenever the camera cuts to the audience, who look like they’d rather be anywhere else. A U.K. source shared that this was because this wasn’t an audience of Tom Petty fans but rather random people who’d put in for tickets and wouldn’t have been encouraged to be enthusiastic. Petty gets his revenge, though, at the last number. (No spoilers!)

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos.

“The Who By Numbers” was released in 1975, but this is still being declared a 50th anniversary artifact. It features 92 unreleased audio tracks, a recording of the band live in Swansea in 1976, the requisite Atmos and stereo mixes, and a video of the full concert of The Who at the Silverdome in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1975.

Also included is what has become a trademark for the band’s reissue sets, a gorgeous full-color 100-page book of liner notes, interviews, lyrics, photographs and other assorted documentation. Even if you buy the CD box, you’re still getting the full-sized book because they put the CDs into an album-sized enclosure. The archivist this time is Andy Neill, one of the two names you want to see behind a Who reissue.

The Who box sets are intended to be complete documents of individual records. So there’s the disc of the remastered album (which sounds fantastic), then the initial Townshend demos. Townshend was approaching 30 when he began work on the songs for “By Numbers,” and he was in the middle of a number of personal dilemmas, as well as struggling with his and the band’s place within rock ‘n’ roll: “I felt detached from my own songs,” he confesses. He also rued the fact that he felt he owed his best material to the band, instead of being able to pursue more of a solo career, which all of his bandmates had done. Townshend’s “Who Came First” came out in 1972, but there hadn’t been anything since.

(Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) The Who, 1975

The demos are lovely, ethereal sketches, documenting Townshend breathing life into his creations for the first time. There are two demos of “Keep Me Turning,” which didn’t make the cut and we wouldn’t hear until it appeared on “Rough Mix,” the warm and affectionate project he recorded with Ronnie Lane of the Faces two years later. A fun game is to take the Townshend demo of “Slip Kid,” where he’s kind of half-speaking, half-singing, and then compare it to Daltrey’s delivery on the finished version, which is the one song from this record that was built on the original demo. (This is a release that you’ll want the good headphones for.) The highlight is probably “How Many Friends,” which is the heartbreaker on the album; Daltrey’s read of it nails the pathos, but this version makes you wish that Pete maybe hung onto it for himself.

Up next is “Tracking Sessions,” which are initial loose takes with the whole band, but not finished vocals. It’s basically how the band taught themselves the new material, and it includes listings like “Ramport Jam” where they (sans Keith Moon, still making his way back to the U.K. after hanging out in L.A. and working on his solo record) fart around on a variety of instrumentals and a Faces song. This lasted about half an hour, but we’re getting only eight minutes; given the nature of the release, just give the fans the entire unedited mess. Throughout the sessions, you hear the band members making jokes and laughing; you hear Glyn Johns in the control room offering his thoughts; you hear Pete Townshend complaining about not being able to obtain a suitable breakfast. This stuff is gold.

Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”

There are also lovely early run-throughs of “Imagine A Man” with a solo Townshend on acoustic and Nicky Hopkins on piano, and similarly, “They Are All In Love” (a song that Daltrey did not initially want to sing) is also offered solo Pete. A prototype of “Blue Red and Gray” is here as well, thanks to Glyn Johns’ insistence: “I find that the hardest thing for me to do as a writer is to express optimism, general warmth and a feeling of good will to all men in a song,” Townshend said. “It feels trite and I hate it. That song, ‘I Love Every Minute Of The Day’ . . . is a prime example. Glyn Johns wanted it on the album; I cringed when he picked it. He heard it on a cassette and said, ‘What’s that?’ I said, ‘Nothing.’ He said, ‘No. Play it.’ I said, ‘Really, it’s nothing. Just me playing a ukulele.’ But he insisted on doing it. I said, ‘What? That fu*king thing. Here’s me, wanting to commit suicide, and you’re going to put that thing on the record’.”

Disc 4 is billed “Early Mixes & Guide Vocals” and is by nature more structured than the Tracking Sessions. The songs are taking shape now. Entwistle offers his approach to his “Success Story,” Pete sings the lead on “However Much I Booze,” there’s a version of “Squeezebox” that the liner notes state is “accented by tambourine” but sounds like the cowbell on the “SNL” “Don’t Fear The Reaper” sketch, and “Dreaming From The Waist” is a fantastic illustration of why Pete Townshend needed Roger Daltrey to sing most of his songs.

As a way to track the evolution of the song from start to finish, the inclusion of all of these different versions is an established and useful presentation device, but given their formative nature, it’s not likely that you’re going to go back to them with regularity. But that’s not why this record exists. Whereas the Tom Petty box set is intended to show you how they got to the first two albums, this release is trying to show you why this was the record between “Quadrophenia” and “Who Are You.”

But it’s probably more accurate to state that “The Who By Numbers” was the record between the “Tommy” movie and “Who Are You,” which isn’t a small distinction; the “Tommy” movie made the band into a larger and different flavor of rock star, one that brought in the girls because of shirtless golden god Daltrey and delivered your average punters who might not have found their way past the tunes they’d heard on the radio. And it’s not unimportant to note that the “Tommy” movie brought the band the kind of money they hadn’t yet seen.

That’s part of the cri de coeur you hear on “By Numbers.” It’s by no means the main thread, but it absolutely underpins Townshend’s personal anxieties. He’s annoyed that his bandmates are off doing their own thing. He’s perturbed that he doesn’t have the time or material to make another solo record because he has to offer his best songs to The Who (and conversely, it’s kind of hilarious that he then seems panicked when he presented Daltrey with the songs he’d written for the record and ended up shocked that Rog picked “the more personal ones”.) NOTE: Daltrey is not responsible for the abomination that is “Squeeze Box,” that we have to blame on Ronnie Lane, who was enchanted by it.

The Swansea show from 1976 here isn’t complete, but it is Keith Moon’s last proper show before a U.K. audience. (It was recorded with the intention of being released as a live album, and one of the original tapes went missing at some point in the 1990s, which is why the first two songs are missing.) “My Wife” will sound familiar to anyone who owns the “Maximum RnB” box set, “Squeezebox” is palatable because of Townshend’s giant power chords, “I’m Free” (introduced by Moon, who dedicates it to the occupants of the prison across the street from the venue) sounds more like the version from the “Tommy” soundtrack, and there’s a hilarious comedic bit over “Bellboy.”

But it’s the last live artifact here that’s a truly delightful surprise. It’s on the last disc with the Atmos remixes, and at first I feared it would be poor-quality footage added simply because it existed. But it’s far, far better than that. It is the complete show from the Pontiac Silverdome in December of 1975, cleaned up and remastered. This show set the record for the largest ever indoor rock concert attendance of 76,896, which would be broken by Led Zeppelin in the same place two years later. Because of the size of both the venue and the crowd, a large screen was set up to project closed-circuit video, a thing we’d think absolutely nothing of now, but at the time was a revolutionary development.

There were four cameras, and they do a more than decent job of capturing the action but don’t expect any fancy camerawork or closeups of guitar solos. The sound is in mono — as the liner notes point out, “the sound was captured via a direct line mono feed from the PA — no attempt was made to professionally record the concert for synching purposes.” Part of the “Join Together” / “Road Runner” / “My Generation” medley ended up in “The Kids Are Alright,” but this is the first official release of this footage.

You know what? The sound quality is more than adequate, and where it falls down the electricity coming off of that stage in this performance makes up for a multitude of sins. Roger is in Woodstock buckskin fringe, and even this primitive setup can capture that those trousers were, shall we say, form-fitting. (Wait for “Magic Bus,” which swings so much harder and better than it did later.) Daltrey introduces the “Tommy” portion by noting, “This is how we used to do it,” and then the band proceeds to light the stage on fire. The band seems perplexed and concerned about the size of the crowd, with both Roger and Pete each taking turns to ask the crowd to take a few steps back.

This Silverdome footage is absolutely a text, and even this rudimentary capture that was meant to make sure the 76,896th guy in the back could see something is still full of electricity and life. If you were lucky enough to see the band with Keith Moon in those days, you’ll remember, and if you weren’t, this at least brings some of that fairy dust into your life and your house. Put it on, turn it all the way up, and enjoy it without 76,896 people stepping on your feet.

#6183. American Airlines Adds New App Option When Flights Go Wrong—Try For An Earlier Flight Without Giving Up Your Confirmed Seat

American Airlines is making it easier to try for an earlier flight when your travel falls apart. Its app and website will now offer standby options when you’re dealing with a travel disruption while keeping your new confirmed flight. You don’t need an agent for this – it’s part of their self-service tool. The change to list yourself for free standby on an earlier flight went into effect this week. During a disruption, the flight you can confirm may be hours later than one you could actually get on if a seat opens up. You no longer need to deal with customer service to get on the standby list. . How The New Standby Option Works American calls its tool Dynamic Rebooking. Here’s the sequence described in an internal company memo: Open your disrupted trip on aa.com or in the American Airlines app. Start with Flight Options or Rebook Trip in the disruption banner. If your flight was canceled and you don’t have a replacement, confirm one first. Choose a flight with availability, then return to Flight Options to look for standby. Look for earlier nonstop flights. Up to three standby options may appear when American can’t confirm the earlier rebooking. Pick one. You can join one standby list at a time through this tool. You can remove yourself or switch to another option without contacting an employee. Keep your confirmed flight while you wait. Your itinerary changes only if you clear onto the standby flight. If you’re confirmed for an 8 p.m. flight and the app can’t confirm you on the 5 p.m., you can standby for it while remaining confirmed on that 8 p.m.. If you don’t clear, your confirmed itinerary remains intact. Employees are told, Do not cancel the customer’s confirmed flight because the customer joined standby If you do clear standby you lose the confirmation on your original flight so if you can’t make it you need to remove yourself from standby. What American Is Actually Adding For Passengers American has offered same day changes and standby through its app since 2017. And keeping your original booking while standing by for an earlier flight was already part of published policy. The improvement is putting standby inside the flight disruption rebooking process. Here’s one example of where this matters: an Executive Platinum member facing a seven hour Dallas–Charlotte delay could see confirmed alternatives in the disruption tool, but couldn’t find a way to request earlier standby. Even accepting a later confirmed flight didn’t solve it. An agent eventually added them to standby and they cleared. I covered American’s new disruption banners in January, alongside rebooking, baggage tracking, and digital hotel and meal vouchers. Standby was one of the additions they said was coming. American also described the feature in its October 26 iPhone app release notes. American is trying to offer more tools for managing disruptions. That’s both a cost savings and also empowering to the passenger. A customer who feels in control of their options is going to have a better view of the airline than one who feels at the mercy of broader forces. It’s about raising net promoter scores when things go wrong, which is part of customers being willing to be repeat purchasers, purchasers of premium products, and passengers willing to pay more to fly American. That’s the strategy anyway. In contrast, in 2024, American restricted most passengers to digital standby even when its systems couldn’t handle their requests. They restored agent assistance in July 2025. Improving digital tools and offering agent help is ultimately the right direction to be moving. The Limits Customers Should Know Nothing is being taken away here, but the new tool has limits: Three displayed choices means one standby request. Owning the building made this easy. Minor didn’t need anyone’s money to put its wellness brand inside a Marriott-run hotel. Getting an outside owner to pay for one, and agreeing with another brand on who keeps the client, will be harder.

Minor Hotels has put the first city outpost of its new wellness brand inside a hotel it owns but doesn’t run. It is a test case meant to show other hotel owners that the concept can work under brands other than Minor’s own.

Bangkok Life, which was announced last month, pairs medical diagnostics with traditional medicine, nutrition and fitness. The new offering sits inside The St. Regis Bangkok, which Marriott manages under its St. Regis brand. The hotel is one of several Minor owns but other companies operate.

Thailand-headquartered Minor launched Life Longevity as a standalone wellness brand in October, building out its flagship, Layan Life by Anantara, at Anantara Layan Phuket Resort. Opting for a Bangkok roll-out in a hotel it owns also lets Minor invest its own capital first.

Minor Hotels has opened the first urban location of its Life Longevity wellness brand inside The St. Regis Bangkok — a hotel Minor owns but Marriott operates under its own brand. The move follows Layan Life by Anantara at Anantara Layan Phuket Resort, which Minor spent more than $11 million developing, and replaces the property's former Longevity Hub by Clinique La Prairie. Minor Chief Commercial Officer Ian Di Tullio said the brand was designed from the start to work independently of Anantara, giving Minor the freedom to place it in its own luxury properties or someone else's. Minor still owns or leases almost 70% of its portfolio under what it calls an asset-right strategy, and Di Tullio said that lets the company fund a concept itself, test the economics, and then approach third-party owners. He named three formats for the brand: a resort retreat, an urban hub, and eventually a residence. Di Tullio declined to say whether Marriott approved the concept under its brand standards or shares in revenue, citing confidentiality. Marriott did not immediately respond to Skift's request for comment.

#6179. Will the midterms live up to the hype? 6 key stories we’re watching

Across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans. Inflation is up, consumer confidence is down, gas and diesel prices are through the roof, largely due to the presidentâs war of choice in Iran. The cruelty of his MAGA agenda has roiled the country and left a bad taste even in the mouths of some of his erstwhile supporters.Â

Each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype. As we await the results, itâs worth taking note of several questions:

A tsunami, a trickle âÂ or something in the middle? All are possible, but signs are pointing to significant Democratic gains, likely up to 25 seats in the House, as well as a Senate majority. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed looks increasingly likely to win in Michigan, and James Talarico has Democratic hopes up in Texas. Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska are in play, and itâs worth keeping an eye on South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana as well.

One sign will come at 6 p.m. when polls close in Kentuckyâs 6th Congressional District, where Democrat Zach Dembo is facing off against Republican Ralph Alvarado. Once a Democratic stronghold, the seat went Republican in 2012 and, despite a close call in 2018, has remained in GOP hands since. Although the district has been gerrymandered to favor Republicans, the energy on the ground is with Dembo. If he posts and maintains a healthy lead, look for significant Democratic gains to unfold throughout the night.

What effect did redistricting have on the GOPâs chances?

The midterms will be the first test of the GOPâs redistricting strategy, which saw the party redraw congressional districts in Florida, Texas and other states, partly in response to the gains Trump made with Black and Latino voters in 2024. But polls show those margins have been largely erased as the electorate has turned on the president after nearly two tumultuous years in office, while Democratic legislatures in California and Virginia have imposed their own gerrymanders. According to a Politico poll, the GOP increasingly sees the coalition that returned Trump to office as âcrumbling,â and may have gained little or nothing from all this adventurous map-drawing.

Will progressives be bolstered or chastened?

Losses â or even narrow wins â by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the partyâs establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

The size of the blue wave could well come to be seen as a measure of progressivesâ influence and power within the Democratic Party. Losses â or even narrow wins â by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the partyâs establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins â and victories in unexpected places, such as Michiganâs 7th Congressional District where William Lawrence, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, stands a real chance of unseating incumbent Republican Tom Barrett â would provide rocket fuel to the movement.Â

Progressive groups are already on the offensive, getting a head start on spinning tonightâs election results, particularly in anticipation of a narrow El-Sayed win in Michigan. âExpect to hear narrow victories cited as evidence of weak electability,â a Progressive Change Campaign Committee memo obtained by Politico reads. âBut a candidateâs first winning margin is not their electoral ceiling.â

Will the Haley Stevens drama matter in Michigan?

Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michiganâs Senate primary, has brought the drama in the raceâs closing days. As late as Saturday night, she pledged to colleagues and friends that she was backing El-Sayed, only to turn up hours later at a church service with his Republican opponent Mike Rogers, and endorse the former congressman in a video. The cold-dish move has virtually drowned out El-Sayedâs closing message, with Stevens being formally kicked out of the Michigan Democratic Party.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

The question now is if any of it will matter, especially in light of a New York Times/Siena poll taken before Stevensâ move that showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 11 points. Michigan Republicans seem to think it wonât, telling Politico they wish the congresswoman had crossed the aisle earlier. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report agrees, moving the race in their ratings to âLeans Democratic,â a shift that was already in the works before Stevens detonated her bomb.Â

Still, the results in the stateâs Democratic primary were far narrower than the polls showed, with El-Sayed besting Stevens by only 1%, or 14,893 votes.Â

The New York Times reported yesterday that the worldâs first trillionaire has dropped a staggering $474 million this election cycle, an historic first. The amount has been spread out across a variety of groups, PACs and funds, but it doesnât include the âdark-money donationsâ the Times reports he has also made. Most of the $168 million he contributed to the Senate Leadership Fund has served to shore up Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas, who is locked in a tight race with Talarico.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesdayâs results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations.

Musk has a lot riding on Tuesdayâs results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations. If the blue wave materializes, Musk can expect congressional inquiries of his activities, including his reported interventions in Russiaâs war against Ukraine and his leadership of DOGE during the early months of Trumpâs second administration.Â

Each election brings surprises. Think not one but both of Georgiaâs Senate seats going to Democrats in 2020, or Republicans making big gains in New York two years later.Â

This is the year we could hear the echo of Georgiaâs 2020 election results in another Southern state. Despite boasting large Black populations, Senate seats in South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana have long been out of reach for Democrats. But there is now a path to victory for the partyâs candidates in each of those states.

In South Carolina, the GOP incumbent Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat at Donald Trumpâs command following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, has proven to be a lackluster candidate, alarming even some Republicans with her performance in debates and on the stump. Democrat Annie Andrews has run a more nimble campaign, and between Grahamâs performance and the national state of affairs, she appears to have narrowed the gap.

Mississippiâs incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has also run a lazy campaign, expecting to coast to victory. But the national political environment under Trump, coupled with campaign gaffes, large Black turnout in the aftermath of the Supreme Courtâs decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and clever campaigning by Scott Colom, her Democratic opponent, have helped to put the race in play.Â

Louisiana is also a wild card. The state, which is one-third African American, has also seen a surge in early voting among Black residents, and according to a recent poll, the race between Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis, who is Black, is tied.

Polls are not predictive. The political history of these states continues to favor Republicans, but any of them could deliver one of 2026âs electoral surprises. If that happens, it will signal that the blue wave has become a blue tsunami.

#6177. KLM to Cut Workforce by Nearly 15% in €1 Billion Cost-Saving Drive

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: A KLM Boeing 737 at Amsterdam Schiphol Airport. KLM/Capital Photo

Despite improving profits, the Dutch airline says its future is far from guaranteed, with big changes needed to bring costs under control and restore competitiveness.

KLM is preparing to shrink its workforce by almost 15% as part of a major restructuring aimed at cutting costs and improving its long-term competitiveness.

The Dutch flag carrier announced the measures on Thursday alongside parent company Air France-KLM's third-quarter earnings. Around 5,000 positions have already been or will be affected, with jobs eliminated, outsourced or transferred within the wider airline group.

The overhaul aims to deliver an additional €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in annual earnings improvements, bringing the total targeted improvement to €1.4 billion.

Speaking on Thursday, Marjan Rintel, KLM's CEO, delivered a stark message about the need for change: "KLM's future is not guaranteed… That's why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we're taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures. Every department and every division will be asked to contribute."

KLM will cut, outsource, or transfer about 5,000 positions — close to 15% of its workforce — in a restructuring announced Thursday alongside Air France-KLM's third-quarter results. The plan targets an additional €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in annual earnings improvements, lifting the total goal to €1.4 billion. Roughly 1,250 catering jobs have already moved to Gategroup, 800 ground services roles are expected to go to third-party providers at Schiphol and for KLM Cityhopper, and 2,000 positions, including 1,500 at contact center Cygnific, will transfer to parent Air France-KLM. Another 1,000 reductions are planned through productivity gains, and KLM is seeking union agreements covering at least an 8% productivity improvement by 2028 and restrained wage growth. The fleet is being resized too: A321neos stay, Embraer E195-E2s replace previously planned A320s, and older 737s and E190s will be phased out, giving Cityhopper a bigger role in Europe. The cuts come despite improving numbers — KLM's third-quarter operating profit rose €106 million to €458 million, and group operating profit hit €1.35 billion, sending shares up about 12% — with CEO Marjan Rintel saying the cost base remains too high and that "KLM's future is not guaranteed."

It’s been two years since Singapore Airlines began teasing all-new business- and first-class cabins, and nearly 10 years since the last time the airline unveiled a new generation of flagship products.

But, after much anticipation and a flurry of recent announcements about upgrades and refreshes to everything from the airline’s dining program and inflight meals and serviceware to its KrisWorld entertainment system and amenity kits, today we finally got to see what the new Singapore Airlines business- and first-class seats are like along with a preview of the new economy and premium economy seats coming to its Boeing 777-9s.

We joined a slew of international media for two days of announcements and executive interviews culminating in the big reveal at Marina Bay Sands.

The new products represent a multiyear investment of over 2 billion Singaporean dollars ($1.56 billion) in addition to the S$130 million ($102 million) the airline has spent renovating its SilverKris lounges around the world.

“This is our biggest investment in improving the customer travel experience,” said Siva Govindasamy, divisional vice president of public affairs, “because we’re not just talking about seat development. We’re talking about improvements in the customer service journey from end to end.”

The airline surveyed over 5,000 frequent flyers, incorporating their feedback on what they were looking for from the travel experience, what elements of Singapore Airlines’ current seats and service they liked, and what needed to evolve.

“Our development process has been shaped by extensive research and feedback to help us understand how our customers work, dine, relax, sleep and use technology in their journeys,” explained Lee Lik Hsin, Singapore Airlines’ chief commercial officer. “This launch represents a significant milestone, but not an end point,” he continued. “We are committed to continuously investing in our product and services and elevating the end-to-end customer journey.”

Here’s how, based on what we saw of the new seats and service elements, and all the fancy, industry-leading features in store for passengers.

Related: Singapore KrisFlyer: Ultimate guide to earning, redeeming and elite status

Perhaps the most exciting announcement of the bunch was the unveiling of Singapore Airlines’ new long-haul first-class seats.

Designed by PriestmanGoode and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, these fixtures were initially slated for the airline’s upcoming order of Boeing 777-9s, but given the delays on those aircraft deliveries, Singapore is also installing them on its ultra-long-range subfleet of seven Airbus A350-900ULRs starting in the second half of 2027. This will be the first time the airline’s A350s have sported a first-class cabin.

The A350s will have just four of these seats on board in a 1-2-1 configuration at the very front of the plane. The 777-9s will eventually have six of them on board — two running down either side of the cabin and two in the center. They have 89 1/2 inches of pitch, giving them a fairly large footprint, though not as big as the Suites aboard the airline’s Airbus A380s. Singapore Airlines does not have plans to update the first-class cabins on board its Boeing 777-300s or A380s.

In one of the lighter moments during the pre-reveal press conferences, one journalist asked Singapore’s Hsin how flight crew would address couples who might want to use the space inappropriately. Without missing a beat, Hsin replied, “We will address it,” prompting chuckles around the room. “We want every passenger to be able to enjoy the comfort that we have provided without disturbing the comfort and experience for any other customer.”

Back to the seat, though, it incorporates a cocktail tray for inflight aperitifs and wardrobe areas on the aisles where passengers can stow their clothes (after slipping into the airline’s new pajamas, of course…more on that below!). Those with a keen eye will also notice a subtle batik motif on the soft wall panels hearkening to the airline’s famous uniforms and branding.

The chairs are upholstered in Poltrona Frau leather, are 23 inches wide (30 with the armrests lowered) and recline to 80-inch lie-flat beds that flight attendants will make up with 100% cotton linens, a duvet and a selection of pillows, as well as a breathable new mattress topper from German luxury brand Paradies.

Passengers can adjust the various components of the seat including the arm and legrests, the ottoman and lumbar support as well as the lighting using the inflight entertainment system control and can create a profile so that their settings will carry over to their next flight.

Passengers can dine face to face thanks to large, sturdy tray tables and will find a wireless charging pad, USB-C ports and a universal AC power port to keep their devices charged. The 777-9 seats will have a USB-A port as well.

The storage areas include a slim personal wardrobe, a vanity drawer lined in leather and a small compartment for a cabin bag beneath the ottoman.

The inflight entertainment system is a 32-inch 4K touchscreen loaded with the airline’s KrisWorld content system. It will include an integrated touch panel display for flight information, destination weather, inflight Wi-Fi connectivity status and the availability of lavatories.

Passengers will be given Bang & Olufsen wireless headphones to use, but will also be able to connect to the entertainment system using their own Bluetooth headsets.

Overall, the new first-class seats are a big step forward from the first-class cabins you’ll find aboard the airline’s Boeing 777-300s and sit somewhere between those and the A380 Suites. Their look feels like an evolution of the palette and finishes of the Suites, with welcome tech updates that should keep travelers happy and connected.

Related: The ultimate guide to Singapore Suites

Lest you think first class is the biggest news, the airline also unveiled its all-new business-class seats, designed from the ground up in conjunction with seat manufacturer Recaro and BMW’s DesignWorks.

These seats will appear on the Boeing 777-9 and both the A350-900ULR and the long-haul A350-900 but not the airline’s medium-haul A350s. If you’re losing track, don’t worry, we have tables laying out the details below. We also got a few exclusive shots from a mockup cabin at Singapore Airlines' headquarters the day before the official unveiling, which you can see below. Just note that they don't have all the finishes and other details the final seats on board will have.

“We wanted to bring an automotive-inspired seat and our knowledge from experiential design into the cabin,” explained BMW DesignWorks CEO Julia de Bono. Thus the seats feel like a mix between seats in a luxury sedan and a racecar with mineral gray-toned leather and bright yellow trim, meant to convey balance and stability on the one hand and energy and creativity on the other, according to de Bono.

The seats are laid out in a front-facing 1-2-1 pattern — this was a direct result of customer feedback, with frequent flyers telling airline executives that they wanted to move past an angled orientation, which could feel constraining at times.

Passengers will also receive new padded seat covers with memory foam for cushioning and support.

The tray table placement and stowage — it pops out from under the entertainment screen and can be maneuvered flexibly — also allows the seat to have a larger ottoman, alleviating a common complaint about the airline’s current business-class seats.

Like the new first-class seats, these will allow passengers to create a profile via the inflight entertainment system so their preferred seat and lighting settings are saved from flight to flight.

They have 22-inch 4K touchscreen entertainment systems (20 inches on the 777-9) with Bluetooth pairing capability. Among the storage spaces are a small cubby that slides out from the chair-side seatback and a little cupboard next to the entertainment screen. Passengers will also find wireless charging pads, USB-C ports and universal power plugs.

Related: Which Singapore Airlines business class is better? A380 vs A350

Singapore Airlines worked with FactoryDesign and Collins Aerospace to create updated versions of its economy and premium economy seats specifically for the Boeing 777-9. There are currently no plans for these to be installed aboard the airline’s other jets.

The new premium economy seats have a swanky, contoured look with dark gray leather upholstery and vibrant orange accents. They will see their seat pitch increase from the 38 inches previous versions offer to 40 inches and they will get an extra inch of recline, rounding it up to nine instead of eight. They will be 19 inches wide and have adjustable leg and footrests plus adjustable headsets.

Their entertainment screens will be 16 inches wide with 4K resolution and Bluetooth pairing capability. The seats will also feature universal power plugs, USB-C ports and USB-A ports on some aircraft.

As for economy seating, these look a lot like current versions and are squeezed into a tight 3-4-3 layout, with just 17.6 inches of width per seat. Their screens get an upgrade to 13 inches and 4K resolution with Bluetooth pairing available. They will also have USB-C ports (and A versions on some aircraft) plus universal power plugs.

Related: Worth the upcharge? Flying Singapore Airlines premium economy

So how exactly are all these new seats going to get onto planes and when will passengers start seeing them? Here’s the plan.

Singapore Airlines currently has 58 Airbus A350s. Seventeen of those are configured for medium-haul and regional routes.

Of the remaining 41, 34 are long-range A350-900s with business class, premium economy and economy on board. These will be kitted out with new business class seats with the following adjusted seat numbers in each class. The process is expected to start in the second half of 2027 and to last through 2030.

The other seven A350s are the airline’s A350-900ULRs, which stands for Ultra-Long-Range, and which are deployed on the airline’s longest routes from Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). These ULR jets will get a full overhaul with the new first- and business-class seats. The changes will reduce the plane's overall seating capacity to 132, down from 161.

All the seats on this jet will be new, but here’s how it breaks down.

So the good news is that the majority of Singapore Airlines' long-haul fleet will have new first- and business-class seats on them once this retrofit is complete and the 777-9s are in service. The bad news is that we don't know how long that will take, exactly, and we don't know what routes will see the new seats first.

In the meantime, here are some of the other fun things the airline has cooking up. Quite literally, in some cases.

Related: A review of Singapore Suites first class from Frankfurt to New York

As if new seats weren’t enough, Singapore Airlines is making major updates to its meal service as well.

The airline is already well-known for offering a “Book the Cook” meal preorder service with dozens of dishes available to flyers in Suites, first, business and premium economy, but there are about to be a lot more options.

The airline is touting over 100 new and refreshed dishes on offer, including appetizers, mains and desserts, which will be introduced across all four classes of service under a new category titled “SIA Chefs’ Selection” developed by the airline’s partner guest chefs, who include Monica Galetti, Nandu Jubany, Sanjeev Kapoor, Sid Sahrawat, Yoshihiro Murata and Zhu Jun.

Among the new dishes you might spot are poached Maine lobster with champagne sauce in Suites and first class, a Japanese-inspired prawn cocktail in business class, beef short rib in coconut-based sambal percik with nasi kerabu rice in business class, tandoor-roasted paneer in tangy pasanda gravy in all classes and Irish lamb stew with buttered cabbage and caraway seeds in premium economy.

And take a closer look at what those dishes will be served on in business and first. The airline is introducing an all-new line of chinaware from French luxury brand Christofle, making it the first airline to partner with the longstanding luxury house. The patterns are inspired by Christofle’s Malmaison Impériale collection and incorporate an interpretation of Singapore Airline’s floral batik patterns. There will also be new custom-designed Christofle glassware with tulip-shaped champagne flutes and wine glasses with long stems for more utility.

A new selection of spirits across the board and new wines for business and first class passengers is coming, too. First-class and Suites passengers will be treated to an expanded selection of champagnes including Krug Grande Cuvée, Louis Roederer Cristal, Taittinger Comtes de Champagne, Charles Heidsieck Blanc des Millénaires and Bollinger La Grande Année while those in business class will find Charles Heidsieck Brut Reserve N.V. and Piper-Heidsieck Vintage.

Among the new spirits to be carried on board, there will be a blended whiskey from Japan’s Komoro Distillery created exclusively for Singapore Airlines first class, Bowmore 19 Year Old Pinot Noir Cask Finish single-malt Scotch whisky and Roky Botanical Kasane Edition gin in business class and Whyte & Mackay blended Scotch whisky in premium economy and economy.

Related: Behind the scenes with Singapore Airlines' wine experts as they choose the Champagnes that will be on board soon

For a carrier with such a premium reputation, one thing that surprises some business-class passengers is the fact that Singapore Airlines has not traditionally handed out amenities in business class (first-class passengers do get them, though). That’s all about to change, starting this week.

In fact, Singapore Airlines is introducing all-new amenity kits available on flights over six hours. Here’s what’s in store for passengers.

When Singapore Airlines launched its second-generation A380 First Class Suites in 2017, it also formed a partnership with French luxury house Lalique to create onboard amenities including pajamas, linens and amenity kits with fragrances and skincare products.

Now, with the introduction of its third-generation suites, the airline is turning to French cosmetics brand Sisley to create all-new men’s and women’s kits for first class passengers featuring anti-aging Sisleÿa (for women) and Sisleÿum (for men) products.

Passengers will also find Sisley’s Eau de Campagne fragrance, moisturizing body lotion and floral spray mist along with dental kits in the first-class lavatories.

As for pajamas, customers will receive all-new sleeper suits in dark gray cotton with a subtle imprint of the airline’s batik pattern on the plackets and side seams, along with new, better padded slippers. They will be available in four sizes.

While visiting the airline’s fancy The Private Room lounge and the First Class SilverKris Lounge at Changi Terminals 2 and 3, passengers will also find Hair Rituel by Sisley fortifying densifying shampoo and restructuring conditioner in the shower suites, along with Sisley’s Eau de Campagne bath and shower gel, fragrance and moisturizing body lotion.

Singapore Airlines is also introducing new amenity kits and, for the first time, pajamas for business-class passengers.

The sleeping apparel will be navy-blue poly-cotton with a subtle batik print on the tops’ inner collars and the lining of the trousers’ pockets. They will be available in two sizes.

Business-class passengers will also receive new amenity kits from Swedish brand Byredo that include:

The business-class lavatories will have Blanche body lotion and vitamin E and chamomile facial toner.

Don’t worry, the airline hasn’t forgotten about premium economy passengers, who pay a pretty penny for that extra legroom. They will now receive new zip pouches made from recycled materials and decorated with the airline’s recognizable batik motif.

The pouches will contain Australian personal care brand Ink & Water’s white tea-scented lip balm as well as eye masks, socks and dental kits.

Related: Singapore Airlines premium economy review

Even the folks in the back will receive drawstring pouches with a batik motif containing eye masks, socks and a dental kit.

Long flights are tough on kids, so for travelers 12 years of age and under on flights that are over five hours long, the airline will offer collectible Beary soft toys — essentially airline-branded teddy bears. The airline also offers Pixar’s “Toy Story”-themed amenities on all flights including things like infant bibs, activity pads for kids and drawstring bags.

Related: I make my own amenity kit for long-haul flights: Here’s what’s inside

Singapore Airlines will also be updating the KrisWorld inflight entertainment systems on its A350s and offering new systems on its forthcoming 777-9s.

The new systems will have 4K resolution and Bluetooth pairing capability, but interface improvements that include better search functions, content shortcuts, a mini-player function so passengers can browse content while watching something, better personalization and wellness programming.

First-class passengers will receive Bang & Olufsen noise-cancelling Bluetooth headsets to use in flight while business-class and premium economy flyers will receive active noise-cancellation sets. Economy passengers get wired headphones, but all will be able to pair their own Bluetooth devices with the new systems.

The airline will also progressively roll out new Starlink Wi-Fi service starting in 2027 aboard its Airbus A380s, A350-900 long-haul fleet and its A350-900ULRs. Like the airline’s current Wi-Fi offerings, Starlink service will be free for business and first class passengers and passengers in all cabins who are members of KrisFlyer or PPS Club.

New airline seats represent huge investments of time, money and research, let alone the costs of updating onboard services and amenities. That makes Singapore Airlines’ current slate of announcements all the more exciting.

Flyers have a lot to look forward to on board the airline’s long-haul A350s and forthcoming 777-9s. While the first-class seats are not as large as the Suites on board the airline’s A380s, they are still roomy with high-end finishes and up-to-date tech that passengers should welcome.

As for premium economy and economy, hopefully the airline will consider bringing its latest seats to the A350 as well in an attempt to standardize the experience across the fleet. Still, for 777-9 passengers, these updates will be a win.

What do you think of Singapore Airlines’ new seats? Leave a comment with your impressions below!

#6175. Fuel Hedges Kept Emirates Profitable as Earnings Fell Two-Thirds

Photo Credit: An Emirates Airbus A380-800. Vincenzo Pace / Vincenzo Pace

Fuel hedges turned a likely loss into a profit for Emirates. The war’s full cost will show only once that cover runs out.

Emirates airline’s first-half net profit fell 66% to AED 3.3 billion ($899 million), with the result resting on AED 7.1 billion ($1.93 billion) in fuel hedging-derived gains. At open-market fuel prices, the airline would have lost money after the U.S.-Iran war closed regional airspace and caused jet fuel costs to soar.

The Dubai-based carrier’s revenue fell 13% to AED 56.9 billion ($15.5 billion) in the half, despite what it described as strong cargo performance and enduring travel demand across its markets.

“It has been a demanding six months,” Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum, chairman and CEO, said in a statement on Thursday, citing “unprecedented regional challenges and high fuel prices.”

The first six months of fiscal 2026–27, to end-September, posed significant challenges to its operations due to air

Emirates posted a 66% drop in first-half net profit to AED 3.3 billion ($899 million), and the result rested on AED 7.1 billion ($1.93 billion) in fuel hedging gains. The airline said that without those gains, at open-market fuel prices, it would have lost money after the U.S.-Iran war closed regional airspace and sent jet fuel costs soaring. Revenue fell 13% to AED 56.9 billion ($15.5 billion). Passenger traffic dropped 22% to 21.8 million, capacity fell 17%, and seat factor slipped to 72% from 79.5%, as connecting traffic moved to Istanbul, Singapore, and other hubs. Pre-hedge fuel costs rose 60% year over year; hedging cut the net increase to 13%, with fuel still 34% of operating cost. Cargo was the bright spot: tonnage fell 1% but revenue rose 52% as conflict squeezed airfreight capacity and shipping disruption pushed volume to air. Emirates kept spending through the downturn, taking nine A350s, refitting 12 aircraft under a $7 billion-plus retrofit program, and adding Starlink to 36 more aircraft. Linus Benjamin Bauer of BAA & Partners said the core flying business was likely loss-making on an unhedged basis and that the second half will show whether the operating model has recovered. Emirates has not disclosed its hedging position for the fiscal second half.

#6174. Elon Musk is using Anakin Skywalker to cope with the midterm forecast

Move over, Haley Stevens: There’s a new competitor for the most pathetic reaction to plummeting political fortunes. Elon Musk, the former Trump administration member and the world’s richest man, has seen the midterm election forecast for conservative candidates, and he’s responded by petulantly playing with his toys.

The X owner started “Anakin-posting” on Monday. The purely online phenomenon finds far-right and MAGA nerds recasting Star Wars’ Anakin Skywalker, the man who will become Darth Vader, as a tragic hero and paragon of traditional values. A typical post uses generative AI to reframe the “Star Wars” films’ genocidal space monk as a masculine, hyper-conservative, attentive father. Musk’s post shows Anakin, as played by actor Hayden Christensen, sitting on a throne surrounded by his children, Luke and Leia, and his wife, Padme. The AI illustration has pulled liberally from all three trilogies, placing the adult faces of Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher on the children. Natalie Portman’s Padme appears to be wearing her makeup and crown from “Black Swan.” The Sith first family is surrounded by 1970s-era storm troopers and 2010s imperial guards.

“This is what they stole from us,” Musk captioned the computer-generated photo of his sci-fi fan fiction.

For the unfamiliar, Anakin was a member of an order of space knights. As a young man, he began having prophetic dreams of his wife dying in childbirth. Consumed by ambition and anger, and desperate to avoid the fate he envisioned, he was manipulated by several elderly politicians into betraying his chivalric order, killing many of his fellow knights and slaughtering an entire school full of squires for fear of retribution. Unable to save his wife, and grievously injured from a battle with his former mentor, he became a running dog of a fascist empire that aimed to rule the entire galaxy.

Right-wing young men have warped that story through the established MAGA lens of “returning to tradition,” picturing a world where having the conviction to kill a bunch of toddlers is celebrated.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

The typical example of “Anakin-posting” expresses rage at a stagnant economy or lack of prospects by sharing images of Christensen’s Anakin looking stoic. MAGA influencers like Jack Posobiec have added a dash of intergalactic racism, sharing images of a young Anakin surrounded by literal aliens to hint at a pro-segregationist message. Others have reimagined Anakin’s mentors as chiding liberal scolds, grafting pink hair and a keffiyeh onto Obi-Wan Kenobi. In the pathetic galaxy of Gen Z men, anything from mid-century magazine ads to a Disney-owned sci-fi epic for children can be a stand in for their cultural grievances.

Enough time has passed between the prequels and the present that Anakin can be presented as a brooding badass. The primary criticism of the movies at the time concerned Christensen’s portrayal of Anakin as a whiny child throwing a deadly tantrum. The knotty and boring political intrigue subplots of the films have been forgotten, making it easy to gloss over Anakin being a stooge for politicians playing a game beyond his ken.

Musk, in particular, does have reasons to empathize with the “Star Wars” villain. After believing he had found a way to reshape the government toward his own ends via DOGE, he was booted when the program proved deeply unpopular. Seeing visions of a blue wave washout, he used his financial superpower to try and avoid what appears to be an oncoming loss. Separated from the levers of power and now half a billion dollars poorer, Musk has been forced to play-act a scenario where he won. His image-generating toy gave him the happy ending that politics, relationships and wealth couldn’t.

But all the AI bots can’t undo the facts of Anakin’s story. He was ultimately killed by the evil emperor he served, dying in front of the son he abandoned. His “return to tradition” was a last-minute awakening, when he was forced to confront all the harm he had done and the miserable life he had led. Now there’s something for Musk to aspire to.

Its sustainability pillar rests on three voluntary instruments: the EU Model for Tourism Management, a proposed Council Recommendation for Balanced Tourism, and an EU Toolbox for Balanced Tourism that will include shared approaches to short-term rentals. A Cruise Cooperation Dialogue was also proposed. The Commission said €18 billion in EU support is expected to have benefited tourism from 2021 to 2027 but committed no fresh money, pointing instead to the 2028–2034 budget still under negotiation and to combining private investment with financial instruments. Industry voices quoted by Skift welcomed the volume-to-value direction while pressing for measurable targets, simpler funding access, and practical fixes such as interoperable transport ticketing, which the Commission said it would only "explore" by 2028. The strategy also flags that AI trip-planning tools could reinforce existing tourism hubs if destinations stay passive.

#6163. Keisha Lance Bottoms set to become first Black woman governor in US

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

The contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

At least 27 flights across Europe were disrupted Thursday by bomb threats, the second wave in a week, and no explosives were found in any case. French fighter jets intercepted an Aer Lingus Dublin–Rome flight carrying more than 150 passengers and escorted it to an air base in Normandy, Bulgaria's air force escorted three airliners to the ground, and Madrid authorities searched Air Europa and Iberia aircraft after receiving three emailed threats in under 20 minutes. Earlier threats on Monday and Tuesday hit flights operated by Wizz Air, Ryanair, LOT, and Scandinavian Airlines, plus a cruise ship in Greece. No government has said who is responsible, and Bloomberg reported no pattern in the carriers or routes targeted. Matthew Borie of Osprey Flight Solutions told the AP the threats could be copycats, a single person or group, or "hybrid warfare" by state actors, and pointed to a possible Russian link; Moscow has denied European accusations of sabotage this year. The operational math is the problem: each threat an airline acts on means a diversion or stopped departure, a full search, often a replacement aircraft, crews timing out, and passengers rebooked — and Skift has reported that insurance typically doesn't cover those commercial losses. The hoaxes arrive while European carriers are already absorbing jet fuel prices that have more than doubled year over year, Middle East airspace closures that lengthen Asia routes, and drone incursions at airports.
